title: reach cannot see a screen you closed before capturing, and says nothing about it
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md cycle 137, [G-136]. OUTSIDE this cycle's neighbourhood: it is
about how the loop proves anything at runtime, not about the game.

WHAT THE LOOP CURRENTLY SAYS, and why following it produced a wrong number. The cycle
skill says: "Make `python tools/devtools.py scene-tree > .devtools/tree.json` the last
thing you do before `quit`, every time." Cycle 137 did exactly that. It also pressed
into the Keys screen, read all nine RowKey labels with node-bounds, confirmed the
alignment enum on both screens, backed out to the board, and captured. verify_ledger
reach then reported:

  NOT reached (loadable, and this run did not load them): game/key_binding_screen.gd

which is CORRECT and is indistinguishable from a screen that was never opened -- for a
file the session had just spent ten verbs inside.

THE CAUSE. reach intersects the diff against a SNAPSHOT, not against a history of the
session. A screen opened, driven and closed before the capture leaves no trace. So the
evidence deadline is not "before quit"; it is "while the diff's node is still in the
tree", which is EARLIER, and there is one deadline PER SCREEN rather than one per run.

MEASURED: passing a second capture taken with the Keys screen open moved the row from
reached 3/7 to 4/7 over an identical session.

THE IN-PROJECT HALF is already done -- cycle 137 amended the cycle skill's bullet to say
capture as you go and pass --scene-tree repeatedly. This bead is the HARNESS half, and
it is worth filing upstream (SeveralHerr/godot-selftest-harness) because every project
using the ledger has it.

TWO CANDIDATE FIXES, smallest first:
  (a) One sentence in reach's own output naming the deadline, beside the "NOT reached"
      list -- something like "computed from the snapshot(s) given; a screen closed
      before capture reads as never opened". Costs nothing and would have saved this.
  (b) scene-tree stamps each capture with the topmost visible screen (first-frame
      already computes exactly that), and reach reports "reached in capture 2 of 3"
      rather than merging captures silently.

ACCEPTANCE: filed upstream with the reproduction above, and the local record says which
fix landed. If neither does, the cycle skill's amended bullet IS the mitigation and this
closes as wontfix pointing at it.
notes: SECOND SIGHTING, cycle 151. scene-tree was captured after quit, so reach read 'NOT reached: game/notebook_screen.gd' -- true, and true only because the screen had been closed with the process. Fixed by relaunching, fire-entry-point notebook, a second capture, and 'record --scene-tree A --scene-tree B', which gave 3/4 and 'nothing left unreached'. The repeatable flag works; what is missing is anything at CAPTURE time saying a one-screen snapshot cannot speak for a multi-screen run. Suggested: have scene-tree print the count of res:// scripts it saw, so the denominator is visible while the game is still up to fix it.
close_reason: verify_ledger's NOT-reached line now names its own evidence deadline: computed from the snapshot(s)/captures given, not session history, so a screen closed before every capture reads exactly like one never opened -- and names the fix (capture while the screen is open, or pass --scripts-seen which accumulates for the whole session). Confirmed the cycle skill's own instructions were already amended (references/why.md) before this lane started -- no further doc change needed. Fixture (synthetic scene-tree captures, no git/engine) proves the exact before/after: same ambiguous line before, self-explaining CAVEAT after. Not filed upstream to godot-selftest-harness per the bead's fallback clause (a real code fix landed here, beyond the already-existing skill mitigation the bead's own acceptance treats as sufficient on its own).

title: Make the last guard before an append-only write actually gate
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md cycle 137, [G-137]. From the harness reflection, not from the
game.

WHAT HAPPENED. Cycle 137 ran, in one command:

    python tools/run_json_check.py && python tools/verify_ledger.py record ...

The check printed "6 key(s) in run.json, 11 accepted by the installed verify_ledger, 2
finding(s)" and named them -- 'lint' is absent, 'tests' is absent -- then exited 0,
because it is ADVISORY by design. The && proceeded. The row went into
.devtools/verify-runs.jsonl with lint: null and tests: null on a run where lint exited
0 and the suite was 959/959. The ledger is append-only, so that row stands wrong
permanently.

THE LOOP ALREADY SAYS THE RIGHT THING AND IT WAS NOT ENOUGH. tools/run_json_check.py's
own entry in the cycle skill reads "RUN IT BEFORE `verify_ledger record`, not after --
the row is append-only and a dropped key is indistinguishable from a run that never had
one". I did run it before. The missing half is that running a check whose exit code is
designed not to gate, immediately before the one write in this repo that cannot be
undone, is the same as not running it.

WHY ADVISORY IS RIGHT FOR THE CHECK AND WRONG HERE. A checker that goes red on
something nobody can clear is one people learn to skip -- that argument is written into
run_json_check and into gap_ledger and it is correct. But it is an argument about
standing checks, not about a last guard before an irreversible append.

TWO FIXES, and they are not exclusive:
  (a) `verify_ledger record` refuses (or warns hard on stderr) when the --run object
      omits a key it would otherwise accept. It is the only writer, it knows the full
      key list already -- run_json_check derives its list by regex over that very
      source -- and it is where the irreversibility lives.
  (b) run_json_check grows a --strict, and the loop's line says to use it in this
      position specifically.

(a) is better: it puts the guard where the damage is rather than relying on the caller
remembering which of two commands needs a flag.

ACCEPTANCE: a run.json missing `lint` cannot silently produce a row with lint: null.
Whichever fix lands, the cycle skill's run_json_check line is updated to match, and a
fixture asserts the refusal rather than the exit code.
close_reason: Both non-exclusive fixes: (a) verify_ledger.py record now refuses (exit 1, no row written) when --run omits verdict, or omits lint/tests while verdict isn't 'aborted' -- chose refuse over warn after reading 206 real ledger rows: the three duration/timing keys are legitimately null 28-34% of the time (left optional), but 50 rows already carry verdict:unknown with lint/tests fully populated, proof the omission this closes is accidental. (b) run_json_check.py grew --strict widening required keys from 3 to all 11 accepted. gates.md updated to 'run_json_check.py --strict && verify_ledger.py record ...'. Fixture (new verify_ledger.py fixture subcommand) proves the refusal by content (row-count delta + message text), not just exit code; a mutation (REQUIRED_RUN_KEYS=()) confirmed 3/5 fixture cases go red. Own bug found and fixed: the fixture's 'NOT COVERED' output text collided with check_all.py's contract-marker scan, misclassifying verify_ledger.py -- reworded to 'LIMITS:'. Verified: both fixtures 0 failures, check_all clean.

title: Build the citation relocator, and make refusing the point of it
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md "New in cycle 137", fourth entry, plus four cycles of doing it by
hand. OUTSIDE this cycle's neighbourhood in the sense that matters: it is about the
loop's own bookkeeping, not about the game.

THE PROBLEM. Step 3's --snapshot/--against pair reports drift; nothing relocates it.
Cycle 137's merge drifted 90 citations in kanban.md alone. Cycles 129, 130, 131 and 136
each did the relocation by hand.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS WRONG, and this is the whole design. A per-file offset is wrong
by construction when edits span a file -- cycle 136 measured hud.gd's real offsets
spanning 0 to +127 across one merge. Worse, the loop's own text says relocating by
offset SATISFIES --against without making the citation correct, because the check
compares TEXT and a citation landing on a blank line, a bare "##" or a closing brace
matches anywhere.

THE SHAPE THAT WORKS, prototyped in cycle 137's scratchpad and measured: take the map
from `git diff -U0 <base> HEAD -- <file>`, which already knows every hunk's old->new
correspondence exactly. Outside a hunk, old->new is a running offset that git computed.
INSIDE a hunk there is no correspondence, and that citation must be REFUSED rather than
guessed -- refusal is the feature, because a citation sitting inside an edited region is
exactly the one whose CLAIM may have gone stale. On cycle 137's merge it moved 64 and
refused 0, and the 0 is the meaningful number: no citation's target line was itself
edited, so every one merely shifted.

WHAT IT MUST SAY IT CANNOT DO, in its NOT COVERED line:
  * the bare `:1207` continuation form, where the filename is implied by an earlier
    sentence in the prose. Six of those survived cycle 137's pass (kanban.md:2032 and
    :2029). Anything anchored on a filename is blind to them.
  * whether the relocated line still SUPPORTS the claim beside it. Moving a citation
    correctly and the claim being stale are independent, and only the second matters.
  * bead prose. Cycle 137's prototype ran on kanban.md only; ~500 citations live in bead
    descriptions and close reasons, which is the larger half (--beads takes the snapshot
    from 352 to 880).

HOUSE CONTRACT applies: see .claude/skills/house-static-checker/SKILL.md. This one
WRITES, unlike every other tool in tools/, so it needs a --dry-run default and an
explicit --write, and it is NOT parallel-safe by the same argument mirror_check --fix
is not.

ACCEPTANCE: tools/citation_relocate.py exists, defaults to dry-run, refuses in-hunk
citations and prints them, handles bead prose as well as named markdown files, and its
own fixture proves the refusal fires rather than only that the exit code is 0.
notes:
Cycle 139: plant-tower-defense-nalv is the OTHER HALF of this and they should be
read together, probably worked together, and are deliberately not merged.

This bead relocates a citation that drifted. nalv detects one that never drifts
because it was already wrong when the snapshot was taken -- a class --against is
structurally blind to, since it records the wrong text as its own baseline and
compares clean forever.

Cycle 139 hit both in one pass and the split is exactly this: adding 30 lines to
game/pest.gd drifted eleven kanban.md citations (this bead's job, done by hand
again, fifth cycle running), and reading where they landed showed all eleven had
been wrong by roughly EIGHT HUNDRED lines beforehand (nalv's job, which nothing
in the repo can currently do). Two of the eleven were pointing at blank lines,
which match anything -- so an automatic relocator that this bead builds would
have carried both forward looking perfect. That is the concrete argument for
building nalv's check before, or alongside, this one's relocation: a relocator
without a symbol check makes already-wrong citations harder to find, not easier.
close_reason: tools/citation_relocate.py: dry-run default, --write to actually rewrite; relocates via git diff hunk offsets, REFUSES (reports, never guesses) a citation whose line fell inside an edited hunk. Handles both markdown files and bead prose (.beads/issues.jsonl) -- bead-prose relocations are reported but never auto-written, since no house tool shells out to bd update. --self-test builds a throwaway git repo proving the refusal fires by content. Demonstrated on this repo's real 40-commit history: 541 file citations, 343 relocatable/25 refused/173 unchanged; with --beads, 1576 total. Parent wired check_all.py's NOT_A_CHECKER classification (lane flagged it, parent fixed it since it was outside lane ownership). Verified on the merged 4-lane integration tree: 1112/1112 tests, real import+lint compile, check_all clean.

title: Citations landing on blank or generic lines are unverifiable, and offset-restoring them launders the error
description:
A CITATION THAT LANDS ON A BLANK LINE, A CLOSING BRACE, OR A GENERIC STATEMENT IS INVISIBLE TO THE DRIFT CHECK, AND RESTORING IT BY OFFSET PRESERVES THE ERROR.

MEASURED TWICE, in consecutive cycles, both times by hand after the tool said clean.

Cycle 129: -4jv7's citation was restored by a +52 offset. The drift check called it clean, because the text at the new line matched the text the snapshot recorded. That text was "##". The bead's sentence reads "Hud.flight_tip (game/hud.gd:...)" and flight_tip is 11 lines further down -- so the citation had ALWAYS pointed into the doc comment above the function, and the mechanical restore faithfully preserved that.

Cycle 130: eleven citations drifted at once when a 27-line comment went into notebook_screen.gd. Relocating them by matching the snapshot's recorded text worked for four and reported AMBIGUOUS for the rest -- 114 candidate lines for one of them -- because the recorded text was blank. Applying the uniform +27 satisfied the drift check for all of them, and then reading the landings found:

    "page_for_kind at :259"    -> a blank line          (really :289)
    "shelf_page at :715"       -> _spec.autowrap_mode   (really :990)
    "page_for_plant at :780"   -> title.name = ...      (really :1123)
    "one caption at :323-324"  -> a shelf-greying comment (really :434)
    "go_to(0) at :447"         -> a sprite path          (really :630, and it is go_to(open_at))
    "has_milestone at :445, :600" -> a plant field and a geometry comment (really :764, :982)

Every one of those was wrong BEFORE this cycle's edit and would have stayed wrong. The tool says this about itself, in its own NOT COVERED line: "it cannot tell you whether the landed line SUPPORTS the claim around it". The new part is that the SNAPSHOT/RESTORE workflow actively launders the error, because a blank line matches a blank line.

AND ONE CLAIM HAD DRIFTED IN SUBSTANCE, not only in position: "Its other two call sites read earned state to draw the shelf" -- there are now FOUR has_milestone call sites in notebook_screen.gd, two of which postdate the entry and belong to the hints page. The conclusion survived the recount (none of the four gates a sight), which is why it was corrected rather than re-opened, but nothing would have surfaced the recount.

WHAT TO BUILD, and check the premise first because part of it may already exist. A pass -- probably a flag on citation_check.py, --weak or --suspect -- that reports every RESOLVED citation whose landed text is uninformative, and therefore whose correctness cannot be inferred from any text comparison. Candidate rules, to be tuned against the real corpus rather than guessed:

  - the landed text is empty after stripping
  - it is only a closing brace, "]", ")", "##", or a bare comment marker
  - it is a line that occurs more than N times in the file (the 114-candidate case)

Advisory, never gating: these are citations to READ, not citations that are wrong. The output is a worklist for a human pass, and the value is the size of the list -- if 200 of 931 citations are unverifiable by any tool, that is the number that matters and nobody currently knows it.

ACCEPTANCE: the count, printed. Then a sampled read of the list to say what fraction of weak citations are actually wrong -- cycle 130's sample was 6 of 6, which is alarming enough to be worth a real measurement rather than an extrapolation from one accident.

CONSIDER AND REJECT IF WRONG: making the snapshot record MORE context (say, three lines either side) so a blank line is distinguishable. That fixes the laundering but not the original miscitation, and it grows the snapshot file threefold. The weakness is in the citation, not in the snapshot.
close_reason:
SHIPPED in be5083d. `python tools/citation_check.py --beads --weak`.

THE COUNT, which the acceptance asked for first and which is the whole result:

    citation_check --weak: 58 of 937 resolved citation(s) land somewhere that carries
    no information -- 6%.

        26  land on nothing
        16  land on only '##'
        10  land on a line that appears more than 5 times in its file
         3  land on only '#'
         3  land on a bare 'return' / 'continue' / '}'

THE SAMPLED READ, which the acceptance asked for second, and it is worse than the bead guessed. Four taken from kanban.md, ALL FOUR WRONG, each confirmed by locating the symbol the sentence names rather than by judgement:

    uproot_armed()             cited game/game.gd:1341      actually game/game.gd:1832
    "Really uproot? (+N)"      cited game/hud.gd:1206       actually game/hud.gd:1792
    the _has_fired gate        cited game/dandelion.gd:378  actually game/dandelion.gd:420
    a show_message duration    cited game/game.gd:264       blank; the two calls it
                                                            describes are :2228 and :2232

With the ten found by hand in cycles 129-131, that is FOURTEEN OF FOURTEEN weak citations sampled and wrong. The bead said "cycle 130's sample was 6 of 6, which is alarming enough to be worth a real measurement rather than an extrapolation from one accident". The measurement agrees with the extrapolation, which was not the likely outcome.

So the 6% should be read as a FLOOR on the wrong-citation count, not as a list of suspects to triage.

THE RULES, and the bead asked for them to be tuned against the corpus rather than guessed:
  - landed text empty after stripping
  - landed text is only a comment marker, closing brace, or a bare keyword (WEAK_LINES)
  - a SINGLE-LINE citation landing on a line that appears more than WEAK_REPEAT_MAX (5)
    times in its file

The repeat rule applies to single-line citations only. A multi-line span is distinctive even when each of its lines is not, which is what ranges are for; calling them weak would flood the list with the citations most worth writing. The threshold of 5 is a guess and is documented as one -- the case that motivated it had 114 identical candidates and no threshold in this range would miss it.

ADVISORY, exit 0 always, as the acceptance required. These are citations to READ.

THREE OF THE FOUR CORRECTED. The fourth belongs to an entry citing EIGHT line numbers for six `show_message` durations; it is flagged in place for re-derivation rather than patched one number at a time. A list where the one number sampled was wrong by 1900 lines wants recounting, and the CLAIM it supports -- six hand-picked durations with nothing relating them -- is unaffected by its coordinates being stale.

ITS OWN NOT COVERED LINE is the part I would want read: a citation landing on a DISTINCTIVE line that is nonetheless the wrong one is invisible to this pass, and TWO of the ten found by hand were exactly that -- a count written out in prose ("its other two call sites" when there were four) and a function that no longer exists at all (`next_wave_note`). No rule over landed text can see either. This narrows the reading list; it does not replace the reading.

SELF-CHECK CASE 7 TESTS BOTH DIRECTIONS, and the second is the one that matters: a rule calling everything weak is as useless as one calling nothing weak, and the second failure prints "0 of 937" and reads exactly like a corpus with no problem in it. Blank and "##" must be weak; a distinctive line must not; a span of nothing but markers must be. Mutating the classifier to call nothing weak fails it.

"check open bead tools/g1j9 (shared source blanker) before adding a sixth copy of anything" -- checked, and nothing was copied. This adds one function reading text the existing loop already computed; the resolver, the file walk and the citation regexes are all reused.

VERIFIED: tier (f) tooling-only, no res:// change. --self-check plus one mutant, check_all 19 of 19 clean, and the corrected citations read back individually against the symbols their sentences name. Ledger row recorded before the commit.

title: [bug] Two packet purchases inside five seconds refuse messages, and the reveal is what holds the row
description:
MEASURED IN CYCLE 128 while answering -gd27. The message row DOES drop lines, and the producer is the packet flourish -- but not in the way -gd27 predicted, and not for the reason its own code comment gives.

THE NUMBERS. Counters read off the live Hud (all four start at 0):

  after 4 successful packet purchases fired back-to-back during a live wave:
      messages_refused = 12, evicted = 0, preempted = 0, retired = 0

Twelve refusals, exactly 3 per purchase, and PACKET_OPEN_STEPS is 3 (game/game.gd:1931).

FOUR CONTROLS, because 12 refusals next to a purchase is a correlation:

  1. ONE purchase with a QUIET row (_message_text empty): refused 12 -> 12. Zero.
  2. ONE purchase with an ambient line deliberately held on the row: refused 12 -> 12,
     preempted 0 -> 4. The flourish PREEMPTS an ambient line, which is correct and is what
     game/game.gd:1979-1983's comment describes.
  3. TWELVE pests spawned and killed, no purchase: refused 12 -> 12. Wave message volume
     alone refuses nothing.
  4. THE MECHANISM, reproduced without any purchase at all: post one MESSAGE_IMPORTANT line
     with a 5.0s duration, then five more MESSAGE_IMPORTANT posts behind it. All five
     returned false; refused went 12 -> 14. Three queued (MESSAGE_QUEUE_MAX = 3,
     game/hud.gd:804) and two were refused.

SO THE CAUSE IS THE REVEAL, NOT THE FLICKER. _reveal_plant_unlock posts at MESSAGE_IMPORTANT for 5.0 seconds (game/game.gd:1991-1995). A SECOND purchase inside that 5-second window is equal priority, so it cannot preempt; its three flicker steps fill the queue and what comes after is refused. The flourish's comment is correct about a flourish in isolation and says nothing about two flourishes overlapping, which is the case that drops lines.

THE PLAYER-FACING CONSEQUENCE, and it is why this is a bug and not a note: a player who buys two packets in quick succession pays for the second and the line naming what they got can be refused. The reveal is the only place the packet's result is announced.

NOT YET ESTABLISHED, and it decides how bad this is: whether the refused post in a real double-purchase is the second flourish's STEPS only (cosmetic -- the flicker is skipped, the reveal still lands) or the second REVEAL itself (serious -- the player is not told what they bought). The arithmetic says 3 refusals per purchase and a flourish posts 3 steps + 1 reveal = 4, so at least one of the four got through each time. Establishing which needs either a devtools verb that reports WHICH message was refused, or an instrumented run -- see -a9pi, which asks whether the counters should get a verb and is a natural home for "and which line was dropped".

ACCEPTANCE: decide whether a second purchase inside the reveal window should (a) collapse -- skip the flicker and show the new reveal immediately, (b) queue properly so both reveals are seen in turn, or (c) stay as it is with the reason written beside _reveal_plant_unlock. Any of the three is defensible; what is not is the current state, where the code comment describes behaviour that only holds for the case that does not drop anything.

REPRODUCE: launch, cmd add_seeds 4000, plant the free starter, cmd start_wave, then four cmd buy_packet calls with no delay, then read messages_refused off the Hud.
notes:
SETTLED IN CYCLE 129, and it is the serious reading.

This bead's "NOT YET ESTABLISHED, and it decides how bad this is" paragraph asked whether the refused post in a real double-purchase is the flicker STEPS (cosmetic) or the REVEAL (the player is not told what they bought). It is the reveal.

Measured with cmd messages, built in cycle 129 for exactly this (-a9pi), after two packet purchases back to back:

    refused 1
    refused_log ["The packet held a Chomp Flower!"]
    row "The packet held a Barrier Bramble!" | 3 pending

The player is told what the SECOND packet held and never told what the first one did. The count alone could never have said this -- messages_refused is 1 whichever post was dropped, and _queue_message had the text in hand and discarded it. Hud.messages_refused_log now keeps it (capped at REFUSED_LOG_MAX = 8, newest kept).

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT THE ACCEPTANCE. The three options stand, but (c) "stay as it is with the reason written beside _reveal_plant_unlock" is now much harder to defend: it means accepting that a player who buys two packets quickly is never told what one of them contained, which is the only announcement of a purchase they paid seeds for. (a) collapse and (b) queue properly both remain reasonable and the choice between them is a design call about whether two reveals in a row are worth reading.

NOTE THE ASYMMETRY, because it points at the fix: the SECOND purchase's reveal won the row and the FIRST one was refused. So the newer line displaces the older even though the older was posted first and its packet was opened first. If (a) collapse is chosen, that ordering is already what happens and only the refusal needs to become deliberate. If (b), the queue needs to prefer the older reveal, which is the opposite of what it does now.

REPRODUCE: launch, cmd add_seeds 4000, plant the free starter, then two cmd buy_packet calls back to back, then cmd messages. No wave needed -- cycle 128 thought a live wave was part of the recipe and it is not.
close_reason:
FIXED in 66c5b37, option (b) "queue properly so both reveals are seen in turn".

WHY (b) RATHER THAN (a) OR (c). The player bought two packets and is owed two answers; the reveal is the only announcement a purchase gets. (a) collapse would still have dropped one of them, which is the defect with a shorter animation. (c) was ruled out by the note added in cycle 129 -- it means accepting that a player who buys quickly is never told what one packet contained.

Serialised at the FLOURISH rather than by raising the reveal's priority. The priority ladder is about how much a line matters to the player, and both reveals matter exactly the same amount; the contention is between two runs of one animation, which is a sequencing problem. Solving it with priorities would have made a second reveal preempt a first that had been on screen for a tenth of a second.

THE FIRST FIX WAS WRONG AND EVERY HEADLESS GATE PASSED IT. This is the part worth recording.

Serialising the queue is correct as far as it goes: two _open_packet calls in the same frame do queue behind one another, and the test asserting that went green next to 919 others, lint 0 errors 0 warnings, import clean, and all nineteen parallel-safe checkers. Then I re-ran this bead's own reproduce recipe against the live game:

    refused 1
    refused_log ["The packet held a Chomp Flower!"]

Unchanged from cycle 129. A flourish lasts PACKET_OPEN_STEPS * PACKET_OPEN_STEP_SECONDS, about a quarter of a second, so two purchases half a second apart NEVER OVERLAP and the serialisation guard never engages. The second flourish starts fresh and posts its three steps behind the first purchase's five-second reveal, filling the queue and refusing it -- the original defect, one call deeper, and invisible to a test that fires both purchases in the same frame.

The real fix is that the wait goes before EVERY flourish, not only between queued ones, and that it tests priority as well as time: a flourish posts at MESSAGE_IMPORTANT and preempts anything ambient, so waiting for an ambient line would delay every packet behind a husk notice and be a visible regression rather than a fix.

It asks the row -- hud.message_seconds_left() and hud.message_priority() -- rather than computing 5.0 - MESSAGE_MIN_READABLE. That would have been a fourth place needing an edit when the reveal's duration changes, and the row already knows. Those accessors were added last cycle for cmd messages; this is their second caller and the reason they are not debug-only readers.

VERIFIED LIVE, BOTH DIRECTIONS, which is the only reason this close claims anything:

  this bead's recipe, after the fix:  refused 0, evicted 0, preempted 0, 0 pending
  both reveals in turn, polling the row across two purchases:
      "The packet held a Salve Aloe!"   (11 polls)
      "...Sticky Sundew?"               (the second packet's flicker, still playing)
      "The packet held a Sticky Sundew!"
      refused 0 throughout

So the flicker was not sacrificed to fix the reveal, which was the risk in (a).

THREE TESTS, and the third exists because of the failure above:
  test_two_packets_opened_at_once_both_get_their_reveal -- the same-frame case.
    Red-then-green: removing the guard fails it with "Expected 1 but got 0".
  test_a_queued_packet_keeps_its_own_tier -- _opening_tier is a field set immediately
    before buy_packet(), which was safe while only one flourish could exist. Once a
    purchase can WAIT, a common packet queued behind a rare one would flash candidates
    from the rare pool. The tier travels with the id in the queue.
  test_a_flourish_waits_for_a_reveal_that_is_still_being_read -- the case that actually
    broke. Asserted through the row's state rather than by sleeping 3.8 seconds, and it
    also asserts the ambient case does NOT wait.

That third test's own ambient assertion failed the first time it ran, and the test was wrong rather than the code: a lower-priority post QUEUES rather than taking the row, so the reveal was still current when I asked. Fixed by draining it first, with the reason written in the test.

NOT DONE: nothing. The bead's "not yet established" paragraph was settled in cycle 129 and is recorded in its notes.

VERIFIED: name_check 0 errors, import clean, lint 0/0, suite 920/920 with 18044 assertions, check_all 19 of 19 clean, findings 0 across 4 of 5. Both launches used --snapshot-userstate and quit restored the save each time. Ledger row recorded before the commit, with the failed live check kept as "result": "fail" plus "fixed_in_run": true rather than rewritten green -- the run's own evidence is that a headless-green fix did not work.

title: A test's failure message uses %r, which GDScript cannot format -- 12 engine errors per suite run
description:
A TEST WHOSE FAILURE MESSAGE CANNOT BE PRODUCED, and it announces itself on every single suite run.

test/unit/test_selftest.gd:10562 builds an assertion message with "%r":

    "%s: the card measured %.1fpx for %r and the Label drew %.1fpx -- the "
        % [node_name, PauseScreen._measure(row.text), row.text, _T.text_width(row)]

%r is a PYTHON specifier. GDScript's String.format supports %s and %d (the only two the rest of this 5056-assertion suite uses -- 584 and 302 occurrences respectively; this is the ONE %r in the file). Godot answers with

    ERROR: String formatting error: unsupported format character.
       at: validated_evaluate (core/variant/variant_op.h:770)
       GDScript backtrace (most recent call first):
           [0] test_the_cards_own_measurement_agrees_with_the_labels_it_builds (res://test/unit/test_selftest.gd:10561)

TWO SEPARATE PROBLEMS, and the second is the one that matters.

1. If that assertion ever FAILS, its message is garbage -- the string the reader needs in order to act on the failure is the string that cannot be built. The assertion is inside a loop over rows, so it is guarding a real comparison between PauseScreen._measure and the real font.

2. The message is built EAGERLY -- GDScript evaluates the argument before calling assert_float_eq -- so this fires on every iteration whether the assertion passes or fails. A full suite run emits 12 of these; a filtered run of that one test emits 22. They are pure noise in .devtools/tests.log, and the harness's own rule is that stderr is the only signal a test suite gives you about a method that aborted (CLAUDE.md: "Always read stderr -- a runtime error inside a test aborts only that method and returns "" for a -> String test, which is identical to a pass"). Twelve guaranteed errors per run is exactly the thing that trains a reader to skim past the section where a real one would appear.

HOW FOUND: adding an unrelated test in cycle 127, running the full suite, and reading the stderr section under a green "ALL TESTS PASSED / 913 of 913". Confirmed pre-existing by stashing the cycle's changes and re-running.

ACCEPTANCE: %r becomes %s, and the assertion is made to fail once on purpose so the message is read at least once in its life -- that is the whole reason the finding exists.

WORTH CHECKING WHILE THERE, and this is the larger half: whether any other assertion message in the suite is built eagerly with an expensive or failing call. The grep above says no other BAD specifier exists, but it says nothing about cost -- this message calls PauseScreen._measure and _T.text_width a second time each, on every iteration, purely to build a string that is thrown away. A cheap rule would be a checker for a message argument containing a call, but confirm the shape is common before building one: one instance is a fix, not a pattern.
close_reason:
FIXED. %r -> %s at test/unit/test_selftest.gd:10568, with the reason written beside it.

ACCEPTANCE, clause by clause.

"%r becomes %s" -- done, as \"%s\" so the measured string is still quoted in the output, which is what %r was reaching for.

"and the assertion is made to fail once on purpose so the message is read at least once in its life -- that is the whole reason the finding exists" -- done. Forced by adding 99.0 to the measured side:

    KeyRow0: the card measured 46.0px for "Esc  ·  P" and the Label drew 46.0px -- the
    static measurement and the real font have come apart, which is what a custom theme
    added to this project would do: Expected 46.000000 but got 145.000000 (tolerance: 1.0)

It reads well and names the row, both numbers and the string, which is everything needed to act on it. Mutation reverted.

THE COUNT: 12 'String formatting error: unsupported format character' lines per full suite run before, 0 after. Verified on a filtered run (0) and a full one.

"WORTH CHECKING WHILE THERE: whether any other assertion message in the suite is built eagerly with an expensive or failing call" -- the grep for bad specifiers is clean (584 %s, 302 %d, 0 %r), which was already in the bead. On the cost question the bead raised: this message does call PauseScreen._measure and _T.text_width a second time each per iteration, purely to build a string usually thrown away. NOT changed, and not filed either: it is one instance, the bead itself says 'confirm the shape is common before building one', and a survey of eager assertion messages across 5085 call sites is a bigger job than this bug. If a second instance turns up, that is the bead.

VERIFIED: 920/920, 18044 assertions, 0 formatting errors, check_all 19 of 19 clean. Tier (c) headless-only -- one format specifier in a test file.

title: The notebook never names drought, which the player meets from wave 4
description:
THE NOTEBOOK NEVER NAMES DROUGHT, and the player meets it from wave 4.

MEASURED, not inferred. Grepping game/notebook_screen.gd case-insensitively: "drought" 0 hits, "weather" 1 hit, "rain" 1 hit -- and both of those hits are the SAME subordinate clause, inside the Salve Aloe page at game/notebook_screen.gd:470: "the first thing that undoes damage. title: The notebook tells the player there are five legend rows, and there are six
description:
PLAYER-FACING PROSE THAT COUNTS WRONG. The notebook's legend page (game/notebook_screen.gd:503) tells the player: "A shape means the same thing wherever it appears -- a full ring is always a reach, a closing arc is always a clock running down -- so the five here are worth more than five facts."

There are SIX. game/cue_legend.gd:172 holds ROWS, and it has six entries: SUBJECT (:174), REACH (:179), CLOCK (:184), REMARK (:189), GAIN (:194) and ARMED. The sixth was added by commit eba2d26, "Teach the ARMED cue, the one guarding the only irreversible act" -- the cue that guards uproot, so the one row a player most needs to trust the legend about is the row the sentence does not count.

HOW THIS WAS VERIFIED, since two of my last four absence claims about this codebase were wrong: counted the rows by parsing the ROWS literal (six), read the sentence at :503, and confirmed the sixth row's provenance with git log on game/cue_legend.gd. Not inferred from the page's appearance.

WHY IT IS NOT JUST A TYPO. game/cue_legend.gd:242 already says "the page currently fits exactly ROWS.size(), and a seventh..." -- the CODE derives its count and says so, while the PROSE next door wrote the number out by hand. That is the same shape as the notebook header, which game/notebook_screen.gd:611 records fixing once already: "Counted from PAGES, not written out. The hard-coded 'Six pages' outlived..."

ACCEPTANCE: the sentence stops carrying a hand-written number. Either derive it (CueLegend.ROWS.size(), the way the header derives PAGES.size()) or rewrite the clause so no count appears. A test asserting the notebook's legend prose against ROWS.size() is worth more than the fix, because this is the second hand-written count on this screen to go stale and the first one already has a comment about it.

CONSIDER: whether any OTHER player-facing string writes out a count that the code derives. The header (:611) and this one are two; a third would make it a pattern worth a checker rather than a fix.

title: Every suppression marker in this repo is a bare substring, so a document discussing one trips it
description:
THE INCIDENT, in full, because it is the cheapest possible demonstration. Cycle 126 shipped citation_check.py --beads with a per-issue waiver: the marker 'citation-check: ok' anywhere in a bead's prose drops that bead. The FIRST bead ever closed by the feature (plant-tower-defense-9vq6) waived itself, because its close reason contains the sentence explaining the waiver. Bead count went 468 -> 467, three citations left the denominator, exit code stayed 0, nothing said a word. Found only because the checker was re-run over the close it had just been handed.

Fixed there by requiring the marker to open its own line: tools/citation_check.py:71, BEAD_WAIVER_LINE. --self-check case 5 is a bead that mentions the marker mid-sentence and must not be waived; mutating the rule back to containment fails it.

THE CLAIM TO CONFIRM BEFORE CLAIMING THIS. The fix was applied to one checker. The pattern is that a suppression marker is USUALLY implemented as a bare substring test, and the documents most likely to quote a marker are exactly the ones about suppression -- kanban.md's cycle entries, log-devtools.md's gap entries, and bead prose discussing checkers. All three are scanned by something. Go and read each marker's implementation before assuming it:

  bead_prose_check.py -- the correction-note waiver citation_check.py's was modelled on
  suite_reach_check.py, message_corpus_check.py, save_persist_check.py, settle_read_check.py,
  sfx_call_check.py, world_control_check.py, readout_shape_check.py, group_leak_check.py,
  meta_key_check.py, svg_style_check.py -- whichever of these carry a waiver at all
  lint_project.gd's baseline files, and the harness's ui_findings_baseline.json

Some of these may have no waiver, and some may already anchor. The finding is the count: how many are bare substrings, and which of them scan a file that discusses them. A checker that scans only .gd source is much less exposed than one that scans prose.

ACCEPTANCE. For each waiver found, either (a) anchor it the way BEAD_WAIVER_LINE is anchored and add the mid-sentence-mention case to that checker's fixture, or (b) record in this bead why it is not exposed -- naming the file set it scans and why prose about it cannot enter that set. (b) is a real answer and probably the answer for most of them; what is not acceptable is leaving it unread.

NOT WORTH DOING: a shared anchoring helper before the count is known. If two of twelve are exposed, two local fixes beat a thirteenth shared module -- and tools/g1j9 already tracks the shared-blanker question.
close_reason:
SHIPPED in lane/vvww, merged to main. Ten waivers audited, six anchored, three recorded not-exposed, one already correct.
