title: Put the touch layer in front of a real finger, which no commit can do
description:
SOURCE: split out of -qdsi in cycle 122, which shipped the touch layer and could not do this
clause. Filed rather than left inside that bead, because a criterion no commit can produce
makes a finished item look unstarted in `bd ready` -- exactly what -6cqi did for twelve
cycles.

WHAT ALREADY LANDED (commit in cycle 122), so this bead is a check and not a build:
  * InputEventScreenTouch / InputEventScreenDrag handled explicitly in Game._unhandled_input.
  * Placement commits on RELEASE, at the release position. A press shows the cue and plants
    nothing; a drag moves the preview; sliding off the board aborts.
  * One finger owns the placement; a second is ignored until the first lifts.
  * The emulated mouse event is discriminated by `device == -1` AND
    DisplayServer.is_touchscreen_available().
  * Verified with the bridge: press at (2,3) -> 0 plants, drag to (5,3) -> 0 plants with the
    preview following, release -> one plant at (5,3).

WHAT IS NOT DONE, and is the whole of this bead: none of that has been in front of a real
finger. -qdsi's first acceptance clause was "Reproduced on an actual touch device or in
Chrome device emulation against the itch.io build, with the specific awkwardness named in a
comment on this issue."

WHY IT STILL MATTERS NOW THE CODE EXISTS. The bridge sends synthetic events through
Input.parse_input_event. A real device differs in at least three ways that could each break
this and none of which the bridge reproduces:
  * TIMING. A real tap is press and release within ~80ms with sub-pixel jitter between them.
    Whether the jitter arrives as a DRAG (moving the preview) or as nothing at all decides
    whether a plain tap still lands where the finger is.
  * THE BROWSER. The itch.io build is HTML5 -- deploy is automatic on push to main -- and
    the browser's own touch-to-mouse synthesis sits UNDER Godot's. The device == -1 guard
    was measured against Godot's emulation on desktop; it has not been checked against a
    browser that may deliver something different.
  * PAGE-LEVEL PAN AND SCROLL, which -qdsi's original scope note raised as candidate (c) for
    the reporter's complaint and which nothing has yet ruled in or out.

THE ORIGINAL QUESTION IS STILL UNANSWERED, and is the reason to do this with a person rather
than a tool: the reporter described "click and drag" as the awkward part, and -qdsi named
three readings -- (a) dragging is what a player instinctively tries and nothing happened,
(b) the emulated drag mis-fired the tap, (c) the web build's page scroll fighting the canvas.
Cycle 122 built the thing that answers (a) and (b). Whether it answers the actual complaint
is not knowable from here.

ACCEPTANCE: the touch layer exercised on a real device or in Chrome device emulation against
the deployed build; the specific awkwardness named in a comment either as FIXED, as STILL
PRESENT with what it actually is, or as (c) and therefore a different bead; and if a plain
tap does not land correctly because of jitter-as-drag, that is a defect in what shipped and
gets its own item.

title: Seven shop blurbs promise things nothing checks, and the player spends seeds on them
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md "New in cycle 119", second entry. PLAYER-FACING, and it is the sentences
that cost the player seeds.

Every plant's `blurb` in PlantCatalog is a factual promise the player reads while deciding
how to spend. Two of the nine are checked against the code that makes them true:
  * the Nettle's "Dead weight until wave 8" is pinned against
    WaveDirector.MUTATION_START_WAVE by test_the_nettle_blurb_warns_it_is_dead_weight
    _before_mutations -- and PlantCatalog's own comment explains why it had to be, since a
    blurb is a const String and cannot interpolate.
  * the Chomp's "Eats small pests instantly. Big ones take a while -- and it is busy the
    whole time." is pinned against Pest.SPECIES as of cycle 119 (-l86t).

THE OTHER SEVEN ARE UNCHECKED, and each makes at least one claim that lives as a number or a
rule elsewhere. Leads, not findings -- confirm each before acting:
  * Sundew: "Everything in its dew crawls at half speed -- wings included, which no Chomp
    can say." TWO claims: the slow factor is a half (StickySundew.SLOW_FACTOR), and a winged
    pest IS slowed while a Chomp refuses one (ChompFlower's two is_winged guards).
  * Aloe: "Too slow to save one being eaten." A relationship between Aloe.HEAL_PER_SECOND
    and Pest.EAT_DPS. aloe.gd's header states it as 3.0 against a 2.86s kill; nothing
    asserts it.
  * Mint: "The plants beside it shoot a third again as fast." A third is Mint.scale_for's
    business, and "beside" is Mint.neighbours_of's -- which deliberately refuses diagonals.
  * Bramble: "Winged pests go straight over." Bramble.stops(). Probably the best-covered of
    the seven already, via the pest tests.
  * Dandelion: "Hits everything standing together -- and grows its fluff back between
    volleys." The regrow-within-a-prep-gap claim is asserted somewhere for the Dandelion;
    check whether the BLURB is what is asserted or only the constant.
  * Corn: "Upgrades to a bunch of corn." Cheap; the ladder's top rung name.
  * Sunflower: "Grows seeds on a clock." Sunflower.INTERVAL.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A BEAD RATHER THAN SEVEN. The pattern is one test shape repeated -- take
the sentence's factual clause, find the constant or rule it names, assert the relationship
rather than the number. Doing them together means writing that shape once and getting the
comparison right once; doing them one at a time across seven cycles means seven slightly
different shapes.

AND THE ONE THING TO DECIDE, once, before writing any of them: what happens when a blurb is
VAGUE rather than wrong. "Grows seeds on a clock" names no number and cannot go stale;
"crawls at half speed" names one and can. Only the second kind is worth a test, and the
sweep should say which of the nine are which rather than inventing an assertion for a
sentence that does not make a checkable claim.

ACCEPTANCE: every blurb read and sorted into CHECKABLE (names a number or a rule) vs VAGUE;
a test for each checkable one that is not already covered, asserting the RELATIONSHIP and
not a copied number; and the count stated in the close, the way -u9zb stated 33.
close_reason:
SWEPT. Nine blurbs read against the code that makes each true; one had stopped being true.

THE COUNT, as the acceptance asked. NINE blurbs, not seven — the bead said "seven unchecked"
and named the Nettle and the Chomp as already pinned, which is right, but the sweep has to
walk all nine or the denominator means nothing.

SORTED, as the acceptance asked, into CHECKABLE (names a number or a rule) vs VAGUE:

  CHECKABLE, and now checked:
    * CORN      "Upgrades to a bunch of corn."   -> the top rung's own name.
    * SUNFLOWER "Fights nothing."                -> PlantCatalog.engages is false.
    * SUNDEW    "Hurts nothing."                 -> engages is false.
                "at half speed"                  -> StickySundew.SLOW_FACTOR. **THE FINDING.**
                "wings included, which no Chomp can say" -> behavioural, both halves.
    * MINT      "a third again as fast"          -> 1 / Mint.scale_for(1) == 4/3.
    * ALOE      "Too slow to save one being eaten" -> HEAL_PER_SECOND vs Pest.EAT_DPS.
    * DANDELION "grows its fluff back between volleys" -> rearm_seconds() < PREP_SECONDS.
    * BRAMBLE   "Winged pests go straight over."  -> Bramble.stops(true) is false.
    * NETTLE    pinned already (MUTATION_START_WAVE).
    * CHOMP     pinned already (Pest.SPECIES, cycle 119).

  VAGUE, and deliberately not asserted: "Fires kernels down the lane", "Grows seeds on a
  clock", "plant it somewhere the lane doesn't need", "so where you put it is the whole
  point", "this is what makes the last wave's damage stop being permanent". These name no
  number and cannot go stale. The bead warned about exactly this -- "inventing an assertion
  for a sentence that does not make a checkable claim" -- and it was right to.

  NOT MECHANICALLY CHECKABLE, and worth naming rather than quietly skipping: the Bramble's
  "Hurts nothing." It is TRUE and it is an absence of damage code, not a value. `engages` is
  the obvious key and is the wrong one -- the Bramble engages (it HOLDS), which is why that
  key's own header calls it the mirror of the Sundew. There is no `damages()` anywhere, and
  inventing one to make this assertable would be adding a field to satisfy a test.

THE FINDING: the Sundew's blurb said "crawls at half speed". SLOW_FACTOR is 0.55, and the
SELECTION PANEL prints the real number -- Hud.sundew_detail renders "Slowing N pest(s) to
55% speed." So the shop promised half and the panel delivered 55%, both on screen, one click
apart, and a player who read both saw the two disagree about the same plant.

FIXED BY MOVING THE SENTENCE, not the constant. 0.55 is tuned and sticky_sundew.gd:40
carries the overlapping-patch reasoning behind it. Changing a balance number to make a blurb
true is the tail wagging the dog. It now reads "just over half speed".

AND THE ASSERTION IS A RELATIONSHIP rather than a corrected string: the blurb may contain
"at half speed" IF AND ONLY IF SLOW_FACTOR is 0.5. A future retune to an actual half makes
the sentence permissible again, instead of leaving behind a test that pins today's wording
and has to be edited to allow the truth.

THE DENOMINATOR IS THE PART THAT OUTLIVES THIS CYCLE. Every plant must appear in the test --
checked, or explicitly named as checked elsewhere -- so a tenth plant fails here until
somebody decides which category its blurb is in. Without that the sweep is a one-off and the
next unchecked promise ships silently, which is how this one arrived.

SIX OF THE SEVEN WERE TRUE, and that is worth saying plainly. The writing in this catalogue
is careful and the numbers behind it are right. What was missing was anything that would
notice when the code moved underneath the prose -- which is the same conclusion -u9zb
reached about the HUD's sentences, from the other direction.

title: Read all 47 NOT COVERED sentences, and sort cannot-by-construction from not-yet
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md "New in cycle 116", both entries. Filed after breaking one of these and
shipping it.

THE POPULATION, derived: 22 of the 29 files under tools/ carry a `NOT COVERED:` line, 47
occurrences between them. Every one is a factual claim about the code around it, several are
many cycles old, and they are trusted MORE than ordinary comments because they are PRINTED
TO THE OPERATOR ON EVERY RUN. A caveat on screen reads as current by construction.

WHY NOW. Cycle 116 falsified one and shipped it. citation_check.py's line said drift was
"the one nothing can automate"; the same commit made it automatable, and the sentence went
on printing under every run of the tool that had just disproved it. It was caught only
because I went back to verify a claim I had written about my own work in the bead's close.

That is the third instance of one shape in five cycles -- eaten_message (cycle 112),
idle_detail (cycle 115), this -- and the third is what makes it a class rather than three
accidents: A SENTENCE NAMING WHAT SOMETHING CANNOT DO GOES STALE THE MOMENT SOMEBODY MAKES
IT DO THAT.

THE WORK, and it is deliberately a SWEEP and not a checker. -u9zb settled that accuracy
cannot be mechanised (no shared vocabulary between English and code) and that conclusion is
reused here rather than re-derived. Read all 47, give each a verdict, fix what has rotted.
-u9zb found two real defects in 33 HUD sentences; there is no reason to expect a better
ratio here, and these are the sentences a person consults when deciding whether to trust a
green run.

DO IT THE WAY -u9zb WAS DONE, because that shape worked: derive the population by command
rather than by memory, group the verdicts (most will be TRUE BY CONSTRUCTION for one shared
reason and saying so once is worth more than 47 lines of "fine"), and record the verdict
table in the close.

THE SECOND HALF, and it may be the more valuable one. A NOT COVERED line is the one place a
checker admits a gap, which makes it the one place to look for the next feature.
citation_check's admission was a to-do list disguised as a limitation and reading it as one
produced -5sxj in a single cycle. So while sweeping, sort each into:
  * CANNOT, BY CONSTRUCTION -- genuinely undecidable, or needs something the tool must not
    do (open the project, run the game).
  * DOES NOT, YET -- unimplemented. This is a backlog nobody has read.
The two are written identically today and only one of them is work.

TASTE, argue with it: the distinction belongs in the sentences themselves, not in a report.
A checker that conflates "impossible" with "not built" teaches its operator to stop reading
the line, which is the one outcome that would make all 47 worthless.

ACCEPTANCE: all 47 read, each verdicted TRUE / STALE / and sorted CANNOT vs NOT-YET; the
stale ones fixed; the NOT-YET ones filed as their own beads (that list is the deliverable
people will actually use); and a stated decision on whether the two categories should be
distinguishable in the printed text.

title: Make citation drift detectable, since it has happened twice and the checker says it cannot be
description:
SOURCE: cycles 112 and 115, where the same failure happened twice and was caught both times
by hand.

WHAT HAPPENS. Step 3 of the cycle skill says to write kanban entries with a `file:line`
citation for every claim about the code, then to re-read every citation AFTER the code edits
land. That last instruction exists because entries are written in the same cycle as the code
they cite, so a citation written at 14:00 can point at a different line by 16:00 -- and it is
the writer's OWN edits that move it.

It has happened twice:
  * cycle 112: `game/hud.gd:3555` was `eaten_message` when written and `hint_note_text` by
    commit; `game/pest.gd:1279` was the `is_hungry` branch and became `_mark_engaged()`.
  * cycle 115: all THREE new citations drifted, by 39, 8 and 39 lines.

BOTH TIMES citation_check.py reported clean -- 336 of 336, then 351 of 351. It is right to.
Its own NOT COVERED line says it "cannot see a citation that has drifted onto a DIFFERENT
but still-valid line, which is the common case and the one nothing can automate".

THAT LAST CLAUSE IS WHAT THIS BEAD DISPUTES. What cannot be automated is deciding whether a
line SUPPORTS a claim. What can be automated is noticing that the line a citation points at
is not the line it pointed at before.

THE WORK: a snapshot mode for tools/citation_check.py.
  * `--snapshot PATH` records, for every resolved citation, the citation plus a NORMALISED
    copy of the target line's text (strip leading whitespace -- indentation is noise and
    moves for unrelated reasons).
  * `--against PATH` re-resolves every citation and reports the ones whose target text no
    longer matches the snapshot. Those are exactly the drifted ones.
  * A citation absent from the snapshot is NEW and reported as such, never as drifted. An
    entry written this cycle has nothing to compare against and must not gate.

The cycle's flow then becomes: snapshot before the code edits, check after. Same shape as
lint's `--baseline-write` / `--baseline`, which this repo already uses for the "which
findings are MINE" question.

WHAT IT STILL CANNOT DO, and the NOT COVERED line must say so: a citation whose target line
was EDITED IN PLACE reads as drifted when the claim may be fine, and a citation that drifted
onto a line with identical text (two `return ""` lines) reads as clean. Both are better than
today; neither is proof.

ACCEPTANCE: both modes exist; a synthetic fixture proves the check FAILS on a citation whose
target moved and PASSES on one that did not -- both directions, since a drift detector that
always fires is as useless as one that never does; new citations are reported separately
from drifted ones; and the existing 351-citation run is byte-identical when no snapshot is
given.
notes:
CORRECTION TO THE CLOSE ABOVE, made minutes after closing.

The close's last paragraph says: "The tool's original NOT COVERED sentence -- 'the one
nothing can automate' -- is left in place deliberately for the SUPPORTS half, which is still
true and is still the real limit."

That was wrong on the facts and I only found it by grepping to confirm my own claim. The
sentence is not about the SUPPORTS half at all. It reads, in full:

    "Nor can it see a citation that has drifted onto a DIFFERENT but still-valid line,
     which is the common case and the one nothing can automate."

It is specifically about DRIFT -- the thing this bead just made detectable -- so leaving it
was not a deliberate choice about scope, it was a false sentence in the tool's own output
that I had walked past. Exactly the class of defect cycle 115 spent a whole cycle removing
from hud.gd, in the tool I was editing at the time, printed on every single run.

FIXED. The NOT COVERED line now says this MODE does not see drift, names --snapshot/--against
as what does, and keeps a parenthetical recording that the old wording was half right and
survived two cycles after drift had already bitten twice. The SUPPORTS half of the caveat is
untouched and is still the real limit.

Worth recording rather than quietly editing, because the sequence is the lesson: I shipped a
feature that falsified a sentence, wrote a close asserting I had considered that sentence,
and had not read it. The check that caught it was going back to verify a claim I had made
about my own work.
close_reason:
SHIPPED. `--snapshot` / `--against` on tools/citation_check.py, wired into the cycle skill's
step 3.

CLAUSE BY CLAUSE.

"both modes exist" -- yes. `--snapshot PATH` records what every RESOLVED citation lands on,
normalised for leading whitespace (indentation moves for reasons unrelated to the claim; a
block re-indented under a new `if` is not a citation going stale). `--against PATH`
re-resolves and reports the ones whose text moved, printing `was:` and `now:`.

"a synthetic fixture proves the check FAILS on a citation whose target moved and PASSES on
one that did not -- both directions" -- both run, both correct:
  * POSITIVE: insert one line above a cited line -> `DRIFTED: game/bramble.gd:120-120 /
    was: super.take_damage(amount * bite_resistance()) / now: func take_damage(...)`, exit 1.
  * NEGATIVE: nothing moved -> `0 drifted`, exit 0. Reverting the insertion -> exit 0 again.
  * Plus a third: `--against` with no snapshot file is exit 2, not a clean "0 drifted". A
    report of zero against a file that does not exist is indistinguishable from having
    checked, which is what every NOT COVERED line in this repo exists to prevent.

"new citations are reported separately from drifted ones" -- yes, as NEW, and they do not
gate. An entry written this cycle has nothing to compare against.

"the existing 351-citation run is unchanged when no snapshot is given" -- byte-identical:
`351 citation(s) across 1 file(s), 351 resolved, 0 finding(s)`, exit 0. check_all still 19
of 19 clean.

THREE THINGS THE WORK TURNED UP, none of which was the feature:

1. CONFIRMING THE PREMISE STOPPED ME OVERLOADING AN EXISTING FLAG. citation_check ALREADY
   has --baseline / --baseline-write and I nearly reused them. They snapshot FINDINGS,
   answering "which broken citations are new". Drift is about citations that still RESOLVE.
   One flag meaning both would have made a clean --baseline run read as evidence about
   drift, which it is not. The bead specified --snapshot/--against and was right to.

2. THE NEW MODE'S DENOMINATOR CONTRADICTED THE TOOL'S OWN: 310 against 351. Correct -- the
   map is keyed by file:start-end, so a target cited from two entries collapses to one --
   but printing only the smaller number beside a default run saying 351 reads as 41
   citations gone missing. Both numbers now print in both modes.

3. THE FIRST FIXTURE WAS VACUOUS AND SAID SO. An absolute Windows path's drive colon
   (C:/Users/...) is not matched by the CITATION regex, so it reported "0 citation(s), 0
   resolved" and BOTH controls would have passed over nothing. Caught by reading the
   denominator on the SETUP run rather than on the assertion -- which is the whole argument
   for printing one.

WIRED, NOT JUST WRITTEN. Step 3 of the cycle skill now carries the snapshot-before /
check-after pair with the reason. Cycle 111's entire lesson was that .claude/surveys/ held
three scripts nobody ran; shipping a checker with no caller repeats that one directory over.

WHAT IT STILL CANNOT DO, and the --against output says so on every run: it compares TEXT, so
a citation whose target line was edited IN PLACE reports as drifted when the claim may be
fine, and one that moved onto a line with identical text (two `return ""` lines) reports as
clean. It tells you the line is not the line you cited; whether the claim still holds is a
read, same as always.

The tool's original NOT COVERED sentence -- "the one nothing can automate" -- is left in
place deliberately for the SUPPORTS half, which is still true and is still the real limit.

title: Nothing tells the player they may build on the road, and eight plants taught them they cannot
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md "New in cycle 114", first entry. PLAYER-FACING, and the strongest teaching
gap in the game right now.

THE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS and is deliberate. Three one-shot hints:
RunConfig.HINT_MOVE_PREVIEW (game/run_config.gd:166), HINT_CHOMP_IGNORES_FLIGHT (:195),
HINT_UPGRADE_EXISTS (:212). Each pairs a message-row tip with a notebook card in
Hud.HINT_CARDS (game/hud.gd:3494), and test_every_hint_has_a_notebook_card fails on an id
with no card AND on a card with no id, so the two lists cannot drift.

WHAT THOSE THREE TEACH: a winged pest ignores a Chomp; a plant already down can grow; Uproot
compares before it digs. Each is a rule the board does not state.

"YOU MAY BUILD ON THE ROAD" IS A BIGGER ONE THAN ANY OF THEM, and the difference is the
point. The other three fill a gap in what the player knows. This one CONTRADICTS what eight
plants spent the whole game teaching: Board.is_buildable refused every road cell for the
entire history of this project, and Game.place_plant still answers "pests walk there" for
eight of the nine. A player who has internalised that rule will not try it, and the Barrier
Bramble's shop line ("Grows across the road itself, and everything walking it stops to chew
through") is a sentence they have every reason to read as flavour rather than as a placement
rule.

THE TRIGGER IS THE DECISION, and it should be made deliberately rather than defaulted to
"when the plant is unlocked":
  (a) on first seeing the Bramble in the shop -- earliest, and fires while the player is
      reading the blurb that already says it.
  (b) on first SELECTING it -- fires when they are about to act.
  (c) on the first refusal of a road plant on grass -- i.e. the first time place_plant
      returns "no pests walk there". This is the most teachable moment and the only one that
      fires when the player is already confused, because they have just tried and failed.
Prefer (c) unless it turns out to be reachable too rarely; a player who never tries never
learns, so (c) alone may leave the plant undiscovered. A combination is legitimate.

COST: one const in run_config.gd, one entry in Hud.HINT_CARDS, one producer beside
flight_tip/upgrade_tip, and a corpus entry so the message row's budget prices it -- see
Hud.message_corpus(); a hint the budget has never measured can clip, and hud.gd's header
explains why clipping is silent. The gate keeps the two lists together for you.

ACCEPTANCE: a fourth hint exists with its notebook card, the trigger is chosen with the
reason recorded, the message is priced by message_corpus(), and a test asserts the hint
fires once and not twice (the existing three have this shape -- follow it rather than
inventing one).
close_reason:
SHIPPED. The fourth hint exists, and the notebook page that could only hold three now holds
as many as the list needs.

CLAUSE BY CLAUSE.

"a fourth hint exists with its notebook card" -- RunConfig.HINT_ROAD_PLANTS, in HINTS, with
a card in Hud.HINT_CARDS ("One plant goes in the road"). test_every_hint_has_a_notebook_card
keeps the two lists together and did its job: it is why the card could not be skipped.

"the trigger is chosen with the reason recorded" -- ON SELECTION, not on the first refusal,
and the bead preferred (c) the refusal. The reason for overriding it is in _offer_road_hint's
header: _click_at ALREADY answers a misplaced road plant with "No pests walk there.", so the
confused moment is not silent. What the player lacks is not feedback but the positive
instruction -- where it DOES go. A hint firing after the mistake would be the second thing
they read about it.

The bead's own worry about (a)/(b) -- "a player who never tries never learns" -- is what
settles it the other way: selection is GUARANTEED (nothing is planted without being
selected) where a refusal is not.

BOTH ROUTES, which the bead did not raise. _on_plant_chosen's comment says it is "the only
route in"; that is true of the BAR and not of `selected_plant`. _on_packet_requested sets it
too, so a Bramble can arrive already selected having never been pressed in the bar -- which
is precisely the player meeting the plant for the first time. Wired to both, with a test for
the packet route.

"the message is priced by message_corpus()" -- yes, PER PLANT alongside the two death lines,
for the same reason: pricing only the one plant that can currently show it is a budget that
is wrong the first time a second road plant exists. The per-plant multiplier moves 7 -> 8.

"a test asserts the hint fires once and not twice" -- yes, and it asserts more than asked.
The two-door contract is asserted in BOTH directions: a busy message row DEFERS the hint
(show_message queues an unread line and returns false, leaving it owed) and a free row
spends it. That is not decoration -- my first draft "fixed" the deferral by clearing the row,
and a future change that spent the hint on the CALL rather than on the POST would have passed
every other assertion in the file.

WHAT THE BEAD DID NOT ANTICIPATE, and it was most of the work:

THE NOTEBOOK HINTS PAGE HOLDS EXACTLY THREE. The file predicted this day in prose -- "Three
rows at 98 is 3 + 2*98 + 94 = 293 against DRAWING_BOX's 300, so a FOURTH hint does not fit"
-- and gated it so hint four failed the suite rather than drawing off the matte. Its two
named ways out were "drop the pitch or split the page".

The pitch cannot drop. Four rows need a pitch of 67 against a row that is 94 tall, so the
note height must shrink too -- and the same block records that the 4-line note exists
because the UNSHOWN form is the shown form plus "Not shown yet - ", making it "the state a
reader most needs to read" and the one that overflows first. Compressing a teaching page to
fit a teaching line is backwards.

So the page splits. hint_pages_needed(), hints_on_page(index) and page_for_hint_page(index)
are pure and static, the PAGES entry carries its own hint_page index (so the two pages need
not be adjacent), and _build_hints rebuilds for the page being shown. Capacity is STILL
finite and STILL loud: a seventh hint fails the suite exactly as the fourth did, now against
the number of KIND_HINTS entries in PAGES.

THREE DEFECTS ON THE WAY, and which gate caught each is the useful part:

  * queue_free() on the rebuilt pane is DEFERRED. The old Hints was still in the tree when
    the new one was added, Godot renamed the newcomer, and every get_node("Hints") kept
    returning page one. It presented as "a hint with no row" for a row that existed and
    rendered correctly. remove_child + free() fixes it.
  * TWO freed-object accesses in the updated test -- a cast and a .text read on Labels whose
    pane the next page rebuild had freed. THE SUITE REPORTED 903/903 ALL TESTS PASSED
    THROUGH BOTH. Only run_tests.py's stderr check saw them, which is the exact failure mode
    CLAUDE.md says it exists for.
  * suite_reach_check found road_plant_tip public with no test naming it. I had built the
    entire page split and never written the hint's own tests -- the checker noticed what I
    had forgotten rather than what I had got wrong.

VERIFIED LIVE: the tip on the real message row, hint page 0 holding the three old hints and
page 1 holding the road tip, "4 of 4 seen" counting across both, pager 16/16.

NOT DONE: the second hints page's drawing is bramble_ragged.png at 64px in a ~360px pane,
which is small -- but so is the facing page's chomp_flower_gape.png, so it is consistent
rather than wrong. If the hint list grows to a third page the drawings will want revisiting
as a set.

title: Read every HUD sentence against the game, once
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md "New in cycle 112", first entry, written immediately after finding one of
these by accident.

THE CLASS. Hud.eaten_message (game/hud.gd:3563) read "A hungry pest ate your %s!" and was
correct for every plant death in the game until the ninth plant landed. Pest
._physics_process reaches _adjacent_plant() only inside its `is_hungry` branch
(game/pest.gd:1282-1286), so a hungry pest genuinely was the only thing that could destroy
a plant. A Barrier Bramble is chewed by _blocking_plant(), which every pest runs.

Nineteen checkers, lint and 897 tests were green over that sentence for two cycles. They
had to be: whether a sentence is TRUE is not a property any of them evaluates.
message_corpus_check.py is the closest this project gets to checking prose and it verifies
that a line is PRICED -- that the row is wide enough to draw it -- never that it is
accurate.

THE WORK is a one-off sweep, not a checker. Read every producer in Hud, ask what has to be
true about the game for its sentence to be true, and cite the line that makes it so. The
population, derived rather than guessed: `grep -n "^static func .*_message\|^static func
.*_detail\|^static func .*_note\|^static func .*_text" game/hud.gd` -- plus Hud
.message_corpus()'s literal entries, which are strings with no producer and therefore
nothing to read but themselves.

WHAT TO LOOK FOR, from the one instance already found: a sentence that names a MECHANISM
("a hungry pest", "wings", "the rain") rather than describing an outcome. Those are the
ones that go stale, because the mechanism list grows. A sentence that says "your Corn
Cobbler was destroyed" cannot rot; one that says WHY can.

KNOWN CANDIDATES worth checking first, on that reasoning and not yet verified -- treat
these as leads, not findings:
  * idle_detail() "Idle -- waiting for a pest." Its own comment says it is "the line seven
    of the eight plants show". There are nine plants and the count in that comment is
    already wrong; whether the SENTENCE is wrong for any of them is the question.
  * Anything naming a wave number, since WaveDirector.WAVES has grown.
  * Anything naming what a mutation does, since Pest.SPECIES and the mutation list have
    both grown since most of these were written.

ACCEPTANCE: every producer read, with a one-line verdict each recorded in the bead's close
(TRUE / STALE / UNVERIFIABLE), the stale ones fixed or filed, and a stated decision about
whether ANY of this can be mechanised -- "no, and here is why" is a fine answer and is
probably the right one. Do NOT build a checker as part of this bead; the point is to find
out how big the problem is first.
close_reason:
DONE. All 33 producers in game/hud.gd read against the game. Two findings, both fixed; two
stale claims in a neighbouring file's headers, also fixed; one filed as a follow-up; and a
stated decision about mechanising it (no, and the reason is below).

THE POPULATION, derived rather than guessed: 33 functions matching
`^static func [a-z_]+(_message|_detail|_note|_text|_tip|_line|_headline)\(` in game/hud.gd.

VERDICTS. Grouped, because most of them cannot rot for one shared reason.

TRUE BY CONSTRUCTION -- 21 producers whose every claim is a NUMBER read from the thing it
describes, so the sentence cannot outlive the mechanic:
  packet_button_text, uproot_net_text, uproot_button_text, uproot_armed_text,
  _worst_case_text, selection_line, corn_detail, sunflower_detail, dandelion_armed_detail,
  dandelion_regrowing_detail, chomp_chewing_detail, sundew_detail, next_wave_note,
  wave_headline, wave_note, wave_cleared_headline, wave_cleared_note, prep_depth_note,
  hint_note_text, packet_message, upgrade_message, wave_cleared_line.
  These are the safe shape and the finding is that they ARE the safe shape: a sentence that
  interpolates what it is describing is a sentence that cannot lie about it.

TRUE, and recently checked: resisting_detail and chewed_through_message (cycle 111 and 112,
both new), destroyed_message, upgrade_tip, weather_headline, uproot_armed_message ("it will
not grow back" -- confirmed, commit_uproot has no replant path).

STALE, FIXED THIS CYCLE:
  * idle_detail. "Idle -- waiting for a pest." Every plant without its own branch in
    _refresh_selection gets it, and that is Garden Mint, Salve Aloe and Prickly Nettle. Mint
    speeds its neighbours; Aloe repairs them; NEITHER CAN TOUCH A PEST AT ALL. Both were
    announcing that they were waiting for one.
    The damning part is that the argument was already written down and not applied: the
    Sundew has its own line, and the comment three lines above the fall-through says "A
    Sundew is never busy and never idle -- it is always working, and the only question is
    how many pests are in the patch. 'Idle' was simply the wrong word for the one plant that
    cannot be." Correct, and never extended when Mint and Aloe landed.
    Fixed with mint_detail() and aloe_detail(). The Nettle KEEPS the idle line and should:
    it stings, so it genuinely is waiting for a pest (a mutated one).

STALE, FIXED, IN A NEIGHBOURING FILE -- found by following the mechanism rather than the
producer list, which is the half a producer-only sweep would have missed:
  * game/wave_director.gd, the WHAT A DROUGHT SLOWS header: "three of the eight plants in
    PlantCatalog" and "The other five are untouched". Nine and six.
  * game/wave_director.gd, husk multiplier header: "A drought doubles every plant's firing
    interval". It doubles the interval of every plant that HAS one -- three of nine. A
    Bramble and a Mint have nothing to slow.

TRUE BUT NARROW, filed rather than changed:
  * flight_tip: "That pest flies over Chomp Flowers. Corn Cobblers can still hit it." Both
    sentences are true. It names Corn as THE answer when Dandelion and Nettle also reach a
    winged pest -- and the Nettle exists specifically to hit mutated pests, wings included.
    Not a lie, and arguably better pedagogy than a list. Filed as a judgement call rather
    than fixed, because changing a once-per-save teaching line to be more complete and less
    memorable is a trade, not a repair.
  * weather_note drought: "Everything shoots half as often." Loose but defensible -- nothing
    that fails to slow is a thing that shoots. Left alone deliberately; the row has a width
    budget and the natural reading is correct.

CAN THIS BE MECHANISED? NO, and the reason is worth recording rather than re-derived.
message_corpus_check.py already verifies that every emitted line is PRICED, and that is the
only property of a sentence a static tool can decide. Accuracy is a claim about the
RELATIONSHIP between a sentence and code elsewhere, and there is no shared vocabulary
between them to check -- "hungry", "shoots", "idle" are English, not identifiers.

What IS mechanisable, and is the useful residue of this sweep: the sentences that rot are
the ones naming a MECHANISM rather than interpolating a NUMBER. 21 of 33 producers here
interpolate what they describe and are safe by construction; every defect found in two
cycles has been in the handful that name a mechanism in prose. That is a reviewable
property, not a checkable one -- so the recommendation is a note in hud.gd's corpus header
saying "prefer interpolating the thing you are describing over naming it", NOT a checker.
Filed as its own item so this close is not the only place it lives.

title: Give heredoc_survey a working-tree mode, since it cannot see an uncommitted break
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md [G-129], filed in cycle 111 after I broke the rule the survey
exists to police and watched the survey report clean over it.

WHAT HAPPENED. Wrapping a long assertion message across two lines inside an Edit put a
real newline inside a GDScript string literal in test/unit/test_selftest.gd -- the cycle-97
defect, reached with no heredoc and no script involved. Three tools were asked:

  python tools/name_check.py                  -> errors: 0   (names resolve; its own
                                                 NOT COVERED line says it does not compile)
  python .claude/surveys/heredoc_survey.py    -> SIGNATURE A: 0 hit(s)
  godot --headless --script tools/lint_project.gd
                                              -> exit 1, "Parse Error", the file named

The survey is the project's designated countermeasure for exactly this defect class and it
reported clean over a live instance of it.

WHY, and it is not a bug in the survey. Its own docstring says it "sweeps this repo's whole
git history", and it does -- it reads DIFFS. The defect was in the working tree and
uncommitted, so there was structurally nothing for it to see. It answers "how often has
this happened", which is a genuinely different question from "is the tree broken right
now", and tools/survey_all.py's header (added in the same cycle) says so explicitly.

THE GAP is that the project has no cheap answer to the second question. lint_project.gd
answers it, and lint opens the Godot project and writes .godot/ -- so it is not
parallel-safe, and a fan-out lane, which gets name_check and nothing else, cannot ask it at
all. That is precisely the population most likely to hand-edit a long string.

THE WORK: a --worktree mode for heredoc_survey.py that runs its two existing signature
scans over tracked files AS THEY ARE ON DISK rather than over diffs. Both scanners already
operate on file text -- SIGNATURE A asks gdsource.literal_spans, SIGNATURE B looks for
comment prose with no leading '#' -- so this is a second input source, not a second
detector, which is what keeps it honest: a working-tree hit and a history hit must be found
by the same code or the two can disagree.

If that lands it is parallel-safe (stdlib, no project, no .godot/) and belongs in
tools/check_all.py's pool, NOT in survey_all.py -- at which point the split is worth
restating: the history sweep stays a survey, the working-tree scan becomes a checker. Note
the trap cycle 111 hit while wiring survey_all: giving a file a NOT COVERED line is what
makes check_all adopt and RUN it, so decide which pool a new entry belongs in before adding
the marker.

ACCEPTANCE: reintroduce the exact defect (a literal newline inside a string literal in any
.gd under test/ or game/), confirm the new mode exits 1 and names the file and line, then
remove it and confirm exit 0. Both directions, because a scanner that always fires and one
that never fires are equally useless and only the second looks like a pass. The history
mode's output must be unchanged -- assert it, since the whole point is one detector with
two inputs.
close_reason:
SHIPPED. `python .claude/surveys/heredoc_survey.py --worktree` scans tracked .gd files as
they are on disk, exits 1 naming the file and line, and is wired into the cycle skill's
step 2 beside the rule it guards.

ACCEPTANCE, clause by clause:

"reintroduce the exact defect ... confirm the new mode exits 1 and names the file and line"
-- done, with a fixture that had to be TRACKED, which is the one thing the bead did not
anticipate. `worktree_versions` uses `git ls-files`, so an UNTRACKED fixture is invisible and
the positive control would have passed over nothing. `git add -N .fixture_h613.gd` fixed it:

    === SIGNATURE A  string literal broken across a newline: 2 hit(s)
      worktree  .fixture_h613.gd:5
      worktree  .fixture_h613.gd:6
    exit=1

"then remove it and confirm exit 0" -- done: 63 tracked files, 0 hits, exit 0.

"both directions -- a drift detector that always fires is as useless as one that never
does" -- both above.

"The history mode's output must be unchanged" -- unchanged: 1028 (commit, .gd file)
versions, 0 hits, exit 0. It now also SAYS what it cannot see, in its first line: "from
HISTORY -- this cannot see an uncommitted defect; use --worktree for that."

ONE THING THE BEAD ASKED FOR THAT I DID DIFFERENTLY, and it matters: the bead said "if that
lands it is parallel-safe and belongs in tools/check_all.py's pool". It does not go in the
pool, and the reason is the exit code.

A hit in HISTORY is a defect that already happened and was already FIXED. This file's own
header documents two such incidents, in itself, while it was being written. Gating on those
is a permanently red gate, which .claude/skills/house-static-checker calls worse than no
gate: it teaches its operator to skip the check, and then it is not there for the one that
matters. So the exit code differs by mode -- --worktree gates, history is advisory -- and a
pool that runs a file with one command cannot express that. Putting it in check_all would
either run the wrong mode or make the pool permanently red.

It is in the cycle skill's step 2 instead, next to the sentence describing the defect, which
is where somebody about to make the mistake is reading.

ONE DETECTOR, TWO INPUTS, as the bead required. `--worktree` supplies a different list of
(sha, subject, path) tuples and a different reader; both feed the SAME `gdsource.literal_spans`
and comment-prose passes. The modes cannot disagree about what a break looks like.

AND THE FILE WAS DAMAGED BY THE THING IT MEASURES FOR THE THIRD TIME WHILE THIS WAS BEING
WRITTEN. Its NOT_COVERED constant was written through a shell heredoc, which turned every
escaped newline into a real one inside a string literal -- twice in one patch, unterminated
strings at exactly the lines the patch touched. That is SIGNATURE A, in the detector for
SIGNATURE A, after a header that already records two of these. The constant is now built by
joining a list of plain lines, which has no escape to eat, and the comment above it says so.

Recording that rather than quietly fixing it, because the file's own header says why: "a
survey that reports 554 non-findings and a survey that reports 0 findings look equally like
work", and an incident IS data for the question the survey asks.

NOT DONE: the survey still cannot see a heredoc that ate a backslash somewhere OTHER than a
string literal or a comment marker -- a regex, a path, a format string. Its NOT_COVERED line
now says so explicitly, which it did not before this cycle.

title: [bug] The move preview describes one plant and asks the board about another
description:
SOURCE: found while closing -3mhn (the Barrier Bramble). Named in that close as "what is
not done" rather than folded in, because it predates the bead.

Game._update_preview resolves WHICH plant it is describing at game/game.gd:2114:

    var previewing: StringName = moving.kind if moving != null else selected_plant

That is correct and deliberate -- while an uproot is armed the player is weighing a MOVE,
so the preview describes the plant being moved (plant-tower-defense-qk5q). `previewing`
then drives _preview.reach and _preview.plant_id.

But the PLACEABILITY of the destination is computed from `selected_plant`, not from
`previewing`, in both halves:
  * `free`, at the three _update_preview call sites, now reads
    `board.is_buildable_for(cell, selected_plant)`.
  * `_preview.placeable = free and would_plant_at(cell)` (game/game.gd:2134), and
    would_plant_at consults `selected_plant` too (:1473).

Before -3mhn this could not produce a wrong answer: every plant had identical
buildability, so which id you asked about did not matter. It does now. Arm an uproot on a
grass plant while a Barrier Bramble is selected in the shop and the preview describes the
grass plant while asking the board whether a ROAD plant may stand there -- and the reverse
with a road plant armed and a grass plant selected.

NOT YET REPRODUCED ON A RUNNING GAME. That is the first job: the uproot-move path may
disarm or re-select on its way here, in which case the two ids can never disagree in
practice and the correct fix is a comment saying so plus a test that pins it. Read
_arm_uproot / _disarm_uproot before writing code. This description is a claim about the
code as read on 2026-08-18, not a claim that a player can see it.

ACCEPTANCE: either a test that drives the disagreeing state and asserts the preview agrees
with the click (fix `free`/would_plant_at to take `previewing`), or a test that
demonstrates the state is unreachable, with the reason written at game/game.gd:2114.
Either is a real answer; only "looks fine" is not.
close_reason:
SHIPPED. The bead's one open question -- "NOT YET REPRODUCED ON A RUNNING GAME. That is the
first job." -- is answered: the state IS reachable and the bug was real.

REACHABILITY, which is what the bead asked to be settled before any code. Game._select()
writes `selected_placed` (the board selection). The shop's `selected_plant` is a separate
field and nothing in the uproot path touches it -- _select() only calls _disarm_uproot()
when the clicked plant differs from the armed one. So: pick a Barrier Bramble in the shop,
click a cob on the board, press Uproot, hover a road cell. Both selections live at once.

Confirmed twice rather than argued once: first as a RED test that failed for the stated
reason ("Expected false but got true"), then on the running game.

WHAT THE PLAYER SAW. The ring, reach and coverage dots describe the plant being MOVED
(-qk5q). The green brackets are a promise about what a CLICK does, and a click plants
`selected_plant`. Before the ninth plant those two could not visibly disagree -- every plant
was placeable in exactly the same cells -- so this is a defect the Barrier Bramble created
rather than exposed. Over a road cell it drew a cob's range ring inside green brackets, on
ground no cob can occupy. That reads as "your cob moves here" and plants a Bramble.

THE FIX, and why this shape rather than another. `_preview.placeable` now requires BOTH
that the click will plant AND that the plant being described could stand there. The
alternative -- making `free`/would_plant_at ask about `previewing` -- would have been WRONG,
because the click genuinely does plant `selected_plant`; that version would have moved the
lie rather than removed it.

Requiring both refuses the cell instead of inventing a meaning for the disagreement. That
matters because whether a move should be a single action at all is still open (-h5w6): a
cue that resolved the contradiction in either direction would have decided that design
question by accident, in a hover handler.

NO-OP EVERYWHERE ELSE, which is the safety argument for putting a third term in a path that
runs on every mouse move: with nothing armed `previewing == selected_plant`, so the new term
asks exactly the question would_plant_at just answered. 898 existing tests were unmoved.

VERIFIED LIVE: placeable=false, plant_id=corn_cobbler, visible=true over the road cell, and
the cropped capture shows the brackets rendering BLOCKED while the cob's reach ring still
draws from that cell. That last part is the only claim no headless test can make, since
nothing headless draws them.

ONE THING WORTH KNOWING FOR THE NEXT TEST IN THIS AREA: arm_uproot() returns "confirm
needed" on success, not "" like place_plant(). The first draft of the reproduction asserted
"" and failed on its own precondition -- a test failing for the wrong reason is
indistinguishable from one that works, and only the message told them apart.

NOT ADDRESSED, and deliberately: the preview still shows the moved plant's ring over cells
the moved plant cannot occupy -- it just no longer promises them. Whether an armed move
should refuse to draw a ring over illegal ground at all is a cue-design question, not a
correctness one, and it belongs with -h5w6.

title: Decide what 'held' means now a plant holds without killing
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md "New in cycle 110", first entry, written while shipping the Barrier
Bramble (-3mhn). DESIGN DECISION, needed before a second wall-shaped plant exists.

The post-mortem card has a row headed "Where you held them" (game/run_summary.gd:468),
whose text comes from _stop_cell_text (:838-851). The number behind it is
`stop_cell_stops` -- Board's per-cell losses with escapes subtracted
(game/board.gd:150-162) -- so it counts KILLS at a cell.

The word was chosen deliberately and the reasoning is written out at
game/run_summary.gd:830-837: "'Held' is true of a kill and false of an escape, so it
cannot be read off the tint at all." That argument is sound and it was made when nothing
in the game could hold a pest without killing it.

As of -3mhn something can. A pest stopped by a Barrier Bramble stands still, chews
through, and walks on. It was held in every ordinary sense of the word and contributes
exactly zero to that row. So a run won on a wall of Brambles feeding cobs reports the
cobs' cell, and the seconds the Brambles bought are invisible on the card that exists to
explain the run.

THE QUESTION, which wants an answer before it is built: the card now has one spatial row
and two spatial stories -- where pests DIED, and where they were made to WAIT. Options:
  (a) leave it. "Held" keeps meaning kills; the Bramble is scenery to the post-mortem.
  (b) a second row. Needs a width budget check -- run_summary's rows are measured.
  (c) fold waiting into the existing tint rather than the number, since the map
      underneath already carries a per-cell reading.
Deciding late is what costs: the ambiguity is cheap with one wall-shaped plant and
expensive with two.

ACCEPTANCE: a decision recorded with its reasoning, and if it is (b) or (c), the
implementation plus a test. If it is (a), the reasoning goes into
game/run_summary.gd:830-837 beside the argument it qualifies, so the next reader of that
paragraph is not misled by it.
notes:
CYCLE 137 NOTE, from -i8k9's lane. Not a resolution -- the vocabulary this bead was
missing now exists, and the decision it asks for is still open.

PlantCatalog.damages(id) ships as of cycle 137, derived off each plant's own damage
constant. So "a plant that holds without killing" is now expressible as
`engages(id) and not damages(id)` rather than as a predicate somebody has to invent
while designing the card.

What that changes for each of this bead's three options:
  (a) leave the row and add a note -- the note at run_summary.gd can now cite
      PlantCatalog.damages instead of arguing from first principles.
  (b) a second row -- buildable now without inventing a predicate first.
  (c) fold waiting into the tint -- unaffected.

What it does NOT settle: which option. That is a card-design decision with a width
budget behind it (rows_capacity()), and the lane deliberately made none of it.

title: The Nurse Beetle wears the beetle's sprite, and she is the one pest you must not shoot
description:
SOURCE: plant-tower-defense-gsai, cycle 106. Disclosed by the lane that shipped the
species rather than found afterwards.

WHAT THE GAME DOES NOW (verified 2026-08-17): the Nurse Beetle exists, reaches a player in
campaign waves 17 and 19 (confirmed on a live census: 15 beetle / 17 aphid / 1 nurse at
t=39s of wave 17), and is the second boss -- it heals every other pest within 160px at
2.0 health a second, which the garden's "shoot the furthest-along pest" rule will not
target.

IT WEARS THE BEETLE'S ART. `Pest.SPECIES[NURSE]` points at
`res://assets/sprites/pest_beetle.png` and `pest_beetle_dead.png` at `scale 1.30` -- bigger
than any ordinary pest, deliberately under the Queen's 1.45 so
`test_a_queen_is_a_boss_sized_pest_on_every_axis_that_matters` stays honest.

WHY IT SHIPPED THAT WAY, so nobody reads it as an oversight: a new species sprite needs a
64px SVG in `art_src/`, a render through `tools/render_svg.gd`, a retina variant, and an
`EXPECTED_SIZE` row in `test/unit/test_sprite_style.gd`. A fan-out lane in a worktree can do
none of those -- it has no `.godot/`, may not run the import pass, and does not own the test
file. This is parent work or a solo cycle by construction.

THE PLAYER-FACING COST is real and specific: the one pest whose whole point is that it is
NOT the thing you should be shooting looks exactly like the thing you should be shooting.
A player who cannot pick her out of a beetle column cannot make the decision the species
exists to pose.

ASK: one SVG, following `art_src/STYLE.md` (64x64, top-down, outline a darker shade of the
fill, the sampled palette; `tools/svg_style_check.py` gates all of it). Design constraint
worth stating: she must read as a HEALER at a glance and at 1.30 scale in a moving column --
the Aloe already claims the sand/cream family for mending, so borrowing that hue is an
argument for rather than against, since it is the game's existing visual word for "this one
repairs".

CHECK BEFORE STARTING: `game/pest.gd`'s SPECIES entry documents the placeholder at length;
read it rather than the bead. And run `godot --headless --path . --import` once after adding
the SVG, before the first lint or test pass.

ACCEPTANCE: the Nurse has her own sprite and dead sprite; `svg_style_check.py` and
`test_sprite_style.gd` pass with her EXPECTED_SIZE row; and a screenshot of wave 17 shows
her distinguishable from the beetles she is walking behind.
close_reason: Own SVG + dead variant, rendered 1x and retina, EXPECTED_SIZE rows added, SPECIES repointed. Two channels (value + cross shape). Verified on the board beside ordinary beetles.

title: Make the close reason start from the acceptance, since the instruction alone is not enough
description:
SOURCE: plant-tower-defense-pc3m's audit, cycle 106. It is the one recommendation that
audit made, deliberately filed rather than smuggled into the close.

WHAT THE AUDIT FOUND (the numbers are in -pc3m's close reason):
* 97 of 97 beads closed under the current id scheme carry a real close reason. The "write
  a real close" habit holds without any mechanism.
* But a real reason is necessary and NOT sufficient. -1d07 is a current-scheme bead with a
  262-character close whose acceptance has four clauses: two answered plainly, one
  partially (the illegal mutation pair is asserted at the RULE level in
  test_combat.gd:5333 but not at the ROLL that consumes it, wave_director.gd:1018), and
  one -- "killable by at least two distinct answers the player can buy" -- not addressed
  at all.
* -bxhg, the bead that started this, was the same shape: a good close that quietly skipped
  a clause, unnoticed for four cycles.

WHY A GATE IS THE WRONG ANSWER, established rather than assumed. The audit prototyped one:
split the acceptance on `;` and ` and `, flag a clause whose content words are absent from
the close reason. It flagged 122 OF 146, including plain false positives where the splitter
ate mid-description prose. `.claude/skills/house-static-checker/SKILL.md` is explicit that a
permanently-red gate is worse than no gate -- it teaches people to skip the check, and then
it is not there for the finding that matters. Do not rebuild that checker; the reasoning is
recorded so it is not re-proposed from scratch.

ASK: change `.claude/skills/verify-bd-item/SKILL.md` so the close-reason step STARTS from
the acceptance text rather than from a blank file. Concretely, the close step should say to
write the acceptance's clauses into the reason file first, then answer each one underneath
-- so a skipped clause is a visibly unanswered line in the file being edited, rather than
something that has to be remembered.

That is the whole change: it makes answering the clauses the path of least resistance
instead of an act of discipline. It costs one paragraph in a skill and no new tooling.

CHECK BEFORE WRITING IT: `verify-bd-item` already says to answer the acceptance clause by
clause (that line was added by cycle 95, which is what -pc3m was auditing). So the edit is
not "add the instruction" -- the instruction is there and -1d07 happened anyway. The edit
is to change the MECHANICS of the step so following it is easier than not. Read what it
currently says before rewriting it, or this lands as a second copy of an instruction that
has already been shown not to be enough on its own.

ACCEPTANCE: the close step in verify-bd-item produces a file that already contains the
acceptance clauses; and the next bead closed through it has a close reason with a visible
line per clause.
close_reason:
SHIPPED in .claude/skills/verify-bd-item/SKILL.md.

This close was written by running the very command the change adds, which is the only honest way to close it:

    bd show plant-tower-defense-txme | sed -n '/ACCEPTANCE/,$p' > close-txme.txt

ACCEPTANCE, clause by clause:

"the close step in verify-bd-item produces a file that already contains the acceptance clauses"
    -- DONE. The step now says to seed the reason file from `bd show <id> | sed -n
    '/ACCEPTANCE/,$p'` BEFORE writing a word of the answer, then split it so each clause sits
    on its own line in quotes with the answer underneath. The command is verified, not
    proposed: it is what produced the two clauses above.

"and the next bead closed through it has a close reason with a visible line per clause"
    -- DONE, and the next bead is this one. Two clauses, two quoted lines, two answers. If a
    third clause had existed and I had skipped it, it would be sitting in this file
    unanswered rather than absent from it, which is the entire mechanism.

THE CHECK THE BEAD DEMANDED FIRST, and it changed what I wrote. "verify-bd-item already says
to answer the acceptance clause by clause (cycle 95 added it), so the edit is not 'add the
instruction' -- the instruction is there and -1d07 happened anyway." Confirmed by reading it:
the paragraph at "Re-read the ACCEPTANCE and answer it clause by clause" exists, with the
-bxhg story and the "no mechanism catches this" note. So the new text does not repeat it. It
sits underneath and changes the MECHANICS, and says in its first sentence why a second copy
of the instruction would be worthless.

TWO THINGS I ADDED BEYOND THE ASK:

1. "Do not paraphrase the clause you are answering." Quoting is what makes a missing clause
   visible; the existing paragraph already argues that a close describing what shipped is
   indistinguishable from one describing what was asked for, and a paraphrased clause
   reintroduces exactly that.
2. The rejected gate, recorded in the skill rather than only in this bead: the prototype
   flagged 122 OF 146 including plain false positives, and house-static-checker is explicit
   that a permanently-red gate is worse than no gate. The bead asked for the reasoning to be
   preserved "so it is not re-proposed from scratch" -- a bead is the wrong place for that,
   because the person about to rebuild it will be reading the skill, not the tracker.

NOT DONE, and it is not in the acceptance: nothing enforces this. That is deliberate and
argued above. The mechanism is that the unanswered clause is VISIBLE in the file you are
already editing, not that anything fails.

title: Three copies of get_viewport_width, and two still read the setting
description:
SOURCE: lane 0jye's report, cycle 105. It found this while fixing the same defect in
game/hud.gd and correctly refused to touch files it did not own.

WHAT IS THERE NOW (verified 2026-08-17 by the lane, and the fix it describes has now
shipped in hud.gd so the contrast is live):

`game/hud.gd` used to declare `get_viewport_width()` / `get_viewport_height()` reading
`ProjectSettings display/window/size/viewport_width|height`. That was the whole of -0jye:
the setting is not the live viewport, and under `stretch/mode=canvas_items` with
`stretch/aspect="expand"` the viewport genuinely changes SHAPE at a different window
aspect. Measured live at three shapes: a 1720x720 window produces a 1548-wide canvas, and
the HUD's bar stopped at 1152 with the side panel detached from the right edge by 396px.

`game/title_screen.gd` and `game/overlay_screen.gd` EACH DECLARE THEIR OWN COPY of those
two methods, with the identical ProjectSettings body. Two more copies, same defect, both
untouched -- so the title screen and every overlay (Keys, Options, the Notebook) still lay
themselves out against a number that is not the screen they are on.

WHY THIS IS ITS OWN BEAD rather than a footnote on -0jye: it is three copies of one
method, which is a derive-the-list shape rather than three bugs. The interesting question
is not "fix two more" but "why are there three", and the answer decides the work -- a
shared helper, a common base (OverlayScreen already IS a base for two of them), or a
static on one of them the others call.

WHAT TO CHECK BEFORE PICKING ONE:
* `OverlayScreen` is already the parent of the Keys, Options and Notebook screens, so a
  fix there covers three of the four surfaces for free. TitleScreen is not one of them.
* hud.gd now also has `design_width()` / `design_height()` -- the SETTING, under a name
  that says so -- which the shared version probably wants too. Some callers genuinely want
  the design size; the bug was that they all got it.
* hud.gd's fix connects `get_viewport().size_changed` once and re-derives. A title screen
  and an overlay may not need the signal at all if they are rebuilt on open -- CHECK, do
  not assume, because "it is rebuilt anyway" is exactly the assumption that leaves a
  resized window stale until the player navigates.

ACCEPTANCE: one place answers "how wide is the viewport"; the title screen and the overlay
screens lay out correctly at a non-16:9 window, demonstrated the way -0jye was (bridge
`set_resolution`, then `node-bounds` on the surface, at 1152x648 / 1720x720 / 1024x768);
and a test pins that no file declares a second copy of the method.
close_reason:
DONE. One ScreenMetrics, and the bead's count was wrong in the direction that mattered.

IT SAID THREE COPIES. THERE ARE EIGHT: hud.gd's design_* pair (the cycle-105 fix),
title_screen.gd, overlay_screen.gd, a FOURTH private pair in pause_screen.gd, a FIFTH in
run_summary.gd, and inlined reads in key_binding_screen.gd and options_screen.gd. Finding
the count is what answered the question.

WHY THERE ARE EIGHT, which decided the shape: one name was answering two different
questions -- "how big is the screen I must cover" (the live canvas) and "how big is the
canvas this was composed on" (the design size) -- and only the second had ProjectSettings
as an honest source. The forcing constraint is that half the callers are STATIC on purpose
(TitleScreen.button_rect, menu_capacity, PauseScreen.card_rect, OptionsScreen.rows_capacity
exist so a test can ask "would a seventh destination fit" without building the screen), and
a static function has no get_viewport(). So ProjectSettings was not laziness; it was the
only implementation that could serve them, and once written the instance callers took it
too. At 16:9 the two answers are identical, which is why it drifted invisibly.

game/screen_metrics.gd is the only shape that serves both static and instance callers from
one place. Fixing OverlayScreen alone was rejected because it covers three of four overlays,
leaves TitleScreen/PauseScreen/RunSummary as a fourth, fifth and sixth divergent copy, and
cannot serve the static callers at all.

THE BUG THIS TURNED UP IS NOT COSMETIC. PauseScreen's Backdrop is MOUSE_FILTER_STOP
precisely so the board cannot be played through a pause. Sized at 1152 on a 1548-unit canvas
it stopped 396 px short, and that strip was live, clickable board over a held run. Verified
live at 1720x720: the Backdrop now reads 0,0,1548x648.

WHICH SURFACES CAN BE LIVE DURING A RESIZE, checked rather than assumed by reading every
open/close path: TitleScreen (never rebuilt, and it is the screen a player is on while
maximising), the three overlays (rebuilt on open -- which is an argument about the NEXT
open, not this one), and PauseScreen (worst consequence, and it holds the run still, which
is exactly what a player does before alt-tabbing). All three get size_changed. It works
while paused because signal emission is not gated by SceneTree.paused.

WHAT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT MOVE, recorded and asserted: the compositions. Re-centring a
paper means re-running the builder, which discards a Keys row mid-capture and moves focus
out from under the player. NotebookScreen is a second recorded exception -- its content
constants are absolute viewport coordinates rather than paper offsets.

THE SIX-ROW CEILING STAYS ON THE DESIGN HEIGHT, and that is the trap avoided rather than a
thing left undone: made live, rows_capacity() returns 6 at 16:9, 8 at 4:3 and ~17 in the
headless suite, where a 64x64 root window scales to a 1152x1152 canvas -- which would have
made test_every_row_limited_surface_is_exactly_full go slack ON THE MACHINE RUNNING THE
SUITE while still printing green. expand never yields a canvas smaller than the design size,
so 648 is the worst case a budget must survive, which is what makes a budget against it safe.

A trap caught in passing: TitleScreen.button_column() used the live width, which would have
moved the column's centre 576 -> 768 on a 21:9 window while PLANT_X's hand-placed slots
stayed put -- silently moving the subject of
test_the_title_lawn_clears_the_button_column_and_the_horizon off the invariant it protects.

741/741, 15134 assertions, lint 0/0, check_all 16/16, findings 0 across 5 of 5 at 1548x648.

title: A test run migrated the real save before any redirect could apply
description:
SOURCE: cycle 104, hit while merging -zgzc (the remembered garden speed). Found by
reading the developer's real save after a headless test run, not by any gate.

WHAT HAPPENED: -zgzc bumped the save format v6 -> v7, widening the options line to
`cb0 sfx0 mus0 spd0`. The first `python tools/run_tests.py` after that merge REWROTE THE
DEVELOPER'S REAL `user://highscore.save` into the v7 shape.

Nothing was lost -- scores 3454 and 5008 intact, all six milestones intact, and
`seen_upgrade_tip` still correctly absent -- and the migration is exactly what the game
itself would have done on the player's next launch. So this is not a data-loss bug. It is
a HOLE IN THE GUARD, and the hole is the point.

WHY save_persist_check.py CANNOT SEE IT, and this is the whole bead: that checker asks
"can a function in a test script reach `RunConfig._save()`?" and requires such a script
to have a `setup()` redirecting `RunConfig.save_path`. It was clean for this run -- every
test script does have one. But `RunConfig` is an AUTOLOAD: `_ready()` runs at process
start, loads the real save, sees an old version, and rewrites it -- all before the runner
has called any `setup()`. There is no test function in the chain, so there is nothing for
the checker to find, and a redirect installed later is installed too late.

The general shape: **a redirect that is installed per-test cannot protect anything an
autoload does at process start.** Any future format bump has the same exposure, and so
does anything else RunConfig might decide to write on load.

TWO CANDIDATE FIXES, and they are not equivalent:
1. Make the runner redirect BEFORE the autoloads come up -- an env var or a command-line
   flag `RunConfig` reads in `_ready()` to choose its path. This closes the hole rather
   than narrowing it, and it is the one to prefer if the harness's runner can be told.
2. Make `_load`'s migration rewrite conditional on not being under test. Narrower, and it
   leaves every other process-start write exposed.

Whichever lands, `save_persist_check.py` should gain a NOT COVERED sentence naming this
explicitly: it checks test FUNCTIONS, and says nothing about what an autoload does before
the first one runs. Right now its clean exit reads as "the real save is safe", and on this
run it was clean while the real save was being rewritten.

ACCEPTANCE: a headless suite run against a deliberately old-version save leaves that file
byte-identical; and `save_persist_check.py`'s NOT COVERED line names the autoload
process-start gap so a clean exit stops over-claiming.
close_reason:
Both acceptance criteria met, and the mutation record is the interesting half.

ACCEPTANCE 1 -- "a headless suite run against a deliberately old-version save leaves
that file byte-identical". Done as written, at the REAL path, with two byte-identical
backups held first:

  planted v6 at user://highscore.save     md5 4754e2134a7e56c8dba0bc2a4e06becb
