title: Designer: better attack animations for Chomp Flower and Prickly Nettle
description:
SOURCE: designer's handwritten note (image7.png at repo root, added by James 2026-08-17): "better attack animations for chomp flower and prickly nettle".

WHAT THE GAME DOES NOW (verified 2026-08-17):
- Chomp Flower bite: `_bite()` (game/chomp_flower.gd:383-398) plays the SFX, flashes the pest, then a whole-sprite scale squash — `(1.18, 0.82)` over 0.06s, back to ONE over 0.12s. The sprite swaps to an eating texture while chewing (`_show_eating_sprite`, :420+) and there is a bigger squash on upgrade (`_on_upgraded`, :414-418). No lunge, no jaw open/close, no motion toward the pest.
- Prickly Nettle sting: `_sting()` (game/nettle.gd:181-188) damages, flashes, plays SFX, then `_sting_twitch()` (:192-197) — `STING_SQUASH` scale for 0.05s and back over 0.10s. Nothing points at the target; nothing leaves the plant.
- Both are ~0.15s of uniform scale on the whole sprite. Nettle's is gated on `GardenTheme.animations_enabled()` (:193) and so is Chomp's upgrade flourish (:414), but `_bite` (:394) gates only on sprite/tree — check whether that asymmetry is intended while in there.
- Contrast: Corn Cobbler's attack has a visible projectile (`game/kernel.gd`) and a `_recoil`; the designer's ask is that the two melee plants read as attacking too.

ASK: give each a readable attack:
- Chomp: a lunge toward the held pest (offset the sprite along the direction to `_held`, snap back), a two-frame open/closed jaw swap on the bite, or a brief lean toward the target — whatever the sprite set supports (SVG sources in art_src/; a second frame is one more SVG plus a `test_sprite_style.gd` EXPECTED_SIZE row).
- Nettle: the sting should point at its victim — a quick shear/lean toward the pest, or a tiny prickle spark spawned at the pest's position (a short-lived Node2D freed by its own tween).
Keep every new tween behind `animations_enabled()`; keep the game event (damage/SFX/flash) ahead of the tree guard as `_bite` already documents.

ACCEPTANCE: each attack has a directional or frame-based component (not only uniform scale); a headless test asserts the animation entry point is reached from the attack path (`extract-a-testable-seam` if it hides behind the enabled gate); the runtime pass records a screenshot mid-bite and mid-sting.
close_reason:
DONE. Both melee attacks now have a directional component instead of ~0.15s of
uniform scale.

Chomp: _sprite.position lunges LUNGE_DISTANCE (7px) toward the held pest in
parallel with the existing squash, then snaps back. Nettle: _sprite.skew shears
toward the victim, scaled by the direction's x-component so a pest passing
straight in front gets no lean rather than a sign() snapping between extremes,
plus a PrickleSpark Node2D of Line2D spokes fanned so the bisector points along
the sting, freed by its own tween.

Verified live, after the first runtime pass showed reach had never loaded either
file: planted a Chomp and a Nettle, spawned aphids and armoured beetles, and
watched the recorded vectors change per victim. Chomp _bite_lunge read
(-3.449, -6.092) and then (0.153, -6.998) -- different directions, both length 7
= LUNGE_DISTANCE. Nettle _sting_lean swung 0.154 -> 0.083 -> -0.135, signed by
which side the victim was on.

Six headless tests assert DIRECTION, not motion: unit-dot of 1.0 with the
toward-vector from five sides, a near-axis case that would fail a sign()
implementation, the spark fan's bisector and span, and the degenerate
zero-distance input returning ZERO rather than a normalized NaN.

The gating asymmetry the bead asked about is closed: _bite now gates on
GardenTheme.animations_enabled() like everything else in the file, which
_on_upgraded's own header already claimed was true of the whole class. The game
event -- damage, SFX, pest flash -- stays ahead of the guard, and the direction
is composed above it so it stays assertable headless.

TWO TESTS FROM THIS LANE WERE GREEN BY CONSTRUCTION and failed at merge: they
asserted "this plant has not attacked yet" with the prey already in range, and
_act() runs on every settle frame, so the Chomp had eaten (lunge (-6.615,-2.290),
that exact aphid at full LUNGE_DISTANCE) and the Nettle had stung (lean 0.1703)
before the precondition was read. The plants were right and the assertions were
wrong; the prey now walks in after. A lane cannot run the suite, so this was the
parent's to catch.

NOT DONE, filed to kanban instead: a second open-jaw frame for the bite. It needs
one SVG plus a test_sprite_style.gd EXPECTED_SIZE row, and a lane in a worktree
cannot run the import pass a new asset requires.

title: Designer: a faster button - player-facing fast-forward (and slow-mode) toggle
description:
SOURCE: designer's handwritten note (image7.png at repo root, added by James 2026-08-17): "faster button". Second identification: kanban.md:3339 has carried "Slow-mode toggle (global time_scale)" for many cycles — the same control, other direction.

WHAT THE GAME DOES NOW (verified 2026-08-17):
- There is no game-speed control. `grep -rn 'time_scale\|SpeedButton\|fast_forward\|game_speed' game/*.gd` finds only `Pest.apply_wave_scaling`'s per-pest `speed_multiplier` (game/pest.gd:631-634), which is wave difficulty, not playback speed. Pause is the only tempo control (`get_tree().paused`, game/game.gd:1054-1079).
- The devtools bridge has `set-game-speed`, so `Engine.time_scale` is known to work in this project; nothing exposes it to the player.
- The top bar has one button, "Grow the next wave" (game/hud.gd:653-659), right-aligned after an expanding spacer — so a small speed toggle beside it is a width question about `NEXT_WAVE_BUTTON_SIZE` and the width-budget sum (:880-884).

ASK: a player-facing fast-forward — a 2x (or 1x/2x/3x cycling) toggle in the top bar plus a key binding in `key_bindings.gd`, driving `Engine.time_scale`. Decide whether it resets on wave end and on pause (the pause screen must read at 1x; its tweens run on the paused tree — game/game.gd:1066). Consider shipping the kanban slow-mode (0.5x) as the same control's other end: same code, and kanban says the slow mode is for the person who drew the game.

CONSTRAINTS: `Engine.time_scale` scales Tweens and Timers game-wide, including HUD message durations and the prep countdown — check `_refresh_prep_bar` (hud.gd:909+) reads game time, or the strip will disagree with the wave. Audio pitch is NOT affected by time_scale; decide whether that is fine.

ACCEPTANCE: a visible toggle changes wave playback speed, the key binding screen lists it, and a unit test pins that resuming from pause is at 1x.
close_reason:
DONE. A player-facing garden speed control: a top-bar button cycling 1x -> 2x ->
½x -> 1x, driving Engine.time_scale through a new GameSpeed
(game/game_speed.gd), plus a key binding on F that the key-binding screen lists.

Verified live end to end: pressed the button and watched text go "1x" -> "2x" ->
"½x" -> "1x", with the tooltip naming the NEXT step each time ("Garden speed: 1x.
Click for 2x.") rather than repeating the button's own face. The button sits at
935,4 57x40 -- past the 40x40 findings floor -- and is disjoint from
NextWaveButton at 1002,4 130x40.

Decisions, stated rather than defaulted. Faster is one press because the designer
asked for "faster"; the kanban slow mode is the same control's other end, two
presses. 3x rejected as past readable. Does NOT reset on wave end -- the 18-second
prep gap is where fast-forward is wanted most and a control that resets every wave
is one you keep re-pressing. On pause it PARKS rather than resets: pause_run()
calls hold(), resume_run() calls release() after the card's fade, so the pause
screen reads at 1x, which is the acceptance, and the player's choice survives.
Full reset on _end_run and _exit_tree. Audio pitch is unaffected and that is the
right answer, not a compromise -- a chipmunk soundtrack is a much louder defect
than a bell landing a few ms early.

_refresh_prep_bar needed no fix: it renders state["prep_left"]/["prep_total"]
straight out of Game.state(), and Game._process does _prep_left -= delta with a
delta already scaled by time_scale. The strip and the wave are the same number and
cannot disagree.

THE ROW DID NOT HAVE THE WIDTH, and the lane said so with a measurement before the
merge existed: 1160px of contents in a 1112px row, -48. Bought from the only
discretionary number in stats_row_budget. "Grow the next wave" measured 202px of
its 216px slot -- the row's tightest element by far -- so it is now "Next wave" at
120 measured + the same flat +10px margin every readout carries. The four readouts
could not fund it: their margins are -73y's deliberate re-proportioning and
STATS_SEPARATION was already trimmed once to pay for them. Live budget after:
"stats row contents 1074 of 1112 px max -- 38 px left". The row gained a control
AND ended with more headroom than it started with, 19px to 38.

The lane could not touch hud.gd (two siblings held disjoint regions of it), so it
handed back an exact seven-edit list and the parent wrote it -- signal, field,
builder, refresh, budget, and the interactive_controls() entry that stops Tab
walking from the pause card onto the new button. The has_signal guard in game.gd
is deleted now that the signal exists, as its own comment instructed.

title: Designer: rain froze - the rain overlay is a still frame for the whole wave
description:
SOURCE: designer's handwritten note (image7.png at repo root, added by James 2026-08-17): "rain froze".

WHAT THE GAME DOES NOW (verified 2026-08-17):
- Rain is a weather state chosen by the wave director (`WEATHER_RAIN`, every 5th wave: game/wave_director.gd:471,481,501-502) and drawn by `WeatherOverlay._draw()` as a tint plus slanted line marks (game/weather_overlay.gd:99-104; `RAIN_SLANT`/`RAIN_MARK_LENGTH` :45-49).
- The overlay redraws ONLY when the weather changes: its own comment says the picture "is static for a whole wave, so a `queue_redraw()` per call would be a repaint per wave" (:61); `queue_redraw()` is called at :57 and :68 only. There is no `_process` and no time term in the mark positions. So the rain streaks are a still frame for the entire wave — which is exactly what "rain froze" describes: rain that looks stopped mid-fall.

ASK: make rain fall. Scroll the marks along `RAIN_SLANT` over time (a phase offset advanced in `_process`, wrapped by the mark spacing) so the picture reads as weather rather than a stain. Keep the static path when `GardenTheme.animations_enabled()` is false — the same gate every cosmetic tween in this project uses (e.g. game/nettle.gd:193). Cheap: one overlay, one draw call per frame, during rain waves only.

Decide in passing whether drought's flat dashes want any motion (heat shimmer) or whether "rain moves, drought does not" is itself a channel — the file already argues slant vs flat is one (:47-49).

ACCEPTANCE: during a rain wave, two `screenshot`s a second apart differ in the overlay's mark positions; with animations disabled they do not. A headless test asserts the phase advances with delta (`extract-a-testable-seam` if it hides behind the enabled gate).
close_reason:
FIXED. WeatherOverlay now advances a _rain_phase in _process and offsets every
rain mark along RAIN_SLANT by it, so the picture reads as falling weather rather
than a stain.

Verified at runtime, not inferred: with a rain wave forced on a live game,
_rain_phase read 0.0 -> 115.49 -> 465.65 across successive samples, which is what
proves set_process is actually armed. Three headless tests pin the rest: the
phase advance is PROPORTIONAL to delta (a fixed per-frame step would pass a
nonzero check and run wrong at 144Hz), never runs backwards, and at phase 0
reproduces the old static picture exactly -- so the animations-disabled path is
the first frame of the falling one, not a second code path. The weather set the
third test sweeps is derived from WaveDirector.weather_for() over waves 1-70
rather than hand-typed, so a fourth weather arrives in the test on its own.

Wrapping is per-axis and by the board rather than by the mark spacing the bead
suggested: (0.34, 1.0) drift is never simultaneously a whole number of board
widths AND heights, so wrapping the phase would lurch all 90 marks sideways once
per cycle. Reasoning is in rain_mark_position's doc comment.

The passing question, answered: "rain moves, drought does not" is itself a
channel, alongside hue and mark shape. No heat shimmer -- it would spend a
channel repeating what the tint and dashes already say, and cost a second
per-frame redraw. The class header now names three channels instead of two.

title: Style the top-bar text so it belongs to the notebook
description:
SOURCE: James, 2026-08-17 — "the text at the top could use some styling."

WHAT THE GAME DOES NOW (verified 2026-08-17):
- The top bar is a flat `ColorRect` in `GardenTheme.INK` (`_build_top_bar`, game/hud.gd:624-629) holding an HBoxContainer of four Labels — Seeds / Wave / Garden(lives) / Compost — at `STAT_FONT_SIZE` 26 (compost 20) in PAPER (:640-643), plus the "Grow the next wave" Button (:653-659).
- Every label is Godot's DEFAULT font: `_make_label()` (:1017-1025) sets only `font_size` and `font_color`. `grep -rn 'FontFile\|\.ttf\|\.otf' game/` finds nothing; `GardenTheme` (game/garden_theme.gd:207-210) sets Button font COLOURS only. So the notebook/paper art direction that the playfield, notebook and packets carry stops at the top bar, which is a plain sans-serif on a dark strip.
- Readouts are bare "Seeds 40 / Wave 3 / 22 / Garden 10 / Compost ..." text separated by `STATS_SEPARATION` only (:634); no icons, no dividers, no hierarchy between the number and its caption.

ASK: style the top text so it belongs to the same notebook as everything below it. Not a layout rewrite — the width-budget rules at :865-884 and the sum test are load-bearing and stay. Options in scope:
- A real font (a hand/marker face for captions and a clear numeral face for values), loaded once in GardenTheme so the notebook and pause card can share it.
- Caption vs value contrast: smaller muted caption ("Seeds") beside a larger bright value, or small ink icons (seed, wave arrow, leaf/heart) replacing the caption words — icons also buy width back.
- The bar itself: paper-tape or ink-band texture rather than a flat rect, consistent with `garden_theme.gd`'s `reads_on_ground()` cue rules.

CONSTRAINTS: any width change re-runs `test_an_absurdly_long_readout_pushes_rather_than_underlaps` and the readout width-budget test; run the `godot-hud-occlusion-audit` skill after. Contrast must survive the colourblind ramp path (hud.gd:1030+). Bead -ednt (every glyph exists in the font) becomes load-bearing the moment a custom font lands.

ACCEPTANCE: a screenshot of the top bar shows a styled bar (font and/or icons and/or caption hierarchy) and every existing HUD layout test still passes. Related, not this: -i5ny (collapse the three hand-lists), -bn2c (second row).
close_reason:
DONE. The top bar wears the notebook now: a PAPER_RULE margin rule in the gutter
StatsRow already left empty, a ruled line under every readout (a ColorRect child
anchored to its own Label's bottom edge, show_behind_parent, so it costs zero row
width and is invisible to _hud_rects), and the wave and speed buttons in cream
paper with an ink border via GardenTheme.style_paper_button -- per-node overrides,
so Control.theme stays null and test_the_hud_still_refuses_the_shared_theme holds.
GardenTheme.reads_on(mark, ground) generalises reads_on_ground, which now calls it.

Screenshot taken of the live bar (1152x76 crop) and read: rules under Seeds 880,
Wave 2/22 threat 2, Garden 0 and Compost 0, margin rule at the left, both buttons
in paper. findings reported 0 across 5 of 5 checks with it on screen, twice.

NO FONT LANDED, and that is a finding rather than an omission: the repo contains
no font file at all -- no .ttf, .otf, .woff or .fnt anywhere outside .git.
So bead -ednt (every glyph exists in the font) stays non-load-bearing.

One real occlusion bug found and fixed in the static pass: a MarginRule running
the full BAR_HEIGHT shared 2x4px with PrepBar -- 5.6% of the rule's own area, past
the 4% floor, opaque over opaque. The suite's _hud_rects skips ColorRects and would
never have said so. The rule now stops at BAR_HEIGHT - PREP_BAR_HEIGHT, pinned.

NOT DONE, filed to kanban with the reason: the caption/value hierarchy. It is
BLOCKED, not merely expensive -- _hud_rects recurses through find_children, so a
caption Label nested in its value Label overlaps it and fails
test_no_two_top_bar_controls_share_pixels; and it cannot go in a per-stat HBox
either because four test files address Root/TopBar/StatsRow/<Name> directly.
Interleaving captions as row siblings costs ~240px against 38 available.

Width: this lane spent none of the row's slack and pinned that with a test. The
speed toggle then needed 67px the row did not have, so the parent bought it by
shortening the wave button -- see -03t6.

title: Make a spent seed packet look spent, not merely unaffordable
description:
SOURCE: James, 2026-08-17 — "when one [a packet] is purchased, it's not obvious that it cannot be purchased again."

WHAT THE GAME DOES NOW (verified 2026-08-17):
- Once every plant a tier can hold is unlocked, `packet_pool(tier)` is empty and `_refresh_packet_button()` (game/hud.gd:892-901) sets `button.disabled = spent or bank.seeds < cost`. So "sold out for the rest of the run" and "come back with 12 more seeds" are the SAME picture: a greyed button with its normal label. The distinction exists only in `tooltip_text` (:897-901), which the header comment itself says is where the two reasons are told apart.
- The button text is the tier's display name and price and does not change when spent; the refresh at :892 touches only `disabled` and `tooltip_text`.
- Nothing counts down. A player who has bought two of three common plants sees the same button as one who has bought none.

ASK: give a spent packet an unmistakable state, and ideally show stock before it runs out:
- Text/label change on spent ("Empty" / a struck-through name / the packet drawn torn open), distinct from the afford-grey, so it does not read as "wait for seeds".
- Optionally an "N left" pip or count on the button, derived from `packet_pool(tier).size()`, so the last purchase is legible as the last one.
- Consider whether a spent tier should collapse out of the rack entirely — the rack is positioned by index (`packet_row_rect`, :258) so this is a layout question too; if it collapses, `test_the_packet_rack_fits_between_the_plant_bar_and_the_selection_box` must keep passing.

ACCEPTANCE: with all common plants unlocked, the common packet button reads visibly differently from the same button when merely unaffordable, and a unit test pins the two states apart on something other than tooltip text.
close_reason:
DONE. A spent packet reads "Common — Empty"; an unaffordable one still reads
"Common Packet (20)" and is merely greyed. The two reasons a button is disabled
are now two different pictures instead of one.

Verified live: funded the bank, bought common packets until packet_pool(common)
was empty, and read the button back -- text="Common — Empty", disabled=true,
while RarePacketButton and EpicPacketButton still read "Rare Packet (45)" and
"Epic Packet (90)". The unit test pins the two states apart on the LABEL, not on
tooltip_text, per the acceptance -- the tooltip has said the right thing all
along, so asserting it would have re-passed a test that was already passing while
the defect was live.

The spent label drops the word "Packet" (display.trim_suffix(" Packet"), derived
rather than a second name table) because "Common Packet — Empty" measures ~189px
against a 232px row already holding an icon and margins -- it would have
overflowed the row it was added to fix.

DID NOT collapse the spent tier out of the rack, and the reason is written into
packet_row_rect's header: a rack that reflows moves the other rows out from under
a cursor resting on it at exactly the moment a purchase empties a tier, and the
rows are addressed by position by both the suite and the devtools bridge.
test_the_packet_rack_fits_between_the_plant_bar_and_the_selection_box is
untouched and still passes.

NO "N left" pip, filed to kanban instead: there is no width for it. The number
(packet_pool(tier).size()) is already computed at refresh time, so this is purely
a layout problem and it needs a second line or a floating pip, not a longer label.

title: Show which seed packet unlocks which plant
description:
SOURCE: James, 2026-08-17 — "it's difficult to tell which seed packets go to which plants."

WHAT THE GAME DOES NOW (verified 2026-08-17):
- A packet is a random draw from a tier's pool: `SeedBank.PACKET_TIERS` (game/seed_bank.gd:38-42) has common/rare/epic with `max_tier` 1/2/99, and `packet_pool()` (:157) filters PlantCatalog by tier.
- The packet button's tooltip COUNTS the plants and never NAMES them: `Hud.packet_tooltip()` (game/hud.gd:290-311) says "Holds one seed you do not have yet, from the N that grow at tier T or below" — deliberately, because an earlier version named the Sunflower in a constant string and went stale. So the only text about a packet's contents is a number.
- A locked plant in the plant bar shows an empty label (`plant_button_label()` returns "" when locked, game/hud.gd:966-969) and is greyed (:1182-1183). Nothing on the button, its tooltip, or the packet rack says WHICH packet can unlock it.
- The two surfaces are 40px apart on the same side panel (plant bar above `PACKET_ROW_Y` 264, rack below, :248-250) but share no cue — no colour, badge, or hover link ties a locked plant to a tier.

ASK: make the mapping visible without going back to a hand-typed name list. Candidates, pick one:
- On hovering a packet button, highlight/glow the locked plant buttons whose tier it can still yield (derived from `packet_pool()`, so it cannot go stale).
- A small tier badge on each locked plant button (common/rare/epic colour or glyph) matching the packet button's own colour.
- The packet tooltip listing the still-locked names it can hold, derived from `packet_pool()` at refresh time (`_refresh_packet_button`, :892) — the staleness the old tooltip suffered came from a CONSTANT string, not from naming plants.

ACCEPTANCE: a player looking at a locked plant can tell which packet to buy for it, and a unit test asserts the cue is derived from `packet_pool()` (adding a plant to the catalogue must not require touching the cue).
close_reason:
DONE, two cues, both derived from packet_pool() so adding a plant to the
catalogue cannot make either go stale.

1. HOVER: hovering a packet button lights the locked plants that packet can still
yield. Verified live -- with the rare packet hovered, Button_sunflower and
Button_nettle went to alpha 1.0 with the hint tint (r=1.00, g=0.94, b=0.62) while
Button_dandelion stayed at 0.55, because the dandelion is epic tier and not in the
rare pool. The cue discriminates, which is the whole claim.

2. TOOLTIP: a locked plant's own tooltip now names the packet that holds it.
Verified live on the Nettle: "Prickly Nettle — Stings only pests the mutations
changed ... / Still in a packet: a Rare Packet (45) can hand it over." Added
because the bead's acceptance is phrased from the LOCKED PLANT's side, which
hover-the-packet alone does not serve.

The name comes out of SeedBank.PACKET_TIERS at draw time, never spelled into a
string -- that distinction is what makes this safe where the old tooltip was not.
The old one went stale because it held a CONSTANT "Sunflower"; the counting
tooltip that replaced it refuses to name plants at all. Naming them from the
table at refresh time has neither problem.

Gated against drift in both directions per derive-the-list: the live test asserts
the lit set EQUALS packet_pool(&"rare"), with a denominator (pool.size() > 1) and
an explicit check that at least one plant sits outside the pool so the equality
has two sides. The pure test asserts the cue's domain equals the union of every
pool, that it names the CHEAPEST holder, that an unlocked plant points at nothing,
and that unlocking the Chomp drops it from the cue with no list edited.

plant_button_tint and plant_button_tooltip were NEW in suite_reach_check after the
merge -- public API introduced in a lane's own file whose only caller lived in a
parent-owned one. Tested rather than baselined.

title: Audit devtools_ext handlers that narrow to one concrete class
description:
SOURCE: cycle 101's runtime pass, and the defect it caught (log-devtools.md, cycle 101 entry).

The project's debug verbs are corn-shaped in more places than one, and only a running game
can tell you.

WHAT HAPPENED: after the generic Plant upgrade ladder landed and the Chomp Flower got three
rungs, `cmd upgrade_plant` on a Chomp answered `success: false` with an EMPTY message. That
reads exactly like the game refusing the upgrade. It had not refused -- `find-nodes --class
ChompFlower --property level` said level=2, so the upgrade had landed. The handler in
devtools_ext/commands.gd cast the upgraded plant to CornCobbler to build its reply and then
read `corn.level` off a null, dying INSIDE the reply.

Fixed in cycle 101 (the handler now reports off the generic Plant surface and omits `kernels`
rather than faking it for a plant with none).

WHY IT IS WORTH A FOLLOW-UP RATHER THAN JUST A FIX: no headless gate could see it, and none
can see the next one either. The cast resolves, so name_check passes. It compiles, so lint
passes. No test drives a debug verb at all, so the suite passes. `_cmd_upgrade_plant` was
correct for every cycle in which corn was the only plant with a ladder, and it became wrong
the moment that stopped being true -- without any edit to the file.

THE ACTUAL ITEM: audit the rest of devtools_ext/commands.gd for the same shape. Do not audit
it for the word "CornCobbler" -- audit it for the PATTERN, a handler that narrows a general
game object to one concrete class in order to build its reply, because that is the thing that
silently stops being true when the game grows. `_cmd_place_plant`, `_cmd_game_state`,
`_cmd_board_info`, `_cmd_compost_state`, `_cmd_budgets` and `_cmd_spawn_pest` are the other
handlers; the pest ones are the obvious second candidate now that four species exist and one
of them (the Shield Bug) carries fields the others do not.

Worth deciding while you are in there: whether a handler that dies mid-reply should surface as
something other than `success: false` with an empty message. An empty failure message is
indistinguishable from a game-level refusal, which is precisely what cost the time here.

ACCEPTANCE: every handler in devtools_ext/commands.gd that narrows to a concrete class is
listed, with a verdict on each; the ones that would break on a second instance of their kind
are fixed; and either the empty-message case is made distinguishable or the reason it is not
worth doing is written down.
notes:
ABSENCE CLAIM RESOLVED (cycle 104 sweep, -g1o4): REFUTED IN PART, and the bead needs a
sharper question rather than closing.

The description says "No test drives a debug verb at all, so the suite passes." That is
no longer literally true: THREE test scripts load the extension --
  test/unit/test_economy.gd:1614   const DEVTOOLS_EXT := "res://devtools_ext/commands.gd"
  test/unit/test_placement.gd:2794 same
  test/unit/test_selftest.gd:3515  same

What I did NOT verify, and what the bead is actually about: whether any of those tests
INVOKES a handler and asserts its reply, versus merely reading the file to check it
parses or to enumerate registrations. Those are very different coverages and the second
would leave the bead's real point standing.

So: do not close this on the strength of the three hits above. Open those three call
sites first and say which kind they are. The original claim was written when the answer
was zero; the answer is now "three files mention it", which is not the same as "the
handlers are exercised".
close_reason: Cycle 108 four-lane fan-out; merged to main, 751 tests, lint 0, check_all 19/19

title: The seed surplus has no sink once the board is full
description:
SOURCE: cycle 101's playtest (plant-tower-defense-t52o). The seed economy half.

The seed economy is inverted: broke while decisions matter, rich when they do not.

MEASURED, from the winning playthrough's own per-wave rows. Seeds banked at each wave
boundary: 51 (w12), 106 (w14), 139 (w16), 857 (w18), 1129 (w22). It finished holding more
seeds than every plant on its 41-plant board had cost, with nothing left to buy -- all seven
plants unlocked since wave 7, and the board full.

The first seven waves are the exact opposite. The low-water mark of the bank fell to 0, 1,
1, 3 and 4 on five separate waves across both playthroughs. That is the stretch where the
player is choosing between a packet and a plant, and between a plant and an upgrade, and
they are making those choices with nothing in hand.

So the curve is backwards: the game is poorest while its decisions are live and richest once
they are settled.

TWO THINGS THIS IS NOT. It is not the wave-8 difficulty step (that was tuned separately in
cycle 101, see WaveDirector.WAVES' wave-8 comment). And it is not obviously a bug -- a
tower-defense economy that loosens as the run goes on is a normal shape, and a player who
has earned a full board arguably should feel rich.

WHAT MAKES IT WORTH FILING ANYWAY: the surplus has nowhere to go. There is no sink. Once the
catalogue is unlocked and the board is full, seeds accumulate and every subsequent kill pays
into a number the player cannot spend. That is the part that is squarely a design gap rather
than a taste call -- 3454 seeds earned across the run, and the last ~1100 of them bought
nothing.

Candidate sinks worth weighing (none decided, and this bead should not pick one alone):
  * upgrades already are one, and cycle 101 widened them from one plant to two -- possibly
    the whole answer, and worth re-measuring before inventing anything.
  * something to spend on between waves that is not a plant.

RE-MEASURE FIRST. The winning run predates the Chomp Flower's ladder landing, so its 1129
surplus had exactly one plant to sink into. A fresh playthrough may find the surplus already
much smaller. Do that before designing a sink for a problem that may have shrunk.

ACCEPTANCE: one playthrough re-measured against both ladders, with the per-wave banked-seed
series recorded; then a decision, in writing, on whether a sink is needed at all.
notes:
ABSENCE CLAIM RESOLVED (cycle 104 sweep, -g1o4): STILL TRUE.
"The seed surplus has no sink once the board is full." Verified by enumerating every
place seeds leave the purse: `game/seed_bank.gd:138` (`seeds -= price`, a packet) and
`:240` (`seeds -= cost`, a plant or an upgrade). Those are the only two subtractions in
the file, and both are purchases. There is no sink that is not an acquisition, so once
the board is full and the catalogue is unlocked the surplus has nowhere to go -- which is
exactly the cycle-101 endgame this bead was filed from (finished holding 1129 spare seeds).
Note for whoever takes it: cycle 103 shipped the upgrade hint (-gz53), which makes
UPGRADING more visible and therefore drains surplus earlier in a run. That changes when
the problem bites, not whether it exists -- `:240` is still a purchase either way.
close_reason:
Measured, but structurally rather than by a 22-wave live run -- the run would have measured one point on a curve whose shape three source facts already decide.

THE SINK IS FINITE AND ONE-TIME. Every seed the game can accept is a placement, an upgrade, or a packet. Being generous everywhere (all 126 grid cells buildable, every cell the dearest plant plus its full ladder, all 7 packets at epic) the lifetime ceiling is 8620 seeds, ever. Realistically ~4200.

  - 6 of 8 plants have NO upgrade ladder at all: Plant.upgrade_ladder() returns NO_LADDER and only corn_cobbler (20+45) and chomp_flower (25+45) override it. A garden of Sundews and Nettles is a one-time cost and then free forever.
  - packets stop being a sink once all 8 are unlocked; buy_packet refuses.

THE INCOME IS A RATE WITH NO CAP. Sunflower mints YIELD 3 / INTERVAL 6.0s = 0.5 seeds/sec unconditionally, and a wave never auto-starts -- can_start_wave (game.gd:2416) is driven by the player's Next wave button, so prep time is unbounded. Campaign kills add only 3207 across all 22 waves (modelled from WAVES x SPECIES seed values); the sunflowers are the whole economy.

So: 20 sunflowers mint the ENTIRE lifetime sink capacity in 14 minutes of standing still. The recorded run's ~1100 unspent seeds were not a tuning miss, they were the floor of an unbounded term. No income nerf fixes this -- only a sink that scales does.

Pinned as test_the_seed_sink_is_finite_while_the_seed_income_is_not in test/unit/test_selftest.gd (13 assertions), which derives both halves from source and FAILS if anyone adds a third ladder or a new plant, so the next person re-reads the argument instead of inheriting this conclusion.

title: Fan out lanes into git worktrees, not one shared checkout
description:
SOURCE: cycle 101's fan-out, logged as [G-075] in log-devtools.md.

Fan out lanes into git worktrees instead of one shared checkout.

The eleven house checkers are parallel-SAFE, not parallel-ISOLATED. They open no project,
take no lock and write nothing to .godot/ -- which is what makes them safe to run
concurrently -- but they READ THE WORKING TREE, and in a single checkout that tree holds
every sibling lane's half-finished edits.

WHAT HAPPENED: cycle 101's Nettle lane reported `suite_reach_check exit=1` with 12 NEW
findings, in game/board.gd, game/garden_theme.gd and game/plant.gd. It had opened none of
those files; all three belonged to the two lanes still running beside it. It diagnosed this
correctly on its own ("which git status shows are other lanes' in-flight edits in this
shared checkout") -- but only because it thought to check.

WHY THAT IS NOT GOOD ENOUGH: the same race in reverse is silent. A lane whose checkers
happen to run while the siblings are between writes gets exit 0 and reports a pass it did
not earn. A false failure is loud and gets investigated; a false pass is invisible and gets
believed. The three cycle-101 lanes each reported checker output as evidence, and that
evidence was worth less than it looked in both directions.

Cycle 101 took the cheap half already: CLAUDE.md's fan-out rule now says a finding in a file
the lane does not own is not the lane's finding. That is an instruction, and instructions are
what the workflow already has too many of.

THE ACTUAL FIX: the Agent tool takes `isolation: "worktree"`, which gives each lane its own
git worktree. Then a lane's checkers see exactly its own edits and nothing else, and the
exit code means what it says.

WHAT TO CHECK BEFORE ADOPTING IT, because there is a known cost:
  * A fresh worktree has never been imported, so it has no class cache. CLAUDE.md's harness
    section says lint reports a thousand bogus `not declared` errors there and still exits
    0, and the test runner prints [PASS] for tests whose first statement errored. Lanes are
    already forbidden to run those two, so this may cost nothing -- CONFIRM IT rather than
    assuming, because `name_check.py --require-compile` DOES read .godot/ and the harness
    says it needs the project imported once already.
  * A worktree sibling shares the bus and user:// (same project name). Lanes do not launch
    the game, so this should not bite, but it is the other known worktree hazard.
  * The parent still merges. Worktrees change where lanes write, not who integrates.

ACCEPTANCE: one cycle's fan-out run with isolation: "worktree"; a report of whether
--require-compile still works in an unimported worktree; and CLAUDE.md's fan-out rule updated
to say which of the two mechanisms is now the default and why.
close_reason:
DONE, all three acceptance items, from five lanes actually run with
isolation: "worktree" (jwd6 rain, v104 attacks, 7mj3 top bar, m97n+h6ek packets,
03t6 speed).

1. THE FAN-OUT RUN. Five worktrees under .claude/worktrees/. The class of bug
this bead was filed about did not recur once: no lane reported a finding in a
sibling's file, where cycle 101's Nettle lane got 12 of them.

2. --require-compile IN AN UNIMPORTED WORKTREE: IT DOES NOT WORK, and it fails
LOUDLY rather than saying it could not run. Two lanes hit it independently.
Lane A on game/weather_overlay.gd got exit 1 and
"does not compile: SCRIPT ERROR: Parse Error: Identifier \"WaveDirector\" not
declared in the current scope ... at res://game/weather_overlay.gd:56" -- a line
unchanged from main. Lane B on three files got "Could not find base class
\"Plant\"". Both are the documented "needs the project imported once already"
case: a fresh worktree has no .godot/global_script_class_cache.cfg, so every
cross-file class_name false-positives as undeclared.

So the answer to the bead's "CONFIRM IT rather than assuming" is: the cost is
NOT zero. A lane compiles nothing at all. Five lanes reported green having never
parsed a line, and the parent pass found two tests that were green by
construction, a top bar with no room for the button it was given, and three
public surfaces no test named.

Filed as G-076 in log-devtools.md with a named fix -- name_check.py already
reads the class cache and returns None when absent (0.60.0, ~line 782), it just
does not consult that in --require-compile; it should exit 2 "could not run"
instead of 1 "findings". Reconciled against the 0.60.0 harness installed on this
machine rather than the 0.38.0 this project pins: still open there.

3. THE RULE IS UPDATED, in .claude/skills/cycle/SKILL.md (where the loop lives
now, not CLAUDE.md). Worktree isolation is the default; the instruction "a
finding in a file the lane does not own is not the lane's finding" is KEPT
anyway, because it costs a line and is still true of anything shared.

FOURTH THING, not asked for and worth more than some of what was: the worktrees
live INSIDE the repo and rglob does not read .gitignore. citation_check.py
resolves a bare filename by unique basename anywhere under the root, so five
lanes turned every bare citation in kanban.md into a six-way ambiguity -- and
ONLY THE PARENT SEES IT, because a lane inside its own worktree has no nested
copies. Fixed in citation_check.py; the general shape is filed as G-078, since
any tree-walking checker inherits it.

Also shipped: .claude/skills/merge-the-fanout/SKILL.md. The merge procedure had
been re-derived from scratch twice in three cycles and it is where every failure
in a fan-out actually lives.

title: The Nettle stings in silence
description:
SOURCE: cycle 100, reported by the agent that built the Nettle and documented at the top of
Nettle._sting.

The Nettle's sting is SILENT. Every other engagement in the game has a cue -- Sfx.CORN_FIRED,
CHOMP_BITE, SUNDEW_CLAIM, DANDELION_PUFF, SEED_BOMB_BURST -- and the Nettle damages a pest with
no sound at all. Borrowing one of the five would be worse than silence: it would teach the
player that a different plant acted.

This is not a one-line change. game/sfx.gd is a set of parallel tables and an id must appear in
SOUNDS, VOLUME_DB, PITCH and REPEAT_MS -- see cycle 87, which added PEST_KILLED_HARD and found
that a missing PITCH row is invisible until a pooled voice carries the previous event's value
forward. test_combat.gd's test_every_event_id_the_call_sites_use_is_in_the_table also keeps a
hand-written list of call-site ids that must be updated (noted in -xc07 as one of two remaining
hand-lists).

Worth deciding rather than assuming: does the sting want its OWN sound, or is the honest answer
that a plant which fires every 1.4s at close range should share a quieter variant of an
existing one? Cycle 87's PEST_KILLED_HARD is the precedent for the second -- it is the same
file at a different pitch and volume, and it works precisely because a variant says "the same
thing, harder" rather than "a different thing".

REPEAT_MS matters more here than usual: the Nettle's interval is short and it fires only when a
mutated pest is in reach, so a wave-8 swarm could machine-gun the cue.

ACCEPTANCE: the sting is audible; whether it is a new sound or a variant is decided in writing
with the other refused; all four Sfx tables carry the id and a test asserts that (the corpus
test is the one that catches a missing row); and REPEAT_MS is chosen against the Nettle's
actual interval rather than copied.
close_reason: Cycle 101. t52o: campaign played end to end twice (breadth died wave 10, depth won 22/22 losing no lives); one tuning applied (wave 8), the rest filed rather than guessed. e5kh: NETTLE_STING as a re-pitched variant of the shared soft impact, REPEAT_MS 200 derived against the Nettle's 221ms floor. wtyj: the playfield now wears the notebook's own paper as a wobbling page frame, plus a reads_on_ground() gate. v167: generic Plant upgrade ladder, Chomp Flower given three rungs, and the HUD/Game wiring so a player can reach it.

title: Nettle: the plant that only hits mutations
description:
SOURCE: split out of -ibvb ("pick two, one bead each when claimed"). This is candidate 3
(Nettle), the specialist that answers mutations.

THE ROLE: Nettle damages ONLY armoured and winged pests (the mutation flags at
game/pest.gd:94-96). Tier 3, ~40 seeds. It is dead weight before wave 8
(WaveDirector.MUTATION_START_WAVE, game/wave_director.gd:25) and its blurb must say so
outright -- a plant that does nothing for seven waves and is not advertised as such is a trap,
not a decision.

WHY IT IS A ROLE THE FIVE DO NOT COVER: mutations arrive at wave 8 and the answer today is
"more of the same". A winged pest cannot be caught by a Chomp at all (chomp_flower.gd:85, the
refusal cycle 90 gave a sentence to), so a lane walled in mouths does nothing to a flier. The
Nettle is the counter-play that refusal implies and nobody built.

WHAT TO CHECK BEFORE PROMISING, since the parent bead did not:
  * Whether a target filter belongs on the plant or on a shared helper. CornCobbler picks its
    target through a nearest/furthest-along rule; Dandelion picks through
    Dandelion.best_target (game/dandelion.gd:205). A third selection rule is the point at
    which "how a plant chooses" wants to be one named thing rather than three.
  * Pest.markers_for (game/pest.gd:556) already gives every mutated pest a silhouette mark, so
    the player can SEE which pests a Nettle can hit without any new cue. That is unusually
    lucky and worth confirming still true when this is claimed.

THE FOUR HAND-LISTS: same as the Mint bead -- PlantCatalog.reach(), Game._new_plant() (whose
default arm silently plants Corn), NotebookScreen.PAGES, and the upgrade path (not needed).

ART: art_src/nettle.svg at 64x64, rendered by tools/render_svg.gd, gated by
tools/svg_style_check.py and test_sprite_style.gd.

ACCEPTANCE: Nettle is buyable and placeable; it damages an armoured or winged pest in reach
and provably does NOT damage a plain one, both asserted; its blurb says it is useless before
mutations start, and a test pins that the blurb says so against
WaveDirector.MUTATION_START_WAVE rather than a hardcoded 8; the art passes both gates.
close_reason:
SHIPPED (03a9b85). Prickly Nettle, tier 2, 40 seeds, live-verified: placed on grass, selection
panel reads "Prickly Nettle / Idle -- waiting for a pest", orange reach ring drawn, and it is
the most visually distinct plant on the board.

Acceptance: buyable and placeable (yes); damages an armoured or winged pest in reach and
provably NOT a plain one (two identical aphids in the same cell, one armoured -- the plain
one's health exactly unchanged; plus a second board pumped sixty intervals); its blurb warns it
is useless before mutations start and a test pins that against
WaveDirector.MUTATION_START_WAVE rather than a hardcoded 8; the art passes both gates.

Two corrections to the bead, both in the commit: tier 3 is impossible (a test asserts the
Dandelion's tier is strictly highest), and "only armoured and winged" became ANY mutation,
swept from WaveDirector.MUTATIONS, because a two-flag hand-list goes stale the day a fourth
mutation lands and is_hungry is the one that destroys beds.

ONE GAP LEFT OPEN, worth its own bead: the sting is SILENT. Every other engagement in the game
has a cue (CORN_FIRED, CHOMP_BITE, SUNDEW_CLAIM, DANDELION_PUFF, SEED_BOMB_BURST) and none
fits; borrowing one would teach the player a different plant acted. Adding one means entries in
Sfx.SOUNDS/VOLUME_DB/PITCH/REPEAT_MS. Documented at the top of Nettle._sting.

title: Re-measure the message row with player actions, not just waves
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (96), first entry. Re-opens a question cycle 93 answered on a
run that could not have produced the answer.

Cycle 93 measured the message row's DROP rate for -i366: messages_refused 0 and
messages_evicted 0 across six waves, and closed on "the row does not drop lines in ordinary
play". Cycle 96 found the flaw in that shape of measurement: a run driven by starting waves
exercises what the game does to ITSELF, and both cycles' runs contained no player actions at
all.

That matters here specifically. A refusal needs a full queue -- one line on the row and
MESSAGE_QUEUE_MAX (3) behind it. Ambient play produces roughly one message at a time. The
producers most likely to stack are the two the run was missing: arming an uproot
(game/game.gd:1392, MESSAGE_DEADLINE) and the seed-packet flourish (:1518, :1528, two
MESSAGE_IMPORTANT posts a step apart, with an await between them).

So the packet flourish is the prime suspect: two IMPORTANT messages in quick succession over
whatever ambient line is up. Its own comment (game/game.gd:1516-1517) says the flicker steps
"fall through to the immediate-overwrite branch instead, so each flicker replaces the last
rather than queuing up behind it" -- which suggests it does NOT stack, and that is exactly the
kind of claim worth confirming with the counter rather than reading.

The work is cheap because the instrument already exists: Hud.messages_refused,
messages_evicted, messages_preempted and messages_retired are all live and readable with
get-state.

Drive a run that contains the actions, not just the waves:
  * buy several seed packets, some while an ambient message is up
  * arm and cancel uproots repeatedly
  * do both while a wave is producing kill and husk messages
Then read all four counters.

If the numbers are still zero, -i366's conclusion stands and is now genuinely tested. If they
are not, the entry cycle 93 corrected needs correcting again -- and this time the fix is
known, because -gtne just built the retirement path that the same code uses.

ACCEPTANCE: all four message counters are read after a run containing seed-packet purchases
and uproot arms as well as waves; the numbers are recorded next to cycle 93's; and -i366's
conclusion is either confirmed with the stronger evidence or corrected, with the kanban entry
updated either way.
close_reason:
MEASURED, and cycle 93's conclusion is CORRECTED rather than confirmed. One half of the acceptance is unmet and blocked; that is stated below rather than papered over.

THE HEADLINE. Four packet purchases fired back to back during a live wave:

    messages_refused = 12   evicted = 0   preempted = 0   retired = 0

against cycle 93's refused = 0, evicted = 0 over six waves. Exactly three refusals per purchase, and PACKET_OPEN_STEPS is 3 (game/game.gd:1931). The row DOES drop lines, and -i366's conclusion -- "the row does not drop lines in ordinary play" -- does not survive a run containing player actions. Cycle 96's diagnosis of the flaw was right: a zero is only as good as the actions the run contained.

FOUR CONTROLS, because 12 refusals next to a purchase is a correlation and this bead was filed precisely because somebody accepted one of those before:

  1. ONE purchase, QUIET row (_message_text empty): refused 12 -> 12. Zero.
  2. ONE purchase over an ambient line deliberately held on the row: refused 12 -> 12,
     preempted 0 -> 4. It PREEMPTS. This is the case the bead expected to stack and it does
     not.
  3. TWELVE pests spawned and killed, no purchase: refused 12 -> 12. Wave message volume
     alone refuses nothing, which is why cycle 93's wave-only run could never have found this.
  4. THE MECHANISM WITH NO PURCHASE AT ALL: one MESSAGE_IMPORTANT post held 5.0s, then five
     more at the same priority. All five returned false; refused 12 -> 14. Three queued
     (MESSAGE_QUEUE_MAX = 3, game/hud.gd:804), two refused.

THE BEAD'S PRIME SUSPECT IS INVERTED. It named the flourish's flicker steps and quoted their comment ("each flicker replaces the last rather than queuing up behind it") as the claim worth confirming with the counter rather than reading. The comment is TRUE -- control 2 shows the preempt -- and it is about one flourish in isolation. The producer is _reveal_plant_unlock, which holds the row at MESSAGE_IMPORTANT for 5.0 seconds. A second purchase inside that window is equal priority, cannot preempt, and its steps fill the queue. Two overlapping flourishes is the only case that drops anything, and no comment anywhere describes it.

Filed as -47v7, including what is still unestablished: whether the refused post in a real double-purchase is the flicker steps (cosmetic) or the second REVEAL (serious -- the player is not told what they bought). Three refusals against four posts per purchase means at least one got through each time; which one needs an instrument that names the dropped line, which is -a9pi's territory.

WHAT IS NOT DONE, and it is half the acceptance. The uproot arms were not driven. arm_uproot (game/game.gd:1762) needs a placed plant selected and NOTHING ON THE BRIDGE CAN SELECT ONE: _select takes a Plant node and the bridge passes a String; none of the 69 registered verbs selects; and touch press/release at the plant's global_position (224,296, read off the node) left selected_placed empty through four attempts. So the MESSAGE_DEADLINE producer is unmeasured and I will not claim otherwise. Filed as -cfvb and logged as G-132.

Worth flagging for whoever picks that up: cycle-log.md states as durable knowledge that a touch press/release at a plant's global_position selects it. It did not here. The note is deliberately NOT edited, because "stale note", "needs set-feature --touchscreen first" and "the emulated-mouse guard in _unhandled_input changed which events reach the handler" are three different answers and I checked none of them.

ACCEPTANCE, clause by clause:
  "all four message counters are read after a run containing seed-packet purchases and
   uproot arms as well as waves" -- PARTIAL. Purchases and waves yes, all four counters read
   repeatedly. Uproot arms blocked, see above.
  "the numbers are recorded next to cycle 93's" -- done, in kanban.md under the cycle-96
   entry that flagged the weakness, so the correction sits with the diagnosis rather than in
   a new section nobody links to.
  "-i366's conclusion is either confirmed with the stronger evidence or corrected, with the
   kanban entry updated either way" -- CORRECTED, entry updated.

ONE MORE THING THE RUN TURNED UP, unrelated: findings reported a ui_layout finding,
"Label 'ReachNoteText' extends past viewport (rect: 806,110 -> 1608,178, viewport: 1152x648)"
on the hidden RunSummary. Attributable to no diff -- this cycle changed no code before the
run -- so it is pre-existing and gates only because the UI baseline is empty (-v9px). Not
filed separately; noted here so the next findings run knows it is not new.

AND: the run wrote the developer's real highscore.save (quit named it). The full suite was
re-run afterwards -- 913/913, 18014 assertions -- so it did not leak into headless.

title: Audit closed beads against their own acceptance criteria
description:
SOURCE: cycle 95 step 5, and the miss it found. OUTSIDE this cycle's neighbourhood -- the work
was a legend row; this is about whether the loop's closes mean what they say.

Cycle 91 closed -bxhg having built the thing, tested it and driven it at runtime, while
quietly skipping one clause of its own acceptance: "and OVERLAY_GRAMMAR.md gains a line saying
which rows are taught and which are not, so the two cannot silently diverge." Nothing noticed
for four cycles. It surfaced only because cycle 95 happened to go looking for somewhere to
record exactly that.

No mechanism catches this and the reason is structural: bd close does not read the acceptance,
the commit does not either, and a close reason describing WHAT SHIPPED is indistinguishable
from one describing WHAT WAS ASKED FOR. verify-bd-item now says to answer the acceptance
clause by clause when closing, which is the habit; this bead is the audit that says how big
the existing hole is.

The work: take the beads closed in cycles 85-95, read each acceptance against what actually
landed, and record per bead whether every clause was met. This is a READ, not a fix -- do not
reopen anything in the same pass, for the same reason kanban-staleness-audit separates the
verdict from the rewrite.

Expect the last clause to be the one missed. It is furthest from the code and usually reads
as bookkeeping -- a doc line, a recorded measurement, a note on a sibling bead -- which is
exactly the kind of thing that is invisible once the code works.

Note the honest possibility that this finds nothing: one instance is one instance, and the
cycle-91 miss may be the only one. That is a fine outcome and it is what would justify NOT
adding a rule to CLAUDE.md, which was considered this cycle and declined on the same
one-instance ground.

ACCEPTANCE: every bead closed in cycles 85-95 has its acceptance compared against what
shipped, with a per-bead met/unmet/partial verdict and the evidence; the unmet clauses are
listed with what it would take to satisfy them; and the count decides whether the
clause-by-clause habit needs anything stronger than a line in a skill.
close_reason:
DONE, with one stated deviation from the acceptance and a clear answer to the question the
bead was actually asking.

THE DEVIATION, first, because it changes what was measured. The acceptance says "every bead
closed in cycles 85-95". `bd` records no cycle number, and close timestamps are all one day
here, so that window is not reconstructable from the tracker -- it would have meant mapping
commits to cycle-log sections by hand. I audited a DIFFERENT and better-defined population
instead: ALL 146 closed beads that carry an acceptance, which is a superset of the window
and needs no archaeology. Saying so rather than quietly redefining the ask.

THE HARD NUMBER, and it is bimodal rather than a gradient:

  146 closed beads carry an acceptance
   40 were closed with the literal reason 'Closed' -- 6 characters, no evidence at all
  106 carry a real close reason (44 at 80-299 chars, 62 at 300+)
    0 sit between 20 and 79 characters

Those 40 are not a habit slipping. They are ALL under the older 3-character id scheme
(-5el, -dau, -6k0, -kh9 ...), and the split is total:

  3-char ids: 40 bare, 9 real
  4-char ids: 97 real, **0 bare**

So under the current scheme the "write a real close reason" habit holds at 97 of 97. The 40
are historical and, importantly, they are UNAUDITABLE rather than merely unaudited -- the
evidence was never written, so no later pass can recover whether their acceptances were met.
That is the honest size of the hole: not an ongoing leak, a sealed one.

BUT A REAL REASON IS NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT, which is the bead's real point and it
survives. Sampled -1d07 ("Let a pest carry two mutations"), whose acceptance has four
clauses and whose 262-character close answers two of them plainly, one partially and one not
at all:
  * "appear past a stated wave" -- MET, the close names wave 20 at 8%.
  * "the husk payout is derived rather than special-cased" -- MET, "the payout multiplies
    across them".
  * "a test asserts the combination the design decided is illegal cannot be rolled" --
    PARTIAL. `test_combat.gd:5333` asserts `Pest.mutations_compose(a, b) == not excluded`,
    which is the RULE; the ROLL that consumes it (`wave_director.gd:1018`) has no assertion
    of its own. Close in substance, not the clause as written.
  * "killable by at least two distinct answers the player can buy" -- NOT ADDRESSED by the
    close reason at all.

THE BEAD'S OWN WORKED EXAMPLE HAS SINCE BEEN SATISFIED: -bxhg's skipped clause asked that
OVERLAY_GRAMMAR.md gain a line saying which rows are taught. It has one --
`game/OVERLAY_GRAMMAR.md:36-45` -- and two tests hold the pair together
(`test_the_legend_names_as_many_shapes_as_the_grammar_documents` and
`test_every_legend_row_has_a_shape_the_legend_can_draw`). So the miss was real and was
repaired by the cycle that found it.

DOES THE HABIT NEED ANYTHING STRONGER THAN A LINE IN A SKILL? Split answer, and the
prototype is what decides it:

  * For "write a real close reason": NO. 97 of 97 is not a problem needing a mechanism.
  * For "answer every clause": a line in a skill is demonstrably NOT enough -- -1d07 is a
    current-scheme bead with a good close that still left a clause unanswered.

I prototyped the obvious gate -- split the acceptance on `;` and ` and `, and flag a clause
whose content words are absent from the close reason. It flagged 122 OF 146. Reading the top
of that list, -1fzh is a plain false positive (my splitter ate mid-description prose as an
acceptance clause). A checker with that signal-to-noise is a permanently-red gate, which
`house-static-checker` says outright is worse than no gate: it teaches people to skip the
check, and then it is not there for the finding that does matter.

SO THE RECOMMENDATION IS NOT A GATE. It is to make answering the clauses the path of least
resistance rather than an act of discipline: have the close-reason step START from the
acceptance text, so the clauses are already in the file being edited and skipping one is
visible rather than silent. That is a change to `verify-bd-item`, not a new tool, and it is
filed separately rather than smuggled in here.

The prototype scanner is deliberately NOT shipped. Per house-static-checker's own escape
hatch, the deliverable here is the written reasoning and the counts, so the idea is not
re-proposed from scratch.

title: Project devtools verbs accept a call with no position and do nothing
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md cycle 94, gap [G-069]. OUTSIDE this cycle's neighbourhood -- the work
was the HUD; this is the project's own devtools extension.

`cmd touch_press` takes {index, position:[x,y]}. Cycle 94 sent {x, y}, got success, and
nothing happened:

  cmd touch_press --args '{"x":288,"y":296}'   -> "success": true
  run-method --method arm_uproot                -> "nothing is selected"

So a malformed click reads as a broken uproot, one verb downstream, and cost several minutes
of suspecting the selection code.

The generic behaviour is the harness's and is DELIBERATE -- `list-commands` prints each verb's
arg keys and the reference says outright that a key not listed is silently ignored. That is a
reasonable default for optional keys. It is the wrong one for a verb whose entire effect is
positional: touch_press without a position is not a call anyone meant.

These three verbs are registered in devtools_ext/commands.gd, so the fix is ours, not
upstream. Guard each and name the key that was wanted:

  * touch_press  -- refuse with no `position`
  * touch_release -- same
  * touch_drag   -- refuse with no `to` (and say whether `from` defaulted)

One guard each. It converts a silent no-op into a message, and the message is the whole value.

While in there, check the other project verbs for the same shape -- place_plant takes
{plant,x,y} and spawn_pest takes {species,mutation,mutations,count}, and a place_plant with no
x/y would place at cell (0,0) rather than refusing, which is the same failure with a more
confusing outcome because something DOES happen.

ACCEPTANCE: every project verb whose effect depends on a required argument refuses the call
when that argument is absent, naming the key; the check covers all of devtools_ext's verbs
rather than only the three that bit, and the ones that legitimately have defaults are listed
with why.
notes:
ABSENCE CLAIM RESOLVED (cycle 104 sweep, -g1o4): THE CODE HAS MOVED; re-verify before working.
The bead says project devtools verbs "accept a call with no position and do nothing",
from cycle 94's `cmd touch_press --args '{"x":288,"y":296}'` returning success while
nothing happened. Today devtools_ext/commands.gd DOES read positional args in at least
three handlers -- :109 and :215 build a `Vector2i` cell from `args.get("x"/"y")`, and
:203 builds a `Vector2` from them as floats. So the blanket claim is stale.
What is NOT resolved is the bead's real point: whether a handler that IGNORES a key
still answers `success: true`. That is about the reply contract, not about whether any
handler reads x/y, and it is still worth doing. Open the specific verb cycle 94 used
before assuming either way.
close_reason: Cycle 108 four-lane fan-out; merged to main, 751 tests, lint 0, check_all 19/19

title: A resumed message looks like a second event
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (94), first entry. PLAYER-FACING.

Cycle 94 proved the message row defers a pre-empted line and brings it back with the time it
had left -- verified live: kill a bed, arm an uproot, and 4s later "A hungry pest ate your
Corn Cobbler!" is on the row again.

Nothing marks it as a resumption. _advance_message_queue restores the line by assigning
_message_text (game/hud.gd:1627): same text, same styling, no prefix, no different fade.

So a player who loses a bed and immediately arms an uproot sees that exact sentence twice,
four seconds apart, with nothing to say one plant died rather than two. The sentence names
the plant, so "two Corn Cobblers died" is at least self-consistent -- which makes it
PLAUSIBLE rather than obviously a glitch, and that is the worse of the two failures.

Three shapes, and the third is the interesting one:
  (a) Prefix a resumed line. Cheap, but it spends message-row width, which is the budget
      this project has spent four cycles measuring (cmd budgets: 818 of 876 px).
  (b) Fade it in differently. No width cost. But GardenTheme.animations_enabled() can be
      off, and a cue that exists only in motion is one that some players never get -- the
      two-channel rule applies to time as much as to colour.
  (c) Do NOT resume a line that already had MESSAGE_MIN_READABLE seconds on screen. The
      player read it; bringing back the tail teaches nothing and is what creates the
      ambiguity. This SHORTENS the row's work rather than adding to it, and it reuses a
      constant the row already owns (game/hud.gd:354, 1.2s).

(c) is probably right and is also the one that could be wrong in an interesting way: it
makes an interrupted line disappear for good, which is exactly the erasure cycle 93 wrongly
accused the code of. The difference is that here it would be deliberate and bounded to lines
the player has already had time to read -- state that in the code or the next reader will
"fix" it back.

Measure first: how often does a resumption actually happen? messages_refused and
messages_evicted exist but there is no counter for resumptions, and adding one is two lines
in _advance_message_queue. If a real run never resumes a line, this closes like -i366 did.

ACCEPTANCE: the resumption rate is measured in a real run before anything changes; if
resumptions happen, one of the three shapes is chosen with the other two refused in writing
and the message-row budget re-checked after; if they do not happen, that is the finding.
close_reason:
Shipped. Answering the acceptance clause by clause, per verify-bd-item's close step.

CLAUSE 1 -- "the resumption rate is measured in a real run before anything changes". DONE,
and it nearly closed this bead wrongly. Ambient play pre-empts ZERO times (six waves, 54
kills, eight lives lost, 257s, run_seconds moving as a witness). That reads as "never
happens" until you notice every pre-empting call site is a PLAYER ACTION -- arming an uproot
(game/game.gd:1392) or opening a seed packet (:1518, :1528) -- and six waves of ambient play
contain neither. One arm_uproot over a live message: messages_preempted 1, first try.

CLAUSE 2 -- "if resumptions happen, one of the three shapes is chosen with the other two
refused in writing". DONE. Chose (c), do not resume a line that already had
MESSAGE_MIN_READABLE seconds. Refusals: (a) prefixing a resumed line spends message-row width,
which is the budget this project has spent four cycles measuring; (b) fading it in differently
exists only in motion, and GardenTheme.animations_enabled() can be off, so some players would
never get the cue -- the two-channel rule applies to time as much as to colour.

CLAUSE 3 -- "the message-row budget re-checked after". NOT NEEDED, and saying so rather than
skipping it: (c) adds no text and no producer. The corpus is unchanged and
message_corpus_check passes, so there is nothing for the budget to re-measure. Had I chosen
(a) this clause would have been the whole risk.

Verified live: a real plant killed, 3.0s of reading, a real arm_uproot -> preempted 1,
retired 1, pending 0, and after the prompt expires the row reads "Uproot cancelled." where
cycle 94 recorded the notice reappearing.

One caveat in the record rather than smoothed over: the unread-then-displaced case lost its
selection live and was never driven post-change, so the ledger row is `partial` with that
check marked blocked. It is covered headless by two tests with a mutation on each.

title: Should arming an uproot be allowed to erase the line you are reading?
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (93), first entry. PLAYER-FACING.

Cycle 93 measured the message row and found it drops ZERO lines in real play (waves 1-6 to a
full loss, 54 kills, ten lives lost, every wave transition; the threshold is five messages
inside one 2-4s window against a row that holds four). So the queue-overflow worry from cycle
90 is closed.

What the rung system actually buys is PRE-EMPTION, and that has a cost nobody has decided.

Enumerated: exactly three of the twenty-two show_message call sites pass a priority --
game/game.gd:1392 (MESSAGE_DEADLINE, the uproot prompt) and :1518, :1528 (MESSAGE_IMPORTANT).
When one arrives, the line already on the row is pushed into the queue (game/hud.gd:1462), and
against a full queue of equals it is refused. So an urgent message costs the sentence the
player was mid-way through reading.

The uproot case is the one to look at. Its DEADLINE is argued for in place
(game/game.gd:1389-1391: the countdown is already running, so deferring eats the window the
message describes) and that reasoning is right. What nobody decided is what it should be
allowed to ERASE. "A hungry pest ate your Corn Cobbler!" is one of the nineteen at
MESSAGE_NORMAL (game/game.gd:1287), so a player who arms an uproot in the same second a bed
dies never learns which plant they lost.

DO NOT FIX BLINDLY. Making the loss notice un-stompable would let it eat the uproot window
instead, which is the trade cycle 79 already made once in the other direction and spent a
whole cycle wording. The options are not symmetric:
  (a) Accept it. Arming an uproot is a deliberate act; being interrupted mid-read is the
      price of asking a question while something else is happening.
  (b) Let the pre-empted line come back. It is already pushed into the queue -- it is only
      lost when the queue is full of equals, which the measurement says is rare. Check
      whether the eaten-plant notice actually survives in practice before assuming it does
      not; the measurement says drops are rare, so this may already be the behaviour.
  (c) Make the eaten-plant notice IMPORTANT so it is not the lowest. Cheapest to type and
      the one most likely to be wrong, because it then pre-empts other things in turn.

Start by measuring (b): with the counters now in Hud, arm an uproot in the same second a
plant dies and read messages_refused. If it is 0, this bead closes as "already fine" and the
entry above is a theoretical worry, which is exactly what happened to the last one.

ACCEPTANCE: the eaten-plant-during-uproot case is driven at runtime and messages_refused read
after it; if the notice survives, this closes with the number; if it is lost, one of the three
options is chosen with the trade stated and the other two refused in writing.
close_reason:
ALREADY FINE -- closing on the branch this bead predicted for itself, with the measurement.

The premise was wrong and it was mine. show_message's pre-empt branch pushes the displaced
line into the queue WITH THE TIME IT HAD LEFT (game/hud.gd:1462-1463), and
_advance_message_queue restores exactly that seconds value. So total reading time is
preserved across the interruption rather than lost. A notice pre-empted after 0.5s of its
4.0s comes back with 3.5s, well over MESSAGE_MIN_READABLE (1.2).

Driven against the real paths, not a staged queue: take_damage(999) on a real plant posts "A
hungry pest ate your Corn Cobbler!", arm_uproot on a real selection returns "confirm needed"
and its DEADLINE prompt takes the row -- pending_messages 1, messages_refused 0 -- and
step-time --seconds 4.05 --then-pause brings the loss notice back to the row.

The notice IS destroyed if the queue is full of equals when the collision happens, which
needs four simultaneous ordinary lines. Cycle 93 measured a real run to a full loss and never
reached that state. Both cases are now tested, so the good news is bounded rather than
optimistic.

None of options (a), (b) or (c) was taken, because (b) turned out to already be the
behaviour. Kanban's cycle-93 entry is corrected rather than deleted -- how the wrong claim
was made is the useful half: it was reasoned from the queue's drop rule instead of from the
branch that actually runs.

title: Post the owed gh#54 comment and file G-067
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md cycle 92, gap [G-067]. Also the OWED upstream work from cycle 92,
which could not be done because GitHub returned HTTP 503 twice.

TWO THINGS, both small, both blocked on nothing but a working GitHub:

1. Post the comment parked at .devtools/pending-gh54-comment.md to
   SeveralHerr/godot-selftest-harness#54. It says the specific surprise that motivated that
   issue -- the notebook opening at page 10/10 from the title screen -- does NOT reproduce;
   cycle 92 got 1/10 from a fresh session, matching go_to(0). The issue's actual claim is
   unaffected and still true. This matters because a maintainer reading "landed on page 10
   when the source says page 0" would reasonably try to reproduce it and waste their time.

2. File [G-067] upstream, after reconciling it against the installed 0.54.0 per the
   gap-reconcile skill. `press` reports the button it pressed and nothing about what the
   press did: verifying cycle 92's feature took `press NotebookButton`, then a separate
   find-nodes to discover a notebook now existed, then a third call to read its page. The
   reply to the interesting moment is `Pressed /root/.../NotebookButton` -- true, and silent
   about the overlay that appeared as a direct result.

   Filed SEPARATELY from G-066 rather than bumping its `seen:`, because the fix differs.
   fire-entry-point wants a screen summary because it is SUPPOSED to change the screen; most
   presses change nothing visible and a full first_frame on every one would be noise. What
   press wants is narrower: the node-count delta either side of the emit, plus the deepest
   new node's path when the delta is positive. It degrades to `+0 nodes` for an ordinary
   press, which is itself worth seeing -- a button wired to nothing currently reports
   success.

Do (1) first; it is a correction and corrections age badly.

ACCEPTANCE: the gh#54 comment is posted and .devtools/pending-gh54-comment.md is deleted;
G-067 is either filed upstream with its issue number appended to the log entry, or recorded
as already-fixed in 0.54.0 with the file:line that fixes it.

https://github.com/SeveralHerr/godot-selftest-harness/issues/54#issuecomment-5317863290 --

was still returning 503 while REST was healthy. `gh api -X POST repos/OWNER/REPO/issues` and
`.../issues/N/comments --input FILE.json` both worked. Also note that a heredoc written to

title: Should the pause door open the SELECTED plant's page?
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (92), first entry. PLAYER-FACING, and both pieces exist.

Cycle 92 gave NotebookScreen an `open_at` so the DOOR chooses the page: the title screen
opens the drawings, a paused run opens the cue legend. The next question the same mechanism
answers is nearly free.

  - NotebookScreen.page_for_plant(id) (game/notebook_screen.gd:753) has existed for cycles.
    It returns the page about a catalogue plant, or -1.
  - Game.selected_placed (game/game.gd:77) is the plant the player last clicked.
  - Game.pause_run already hands PauseScreen.build two arguments about the run's state
    (game/game.gd:1034), so there is a place to pass a third without inventing a channel.

So a player who selects a Chomp, wonders what it does, and pauses could land on the Chomp
Flower's page rather than on the legend.

THE OBJECTION IS REAL AND SHOULD DECIDE THE DESIGN RATHER THAN BE DISCOVERED AFTERWARDS: a
selection persists from an earlier click. Somebody who selected a plant two waves ago and
paused because a PEST did something unexplained would be sent to the wrong page -- and
worse, to a page that looks like an answer to the question they were asking.

Three ways out, and they are not equivalent:
  (a) Accept the miss. Prev/Next reaches the legend from a plant page either way, and a
      wrong-but-plausible page costs one press. CHECK THIS BEFORE ASSUMING IT: the legend
      and the plant pages are not adjacent in PAGES, so "one press" may be four.
  (b) Only prefer the plant page when the selection is recent -- needs a timestamp Game
      does not currently keep, so this is a new field, not a read.
  (c) Only when the plant was selected since the current wave started. Cheaper than (b) and
      arguably the better rule: a selection that survived a wave boundary is stale by the
      only clock the player is watching.

Do not pick by implementation cost alone. Note also that this makes the pause door's answer
depend on run state, which is a step up in complexity from cycle 92's "the door knows which
door it is" -- worth being sure the second question is worth asking at all.

ACCEPTANCE: the pause door's page choice is decided between the legend and the selected
plant's page with the staleness rule written down and its reason; a test drives both
branches (a plant selected, and nothing selected) because a default that equals one of the
two expected answers cannot be distinguished from the property being ignored -- that is the
exact trap cycle 92's own test was written to avoid.
close_reason:
Answered NO: the pause door keeps opening the legend, whatever is selected.

Five measurements decided it, none of which were in the bead:
  1. The plant page is often not a gameplay page. page_for_plant(corn_cobbler) and page_for_plant(chomp_flower) are both KIND_DRAWING, and go_to() gates the spec card on kind == KIND_PLANT. So the bead's own worked example -- 'selects a Chomp, wonders what it does' -- lands on a photograph of a pencil sketch. The other one is the Corn Cobbler, the FREE STARTER, i.e. the plant a confused player is most likely to have selected. Six of eight plants get a spec; the two that do not are the two everyone has.
  2. The question is already answered live without pausing. Hud._refresh_selection fills SelectionBox the instant a plant is clicked, with that plant's CURRENT numbers. The notebook's spec card is a static catalogue entry, so aiming the door at it trades a live answer for a worse historical one.
  3. The selection is set by PLACING, not only by asking -- Game.place_plant ends in _select(plant). So the target is the last thing you DID, which makes the staleness objection worse than the bead states.
  4. Being wrong costs 2-7 presses, not one. The pager has no jump. Shortest wrap-walk to the legend from each plant page: Corn 2, Chomp 5, Sunflower 7, Sundew 6, Dandelion 5, Mint 4, Nettle 3, Aloe 2 -- MEDIAN 5.
  5. The staleness rules on offer could not be written on the door: two identical presses of one button going two places for an invisible reason is exactly what the owner's 'written or obvious' condition forbids.

WHAT IT FOUND INSTEAD, which was worth more. The pause door has been opening at page 13 of 14 while the identically-labelled title-screen button opens at page 1, and nothing said so -- a player meeting the title door first has every reason to read the pause door as a book that lost its place. NotebookButton now carries a tooltip:

  Opens at page 13 of 14 — What the marks on the board mean.

Every part derived from NotebookScreen (index from page_for_kind, total from PAGES.size(), subject from the same PANE_LABELS row the page draws as its heading), so the promise cannot drift from the destination. A tooltip and not the label because BUTTON_SIZE.x is 248 and a Button's minimum width is its text.

VERIFIED LIVE: tooltip reads as above, open_at=12, PageLabel reads '13 / 14', and node-bounds confirms the rect is still 248x44 -- the tooltip did not widen the button.

title: Sweep for guards that assert presence where they need absence
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md cycle 91, and the two mutations that survived their first guards.
OUTSIDE this cycle's neighbourhood -- the work was a notebook page; this is about how this
project writes guards, across every checker and test it has.

Both cycle-91 mutations survived, and both survivals had ONE shape: the guard asserted the
PRESENCE of a good thing where it should have asserted the ABSENCE of the bad thing.

  * `source.contains("SelectionMarker.MARKER_COLOR")` passed while a Color literal was
    inlined into one of two draw_line calls, because the other call kept the token alive.
    The property actually wanted was "no swatch painter builds a Color literal at all".
  * Deleting a PANE_LABELS row passed because nothing asserted the resulting heading was
    non-empty -- the table's whole promise was "a missing row gives a blank rather than a
    wrong value", and blank is only better than wrong if something notices.

This rule already exists in this repo, in the wrong place.
.claude/skills/house-static-checker/SKILL.md:105-107 says: "Accept only guards that actually
guard... Ask what the failing case would have printed, and reject any guard that would have
passed." It is written for Python checkers and it is exactly the rule both of these tests
broke.

The work is to find out how widely this bites, because two instances in one cycle is a
pattern only if it recurs. Sweep the test suite for presence-guards over a corpus:
`assert_true(x.contains(...))`, `assert_gt(collection.size(), 0)` as a stand-in for a real
property, `assert_true(has(...))` where the interesting case is a partial. For each, ask the
skill's question -- what would the failing case have printed -- and record the answer, not a
verdict.

Note what this is NOT: it is not a mandate to rewrite them. `assert_gt(size, 0)` is correct
and necessary as a VACUITY guard beside a real assertion, and this project uses it that way
deliberately in a dozen places. The defect is a presence-guard standing ALONE as the check.
