ACCEPTANCE: the presence-guard sweep covers at least the three test scripts with the most
assertions, each candidate recorded with what its failing case would have printed; the ones
that would have passed their own bug are named; and if the count is under three, that is the
finding and this closes -- two in one cycle may have been the cycle, not the codebase.
notes:
ABSENCE CLAIM RESOLVED (cycle 104 sweep, -g1o4): STILL TRUE, and the worked example still reproduces.
"Deleting a PANE_LABELS row passed because nothing asserted the resulting heading was
non-empty -- the table's whole promise was 'a missing row gives an empty heading'."
Verified: `NotebookScreen.PANE_LABELS` is at game/notebook_screen.gd:180 and the reader
at :190 is `return String(PANE_LABELS.get(kind, ""))` -- an explicit empty-string default,
so a deleted row degrades silently by design. And a grep for a non-empty assertion around
every PANE_LABELS mention in test/unit/ returns ZERO (`is_empty`/`assert_true`/`assert_ne`
count: 0). The two mentions in test_placement.gd (:2705, :4014) are comments about the
table, not assertions on its output.
So the guard the bead describes is still missing and the mutation it names would still
survive. This is a live item, not a stale one.
close_reason: Cycle 108 four-lane fan-out; merged to main, 751 tests, lint 0, check_all 19/19

title: Teach the doubled-width ARMED cue, the one guarding the irreversible act
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (91), second entry. PLAYER-FACING, and the strongest
argument in it is about risk rather than polish.

The legend teaches five of the grammar's ten shapes. The five left out are the straight-line
state (game/OVERLAY_GRAMMAR.md:28), the weather's scattered marks (:30), the doubled line
width (:31) and the husk's pip count (:32).

Doubled line width means ARMED -- "a destructive action is one click away", in the grammar's
own words. It is drawn by SelectionMarker.WARNING_LINE_WIDTH and
SoleCoverMarks.WARNING_RING_WIDTH, on the uproot: the one act in the game that cannot be
undone, and the one cycle 79 spent an entire cycle wording the warning sentence for.

So the cue with the highest cost of being misread is the one the legend does not explain.
That was a deliberate scoping call at the time -- the five taught are the vocabulary of the
first two waves, and a player cannot uproot before they have planted -- and it is the wrong
one to leave standing now that the page exists.

The constraint, and it is measured rather than guessed:
test_the_legend_fits_the_page_it_is_drawn_on asserts CueLegend.content_bottom() against
NotebookScreen.DRAWING_BOX's 300px matte, and the current five rows already sit near it. So a
sixth row is ROW_PITCH coming down, or a second legend page. The test will say which, and it
will say it before any layout is broken rather than after.

A second page is not merely more room: PAGES.size() is what the pager counts and what
test_the_notebook_plant_pages_fit_their_card sums over, so two legend pages means the
"exactly one is the cue legend" assertion becomes "exactly two", and that number should move
deliberately.

ACCEPTANCE: the armed/doubled-width row is taught somewhere a player can reach; whichever of
the two shapes is chosen, the fits-the-page test passes without its threshold being raised to
accommodate the new row -- if the only way to fit is to loosen the budget, that is the finding
and the second page is the answer.
close_reason:
Shipped. The legend teaches six of ten now, and the sixth is the ARMED cue.

The bead's constraint was wrong in the direction that makes work cheaper. It said the five
rows sit at the edge of the 300px matte so a sixth needs ROW_PITCH cut or a second page.
Derived from CueLegend's own constants: five rows end at 248, a sixth at 294. It fits at the
current pitch with 6px to spare. A seventh would not, and the fits-the-page test now says so.

The swatch is deliberately the SAME shape as row one, at SelectionMarker.WARNING_LINE_WIDTH
in WARNING_COLOR, because that IS the grammar -- "doubled line width" means the mark you
already know, thicker. It sits last so the contrast with row one is the lesson. Verified by
screenshot through the pause door: the red brackets are visibly heavier than the yellow ones.

Also paid a debt this bead did not carry: cycle 91 closed -bxhg without meeting one clause of
its own acceptance (OVERLAY_GRAMMAR.md was to record which rows are taught). Written now,
without repeating the list, because a second copy is what would diverge -- CueLegend.ROWS is
the authority and two tests hold the pair together.

Four rows remain untaught: the straight-line state, the weather's scattered marks, the husk's
pip count, and the small-solid-ring marked cell. All are cues a player meets late or rarely,
which is the stated reason, and a seventh row does not fit at this pitch -- so teaching another
is a layout decision, not an append.

title: Shorten the route to the cue legend
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (91), first entry. PLAYER-FACING.

The page that teaches the board is the last page of the notebook. CueLegend ships as
KIND_LEGEND, the tenth of ten NotebookScreen.PAGES entries, and the screen opens on page 0
(game/notebook_screen.gd:370 -- go_to(0) at the end of the build). So the route to it is:
title screen -> Notebook -> NINE presses of Next.

The title screen's own header calls the notebook "a click further away" on purpose
(game/title_screen.gd:56-60). That reasoning was about a designer's scrapbook. It now also
gates the one page that explains what the marks on the board mean, which is a different
kind of content with a different audience.

Three shapes the fix could take, and they are NOT equivalent -- pick deliberately:

  (a) Reorder PAGES so the legend is first. Cheapest, one line. But it makes the scrapbook
      open on a rules page, and the five pencil drawings are the notebook's reason for
      existing (see the KIND_DRAWING header at game/notebook_screen.gd:112).
  (b) A direct route from the pause screen, which is where a confused player already is.
      More code, and PauseScreen's two-column list is a controls reference -- this would be
      a button, not a row.
  (c) Open on the legend the FIRST time only, page 0 thereafter. That is hint-shaped, and
      RunConfig.spend_hint(id, shown) exists for exactly that kind of one-shot as of cycle
      89 -- with the caveat that `shown` means the player SAW it, and "the screen opened on
      this page" is a stronger claim than show_message's, not a weaker one.

Do not pick by which is easiest. Nobody has watched a player look for this, and that is the
missing input rather than the missing code.

ACCEPTANCE: the route to the legend is shortened by one of the three shapes above, the
choice is recorded with the reason the other two were refused, and the notebook's existing
page tests still pass unchanged -- test_the_notebook_plant_pages_fit_their_card asserts a
sum over the four page kinds, so a reorder is safe but a fifth kind is not free.
close_reason:
Shipped, and by a fourth shape the bead did not list. PauseScreen already had a Notebook
button and its own _open_notebook, so "add a route" was not the work -- the nine presses
were. NotebookScreen.open_at lets the door choose: default 0 for the title screen
(browsing), page_for_kind(KIND_LEGEND) for the pause card (looking at a board). None of the
three listed options was taken; (a) would have made the scrapbook open on a rules page,
(b) was already done, (c) was unnecessary once the context could decide.

Verified at runtime through both doors: pause -> "10 / 10" with CueLegend visible, title ->
"1 / 10".

Also collapsed a duplicate the work surfaced: shelf_page() was page_for_kind for one kind
and had been for cycles; it now delegates.

title: Measure how often the message row actually drops a line
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (90), first entry. PLAYER-FACING.

Nineteen of the game's twenty-two message-row calls sit on the SAME rung, and a priority tie
drops the NEWER line.

Enumerated by balancing parentheses across every `show_message(` in game/*.gd, not by
grepping one line each -- these calls wrap, and a single-line grep reports all 22 as
defaulted, which is how this nearly went in wrong. The real split: 19 at the default
MESSAGE_NORMAL, two MESSAGE_IMPORTANT (game/game.gd:1518, :1528), one MESSAGE_DEADLINE
(game/game.gd:1392).

MESSAGE_QUEUE_MAX is 3 (game/hud.gd:355). `_queue_message` returns without appending when
the queue is full and the lowest entry's priority is >= the arrival's (game/hud.gd:1486) --
`>=`, so a TIE discards the new one. With 19 producers tied, a busy moment silently drops
the fourth onward.

What makes this player-facing rather than trivia is WHICH lines are tied. "A hungry pest ate
your Corn Cobbler!" is one of the nineteen (game/game.gd:1287, no priority argument) and so
is "Composted a husk for N seeds." (game/game.gd:1735). A bed destroyed and a click paying
out compete as equals, and in the wave where several things happen at once the loss notice is
exactly as droppable as the receipt.

Cycle 90 made this DETECTABLE for the first time: show_message now returns whether the line
landed. So the fix is no longer a guess.

The constraint that makes this a design job rather than a find-and-replace: the rung also
decides what a line may STOMP mid-read (game/hud.gd:1462-1464). Promoting the eaten-plant
notice to IMPORTANT means it can now interrupt a line the player is halfway through. So this
is not "raise the important ones" -- it is deciding which of the nineteen are genuinely peers
and which are not, and the answer has a cost on both sides.

Suggested shape, not a mandate: read show_message's return at the two or three sites where a
dropped line actually costs the player something, and count how often it comes back false in
a real wave 12+ run. A measurement first, because 19-on-one-rung may be producing zero drops
in practice -- MESSAGE_QUEUE_MAX is 3 and messages last 2-4 seconds, so it needs four
producers inside one window.

ACCEPTANCE: the drop rate is measured in a real run before anything is re-prioritised, and
recorded; if drops occur, the lines that lost are named and their rungs decided one at a
time with the stomp cost stated; if no drops occur, that is the finding and this closes.
close_reason:
Measured, and the answer is ZERO -- so this closes on its own terms ("if no drops occur,
that is the finding and this closes") and nothing is re-prioritised.

Real run: waves 1-6 to a full loss, 54 pests defeated, ten lives lost, a weather change to
rain and back, every wave transition. messages_refused 0, messages_evicted 0.

Threshold, measured live: six show_message calls in one frame gives one on the row,
pending_messages()=3 and messages_refused=2. So the row holds FOUR and the fifth inside one
2-4s window is the first line lost. Ordinary play does not produce four messages that close
together -- the producers are naturally spaced by the events that cause them.

The instrument stays (Hud.messages_refused / messages_evicted, and the pure
Hud.queue_outcome that decides between them), because the next person to suspect this can
read a number instead of reasoning about a queue.

Two corrections to this bead's own description, both worth carrying:
  * _queue_message has TWO drop sites, not one. `return` loses the ARRIVING line; the caller
    thinks it said something. `remove_at(lowest)` loses a WAITING line. The bead and cycle
    90's kanban entry both described only the first.
  * A higher-rung message does NOT evict a queued line. It PRE-EMPTS, which pushes the line
    it interrupted into the queue, and against a full queue of equals that displaced line is
    refused. So the cost of an urgent message is the line the player was mid-way through
    reading, not one they had not reached. The 19-of-22-on-one-rung concern is real but its
    consequence is this, not queue overflow.

title: Ship the second one-shot hint, now that hints have a contract
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (89), first entry. PLAYER-FACING.

Cycle 89 gave RunConfig two doors that refuse each other's ids: spend_hint(id, shown)
(game/run_config.gd:432) and record_milestones. So a hint can no longer be recorded by a code
path that never rendered it. What the game has is the machinery for a set of one-shot tips and
exactly ONE tip in it.

Enumerated rather than assumed: `has_milestone` used as a SHOW gate appears once in the whole
game, at game/game.gd:1355. Its other two call sites (game/notebook_screen.gd:445, :505) read
earned state to draw the milestone shelf, which is rendering, not gating a sight. One member is
the whole set.

THE FILTER THE NEW CONTRACT IMPOSES, and it is a real design constraint rather than a
formality: a hint is spent on being SEEN, so a new one needs a `shown` answer at its call site,
which means the moment must be NAMEABLE the way Hud.uproot_shows_tip (game/hud.gd:1775) is. A
tip that appears "somewhere in the message row, usually" cannot answer the question and
therefore cannot be a hint under this scheme. That rules out the vague candidates and points at
the few places the game genuinely decides something and then says nothing:

  - A Chomp declines a winged pest IN SILENCE. From the player's chair that is
    indistinguishable from a broken plant. The pest wears wings (Pest.MARKER_WINGS) and the
    refusal is already a named decision -- ChompFlower._act declines it -- so the `shown`
    answer exists.
  - The first husk left to rot. CompostMeter.lifetime_for already knows the clock ran out, and
    the player who never learned husks are collectible has just lost seeds they never saw.
  - The first plant eaten by a hungry pest. Plant.MAX_HEALTH / Pest.EAT_DPS is under three
    seconds (asserted in test_a_hungry_pest_wears_jaws_because_a_bed_dies_in_seconds), which is
    fast enough that a player can miss the cause entirely.

Pick ONE, not three. Each is a new HINTS member plus a named predicate plus a message, and
three at once would be three untested sentences competing for the same row -- the message row
has a measured budget (cmd budgets) and cycle 79 already burned a hint by adding a clause that
displaced one.

ACCEPTANCE: one new hint ships end to end -- an id in RunConfig.HINTS, a named static predicate
that decides whether it is shown, a spend_hint call passing that predicate's answer, and a test
asserting the hint is NOT spent when the predicate says no; the message-row budget is re-checked
after, since a new sentence competes with the ones already there.
close_reason:
ALREADY SATISFIED, TWICE OVER (cycle 104 sweep, -g1o4).
This bead says "What the game has is the machinery for a set of one-shot tips and
exactly ONE tip in it", and asks for the second.
`game/run_config.gd:162-164` now reads:
    const HINTS: Array[String] = [
        HINT_MOVE_PREVIEW, HINT_CHOMP_IGNORES_FLIGHT, HINT_UPGRADE_EXISTS,
    ]
Three hints. The second (the Chomp/flight tip) shipped, and the third -- the upgrade tip
that tells a player a placed plant can be upgraded -- shipped in cycle 103 as -gz53,
fired at the first moment the player can afford the cheapest upgrade on their own board.
Both were built on exactly the contract this bead describes: spent on `show_message`'s
RETURN value, so a hint cannot be recorded by a path that never rendered it.
Closing rather than re-scoping: -qoil already covered "point a further hint at something
else" and was itself closed as superseded by -gz53. A fourth hint should be argued on its
own evidence in its own bead, not inherited from a list written when there was one.

title: A repaint verb, so pausing to inspect a drawn cue shows the change
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md cycle 88, gap [G-061], filed upstream as
SeveralHerr/godot-selftest-harness#51. This is the in-project half — the upstream fix, if it
lands, reaches this project only after a version bump and a /scaffold-godot-harness refresh,
and this project is deliberately pinned at 0.38.0 (gh#43 segfault).

`pause` freezes the mechanism that repaints. Cycle 88 paused the game, dropped five husks
through `run-method`, screenshotted, and got the pre-pause frame — because `HuskLayer`
repaints from `_process` (game/husk_layer.gd:87, `func _process(_delta): if compost != null:
queue_redraw()`), and a paused tree does not call `_process`. Nothing in any reply says why.
It cost checking three wrong hypotheses (failed drop, wrong region, dead bus) before reading
the node's source.

The workaround is `run-method --node <the drawing node> --method queue_redraw`, which
requires already knowing which node draws the cue and that it draws from `_process`.

This project has ELEVEN Node2D cues in that shape and no list of them. Enumerate them — grep
for the property, not the API: a `_draw()` override plus either a `_process` that calls
`queue_redraw` or an explicit call somewhere. Known members from OVERLAY_GRAMMAR.md's rows:
husk_layer, sole_cover_marks, placement_preview, selection_marker, weather_overlay,
lane_pressure_overlay, corn_cobbler, dandelion, chomp_flower, pest. That list came from a
document, not from a grep, so it is a starting point and not the answer.

Two possible shapes, and the cheap one first:

  (a) A project devtools verb in devtools_ext/commands.gd — `cmd repaint_canvas` — that
      walks the tree, calls `queue_redraw()` on every CanvasItem, and returns the count.
      Needs no harness change, works at 0.38.0, and is the thing cycle 88 wanted.
  (b) A note in the harness section's Gotchas list. Rejected as the only fix: that section
      is inside the BEGIN/END godot-selftest-harness markers and a /scaffold refresh
      regenerates it, so the note would be silently lost. It belongs upstream, which is
      what #51 is for.

Do (a). It is about ten lines and it turns a three-command workaround that needs source
reading into one command that needs nothing.

ACCEPTANCE: `python tools/devtools.py cmd repaint_canvas` makes a change-while-paused
visible in the next screenshot, demonstrated on a husk drop, with the before-and-after
recorded; the verb reports how many CanvasItems it touched so a zero is distinguishable from
a success.
notes:
ALREADY SHIPPED UPSTREAM — found incidentally in cycle 138 while checking
whether [G-138] was closed in a newer harness.

`templates/tools/devtools.py` in the 0.60.0 cache tree
(C:\Users\gotmi\.claude\plugins\cache\godot-selftest-harness\godot-selftest-harness\0.60.0)
registers 67 verbs and `repaint` is one of them. This project runs 0.38.0, which
does not have it -- `python tools/devtools.py` lists 61 verbs and `repaint` is
absent, which is why this bead was filed and why it still looks open.

So the work here is NOT to build the verb. It is to run
`/scaffold-godot-harness` and re-check: the harness section in CLAUDE.md is
regenerated by that command, `harness-version` already prints the warning ("A
newer harness (0.60.0) is already on this machine than this project runs
(0.38.0)"), and this bead closes on the upgrade rather than on a commit.

Worth doing as one item with the rest of the 0.38.0 -> 0.60.0 delta rather than
alone: 0.60.0 also carries `restore-userstate`, `verb-usage`, `batch` and
`state`, none of which exist here, and at least one of those (`batch`) changes
how a cycle drives the bus. Whether any of them break this project's
`devtools_ext/commands.gd` is the real question and it needs the upgrade run to
answer.

This is also a standing lesson rather than a one-off: `.claude/skills/gap-reconcile`
says to open the harness version INSTALLED ON THIS MACHINE rather than the one
this project pins, and that rule applies to bd items that ask for a harness
feature just as much as it applies to [G-NNN] entries. Nothing was checking
these.

title: Give the player somewhere to look up what a drawn cue means
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (88), third entry. PLAYER-FACING, and OUTSIDE this cycle's
neighbourhood — the husk work was one draw call; this is about a surface the game does not
have.

`game/OVERLAY_GRAMMAR.md` is now ten rows (12 table lines, two of them the header) and is
referenced only from GDScript comments — husk_layer.gd:75, placement_preview.gd:3,
selection_marker.gd:3. No script loads it. It is a developer document, and the game teaches
none of what it describes.

Checked both surfaces that look like they could host a legend, and BOTH ARE THE WRONG SHAPE,
which is the actual finding rather than "the notebook is missing a page":

  - `NotebookScreen.PAGES` (game/notebook_screen.gd:198) is a design-history artefact. The
    entries are the original pencil drawings with notes about where each sprite came from
    ("The portrait the whole game starts from", "\"I want it to be a tower defence game\"").
    A grep for husk or compost across the whole file returns nothing. Putting a rules legend
    in here would be putting a manual inside a scrapbook.
  - `PauseScreen`'s two-column list (game/pause_screen.gd:778 — a key column and a "does"
    column) is a controls reference. A dashed ring is not a key; it has no keystroke to sit
    beside in the left column.

So the gap is that the game has no read-the-board surface at all, and every drawn cue added
since cycle 60 has quietly assumed one exists. A player meets a dashed ring, a doubled line
width and now a row of pips with nothing to check any of them against.

Note before designing: this is a NEW SCREEN or a new section of one, which is a bigger piece
of work than a cue. It may be worth doing as the smallest useful slice first — the three or
four cues a player meets in the first two waves — rather than all ten rows, and finding out
whether a legend is something anyone opens.

ACCEPTANCE: a player-reachable surface explains at least the cues reachable in the first two
waves, each shown as the shape it actually is rather than described in words; the surface
names where it lives in the game's navigation; and OVERLAY_GRAMMAR.md gains a line saying
which rows are taught and which are not, so the two cannot silently diverge.
close_reason: Shipped as NotebookScreen.KIND_LEGEND + CueLegend: five of the grammar's ten shapes, each swatch drawn with the real cue's own constants, reachable in the notebook and verified live at page 10/10 with a screenshot. The bead's premise (both candidate surfaces are the wrong shape, so this needs a new screen) was mine and wrong -- KIND_SHELF had already made the notebook a player-facing surface.

title: Decide whether a 60-seed husk should rot faster than a 9-seed one
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (88), first entry. PLAYER-FACING, and blocked on a design
answer before any code — filed so the question is on the record, not so it gets built.

Cycle 88 fixed the husk's VISUAL saturation with pips and deliberately left the mechanical
half alone. `CompostMeter.lifetime_for` (game/compost_meter.gd:93) lerps HUSK_LIFETIME 10.0
→ MIN_HUSK_LIFETIME 4.5 by `value_fraction`, which caps at FULL_VALUE = 9.

Derived, not remembered: `Pest.SPECIES` (three species, seeds 3 / 9 / 40) crossed with every
multiplier `Pest.mutations_compose` permits (1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0) through
`CompostMeter.husk_value_for` gives ten reachable values — {2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 14, 20, 30, 40,
60} — and six of them are at or above 9. So a 60-seed queen husk and a 9-seed beetle husk
both give the player exactly 4.5 seconds. The pips now say one is worth six times the other
while the clock says hurry equally for both.

THE QUESTION, which must be answered before anything is built, because the two answers want
opposite code:

  (a) 4.5s is a floor on human reaction time. A husk the player cannot physically reach is
      not a difficulty knob, it is a payout the game shows and then removes. Keep the cap;
      the pips are the whole fix and this bead closes as "working as intended, now stated".

  (b) The richest drop should be the one you can least afford to miss. Then the rot clock
      wants its own curve spanning the real range, and 4.5s stops being the floor for
      everything above 9.

Widening FULL_VALUE answers (b) for every husk at once as a side effect, which is why cycle
88 refused to do it while fixing a legibility bug. Do not resolve this by picking whichever
is easier to implement.

ACCEPTANCE: the design question is answered by the user, and then either this bead closes
with the answer recorded next to `lifetime_for`, or the rot curve is split from
`value_fraction` and the new spread is measured against the ten reachable values.
close_reason:
DECIDED AND PINNED. The answer is NO: a 60-seed husk keeps the same 4.5s floor as a 9-seed
one.

THE PREMISE HELD, and re-deriving it independently is what made it safe to build on.
Pest.SPECIES crossed with every composable multiplier gives ten reachable values --
{2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 14, 20, 30, 40, 60} -- six of them at or above FULL_VALUE (9), all getting
lifetime_for == MIN_HUSK_LIFETIME == 4.5s. Same ten the bead lists, computed from the
species table rather than copied from it.

THE BEAD'S QUESTION WAS HALF-ANSWERED ALREADY, and finding that changed what this cycle
did. FULL_VALUE's own comment reads: "FULL_VALUE stays at 9 deliberately. It is the knob
lifetime_for was tuned against, so widening it to 60 would silently slow the rot of every
husk in the game -- a balance change wearing a legibility fix's clothes."

That settles the KNOB. It says nothing about whether rot should distinguish above 9 by some
OTHER means -- a second curve with its own ceiling, say -- which is what the bead actually
asked. So this cycle recorded the decision with its own reasons rather than re-deriving a
constraint that was already written down.

THE DECISION, with the reasoning, now above MIN_HUSK_LIFETIME:

  1. 4.5s IS A REACTION TIME, NOT A DIFFICULTY KNOB. The values above 9 come from the two
     bosses -- Pest.SPECIES puts the Nurse Beetle at 39 seeds and the Queen at 40 -- crossed
     with mutations. So the richest husks drop at the single busiest moment on the board: a
     health bar emptying, plants firing, lives possibly just spent. Going below this makes
     the rarest drop the hardest to claim, which punishes the player at the game's high
     point rather than making it tense.
  2. THE URGENCY IS ALREADY CARRIED, TWICE, above the saturation point -- size and glow to
     9, and HuskLayer.overflow_pips counting beyond it. A player already knows a 60 is
     special. What they do not need is less time to act on knowing.
  3. THE FAILURES ARE NOT SYMMETRIC. Rot too slow and the compost meter is mildly too
     generous. Rot too fast on exactly the rarest drops and the player learns that boss
     kills are not worth chasing -- the opposite of what a boss should teach.

THE INCONSISTENCY THE BEAD NAMES IS ACCEPTED, NOT DENIED. "The pips now say one is worth six
times the other while the clock says hurry equally" is true. The pips answer "how much is
this worth" and the clock answers "how long do you have"; those are different questions and
they are allowed to saturate differently, because value is unbounded and reaction time is
not.

PINNED IN THREE PARTS, and the third is the one that makes it a gate rather than a comment.
test_the_rot_floor_is_a_floor_and_the_curve_still_sorts_below_it asserts:
  * nothing rots faster than the floor, at every reachable value AND at 999 and 100000;
  * everything at or above FULL_VALUE shares the floor, with a non-vacuous count guard;
  * BELOW FULL_VALUE a richer husk rots STRICTLY faster.

The third exists because the first two are BOTH satisfiable by flattening the curve
entirely: making every husk rot at 4.5s would "fix" the inconsistency and pass them.
Confirmed by mutation -- HUSK_LIFETIME = MIN_HUSK_LIFETIME fires only the ordering
assertion, and widening FULL_VALUE to 60 fires only the saturation-count guard. A decision
pinned only where it holds is not pinned.

The reachable values are DERIVED inside the test from Pest.SPECIES rather than listed, so a
new species or a new multiplier moves this with the game instead of leaving it asserting a
table nobody updated.

WHAT IS NOT DONE, deliberately: no balance change. Nothing about the curve, the floor,
FULL_VALUE or the pips moved. The bead said it was "filed so the question is on the record,
not so it gets built", and the answer turned out to be that the current behaviour is right
and was undefended. It is defended now.

title: Make extract-a-testable-seam a default rather than a response
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md 'New this cycle (87)', third entry, and four cycles of the same finding. OUTSIDE this cycle's neighbourhood -- it is about the skill, not the game.

Four seams now exist for one reason: `CornCobbler.spread_arc_span` (cycle 70), `Hud.uproot_shows_tip` (80), `Sfx.tune_voice` (74) and `Sfx.kill_event_for` (87). Every one was created because a mutation survived a test that asserted the INPUTS to a decision rather than the decision itself. Three of the four were earned the expensive way -- write the ternary, write the test, watch a mutation live, then extract.

`.claude/skills/extract-a-testable-seam` describes the fix well and frames it as a response: "use when a mutation survives". After four instances that framing is too late. The cheapest version is a question asked BEFORE writing the code: **is the thing that decides something a test can name?** A ternary at a call site is not; a pure static taking the same inputs is.

Rewrite the skill's opening to lead with the pre-emptive form, keeping the diagnostic form below it -- the survival signal is still how you find the ones you missed. Use cycle 87 as the worked example of taking it up front, since it is the only one that did.

Watch the cost the skill already names and do not lose it: an extracted seam is a public function partly for tests, `lint_project.gd`'s orphan pass will list it, and pre-emptive extraction risks decorative seams. The distinguishing question is whether the decision has a NAME -- "which kill sound has this pest earned" does; "add these two numbers" does not.

ACCEPTANCE: the skill leads with the pre-emptive question; the four instances are listed with which were earned and which was taken; the decorative-seam risk is stated in the same breath as the encouragement.
notes:
CORRECTION to the close reason above, which lost a word to the shell. It read "an
if/elif/else whose  MEANT one kind"; the missing word was the else keyword, in backticks,
which bash substituted as a command. Fourth occurrence of this failure in the project
(cycles 76, 78, 83, 91) and the first through `bd close --reason` rather than `bd create
-d` -- the standing rule named only the latter. CLAUDE.md's rule now covers any bd field
passed as a shell argument.
close_reason: Done in cycle 91, from a better position than when filed. The skill's Cost section said to pay for a seam only after a mutation survives, and cycle 87 had already established the opposite default; cycle 91 gave it the evidence to state plainly -- seven seams now exist, the last three taken up front, and two of those paid inside the hour. NotebookScreen.pane_label_for replaced an if/elif/else whose  MEANT one kind, and the identical defect was then found sitting in the test for the same code. Rewritten to lead with the pre-emptive question (does the decision have a NAME?) while keeping a survival as admissible evidence.

title: Check the transform cues by reading properties, not pixels
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md cycle 86. Sharpens -6e2e rather than duplicating it — read that one first, and note this halves its scope.

Cycles 85 and 86 both paid the same cost by hand: a defect or a surviving mutation in the gap between a value the game computes and the property that draws it. -6e2e was filed as a PIXEL probe, on the assumption that checking a drawing means sampling the screen.

For most of this game's cues it does not. The finding is that board cues split into two kinds:

**Transform cues** — the thing that moves is a node property. `_sway_pivot.rotation` for the sway, breathe and flinch; `_sprite.scale` for every event flourish; `_sprite.rotation` for a pest's facing and gait. These need **no pixels at all**. Pause, step, read the property, assert it against the bound the constants imply. Cycle 86's version is three commands and it caught what a mutation could not: sway alone holds the pivot within 0.014 rad, a bite swings it to 0.130.

**Canvas cues** — drawn with `draw_arc`, `draw_circle`, `draw_line` into a node's own canvas item, where there is no property to read: range rings, muzzle fans, chew rings, husk arcs, sole-cover marks, placement previews, the weather overlay. These are the ones that need a pixel probe, and they are the ones cycle 85's bug lived in.

So the work splits, and the transform half is cheap enough to do first and separately. Doing it first also builds the driving harness the pixel half will reuse.

Do NOT let this close -6e2e. The canvas half is where the shipped bug was, and it is the half that needs gh#49 upstream or a colour-counting probe of our own.

ACCEPTANCE: the transform cues have an automated runtime check asserting each moving property against the bound its constants imply; the check names which cues it does NOT cover and why, so the canvas half stays visible rather than looking done.
notes:
ABSENCE CLAIM RESOLVED (cycle 104 sweep, -g1o4): STILL TRUE.
"Canvas cues -- drawn with draw_arc, draw_circle, draw_line into a node's own canvas
item, where there is no property to read." Verified: `grep -rln "draw_arc\|draw_circle"
game/*.gd` returns chomp_flower.gd, corn_cobbler.gd, cue_legend.gd, dandelion.gd,
husk_layer.gd and more -- all Node2D `_draw` calls with no Control and no property that
holds the drawn geometry. So `findings`' ui_layout check structurally cannot see any of
them, and neither can a get-state read.
Cross-reference: -6e2e is the same blind spot approached from the pixel side, and its
note records that the harness now ships a `sample-pixels` verb. Read that note before
designing this one; the two beads should not build two different probes.

title: Measure whether a drought is noticed mid-wave, not side by side
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md 'New this cycle (84)', third entry. PLAYER-FACING, and a measurement before it is a change.

Cycle 84 put weather on the board: a tint plus scattered marks, drought flat dashes and rain slanted streaks. Photographed, all three states are distinguishable side by side. **Side by side is not the test.**

The real question is whether a player mid-wave, watching pests rather than grass, notices that the ground has changed at all. `WeatherOverlay.DROUGHT_TINT` is alpha 0.20 and each mark is 7 px — chosen to be a texture rather than a filter, on the reasoning that a cue you cannot see past is worse than one you miss.

That reasoning may be wrong in the drought case specifically, and the asymmetry is the argument. A drought doubles every plant's firing interval (`game/wave_director.gd:353`) — a demand for more plants or better ones. Rain heals beds by a fraction: a gift requiring no response. So the two get equal visual weight for unequal stakes, and the one a player must ACT on is the one currently reading as slightly duller grass.

Measure before tuning. Capture the same board region at each alpha in a small sweep (0.20, 0.28, 0.36) with pests and plants present rather than an empty board, and judge which is the first that reads as a change without obscuring anything. Record the numbers so the next person tuning it is arguing with evidence.

Consider also whether the asymmetry should be in the CHANNEL rather than the alpha: rain could keep its subtlety and drought gain a second beat the player already reads — the prep-strip colour, or the tint on the wave readout that `_ease_threat_tint` already drives.

ACCEPTANCE: a recorded judgement at three alphas with the screenshots taken over a populated board; whatever ships, `WeatherOverlay`'s header says why that number and not the one either side of it.
close_reason: Measured on the running board: drought +5.31% luminance vs rain +4.29%, but rain's per-channel excursion (+0.114 blue) is nearly double drought's (+0.059 red). Both are hue shifts; the marks carry the greyscale distinction, not the tint. Ordering pinned as a test; the fix is a taste call.

title: Ask what the board's scarce resource is, before the next full-playfield cue
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md 'New this cycle (84)', second entry.

`game/weather_overlay.gd` is the first cue to draw across the whole playfield rather than on one cell or one plant, and it went in without measuring anything — because nothing measures the board.

Every HUD surface has a width budget: `Game.BUDGET_FLOOR` prices seven couplings and `check_budgets` refuses a build that overruns one, which in cycle 79 turned a feature decision (the armed-uproot prompt's two optional clauses became mutually exclusive). Every overlay screen now computes its row ceiling as of cycle 82. **The board has neither.**

And it is the surface with the most competition for attention. Drawing on it already: the lane-pressure hatch, sole-cover marks, placement previews with their dead-ground bars and gained-cell dots, four plants' range rings, the Chomp's chew ring, the muzzle fan, husk rot arcs — and now weather across all of it.

The question this bead asks is not "add a budget" but **what would a board budget even measure**. Width is the HUD's currency because a Label either fits or is ellipsised. The board's scarce resource is different and probably one of: simultaneous cues on one cell, total ink over the playfield, or how many distinct meanings a player is being asked to hold at once. Pick by asking which one, if exceeded, would actually make the game worse.

Note the precedent for getting this wrong: `-saaw`'s measurement exists because the top bar reached the state where every candidate overflowed by 5-54 px, and nobody knew until someone tried. The board is currently at "whatever fits".

ACCEPTANCE: a recorded answer to what the board's scarce resource is; if a budget follows, it is derived and gated the way the HUD's seven are; if the answer is that the board does not need one, that reasoning is written where the next full-playfield cue will be designed.

title: Audit bead descriptions for words the shell ate
description:
SOURCE: CLAUDE.md step 6, the rule added in cycle 83, and three eaten words across this session.

`bd create -d "..."` passes the description through the shell, where backticks are command substitution. A word inside them vanishes silently — the only tell is an unrelated `command not found` on stderr, which is easy to miss beside beads' own export chatter. It happened in cycles 76, 78 and 83, each time after the standing note in `cycle-log.md` told me not to do it.

A note I ignore three times is the wrong countermeasure. `bd create --body-file PATH` exists (also `--stdin`, and `--design-file` for the design field), and a file written with an editor tool never touches a shell at all: no quoting, no substitution, no escaping, and `file:line` citations in backticks survive — which matters now that step 3's citation rules apply to bead descriptions.

This bead is the audit half. The rule itself is already in step 6; what is not done is checking what earlier descriptions lost. Three are known and corrected by notes (`-e1u3`, `-a4hk`, `-b3nt`), but those are the ones where the shell happened to print an error for a word that looked like a command. A backticked word that IS a valid command — `date`, `test`, `find`, `time` — would have been substituted silently, with its OUTPUT landing in the description.

ACCEPTANCE: every open bead description is scanned for the signature of a substitution (an empty gap where prose expects a word, or a stray timestamp/path); anything found is corrected with a note rather than silently rewritten, so the record of the mistake survives.
close_reason:
AUDITED, and the answer to the question the bead could not answer is: none.

Scanned all 419 issues / 1166 prose fields (title, description, design, notes,
acceptance_criteria, close_reason) for the three shapes a shell substitution
leaves: a hole where a word was, command OUTPUT landing in the field, and an
unpaired backtick.

RESULT: zero silent-output substitutions. No `date`, `time`, `pwd`, `ls` or
`find` output appears anywhere in the corpus. That was the bead's actual worry
("a backticked word that IS a valid command would have been substituted
silently, with its OUTPUT landing in the description") and it did not happen.

FOUR eaten-word incidents found, all already self-documented, none new:
-a4hk ("resolving every  or  backtick citation", two words), -e1u3 ("measured
with  rather than eyeballed"), -b3nt ("ever grows a  flag on an entry point",
already carries a CORRECTION note), and -jmxb's notes AND close_reason
("whose  MEANT one kind") from cycle 91. Nothing was rewritten; the damaged
text stands, which is what the acceptance asked for.

Three findings were false positives and each taught the checker something:
-saaw's measured literal 'Wave  9999 infinity   threat 99' (padding, not a
hole), and -j11/-pjk's C:\Users\gotmi\...\log.md (the real location of the
skill-ideas backlog, deliberately written).

SHIPPED tools/bead_prose_check.py rather than only the audit, because the bead's
own argument applies to itself: the "never pass prose as a shell argument" note
has been broken in cycles 76, 78, 83 and 91, the last one inside a close reason
about being careful. A note ignored four times is the wrong countermeasure.

The checker's waiver is the correction note itself -- an issue that records what
the shell ate stops firing -- so the record of the mistake is what silences the
gate, and there is no hand-maintained waiver list to drift. Registered in the
parallel-safe list in .claude/skills/cycle/SKILL.md.

Baseline on the real corpus: 0 gating, 4 advisory (all closed), 3 waived, exit 0.

Fixture written and run per .claude/skills/house-static-checker/SKILL.md; it
caught two bugs in the checker that reading it did not -- the Git-Bash `pwd`
pattern was `/(c|mnt)/[A-Za-z]/Users/`, which matches neither /c/Users nor
/mnt/c/Users and had never fired, and the `  +` quantifier flagged -saaw's
padded literal. Three mutations recorded in the module docstring with OBSERVED
numbers; mutation C is the one worth keeping, because it is a real regression
that this tool's own exit code reports as clean.

title: Point the UI checks at surfaces that actually move
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (83), first entry.

Cycle 83 made three overlay screens reachable and swept them: 0 findings each. That is a real result and it bounds what the sweep is worth. Those screens are STATIC -- they build once from constants and nothing animates or reflows on them, which is the case a layout checker finds least.

The surfaces where a ui_layout finding is actually likely are the ones that change during play. There is essentially one: the HUD, which is already checked every cycle. So the honest reading of 83's clean sweep is that the checks work, not that the game is checked.

What would raise the yield: drive the screens into their MOVING states rather than their opening ones. The notebook turns pages (NotebookScreen.TURN_SECONDS with a tween per turn). The options screen flips rows. The key-binding screen has a capture state waiting for a keypress. Each of those is a reflow that no findings run has ever seen, and each is one press away now that the screens are reachable.

Note the ordering constraint cycles 60 and 65 paid for: settle before reading, and never sample a container mid-sort. A page turn is a tween, so read-a-moving-value applies -- pause before starting it, then step.

ACCEPTANCE: each reachable screen is checked in at least one state that required an interaction to reach; anything found is filed; if all are clean again, the report says which states were driven so the next person knows what is still unswept.

title: Give the other screens named entry points so a runtime check can reach them
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (82), second entry. A config edit with a large payoff.

devtools_config.json entry_points has exactly one entry, campaign, which is also the entry_hook. So a session lands on the board and nothing navigates. Cycle 82 changed four files across the options screen, the notebook and the run-summary card, got a clean findings across all five checks, and recorded reached 0/4 changed file(s). The launch verified nothing about the diff and looked identical to one that did.

Adding entry_points for the notebook, the options screen, the key-binding screen and the pause card converts them from verified by unit tests only to drivable. Each needs a node_path and a zero-arg method that opens it -- the same shape skip_to_game already has.

This is what -iiyg needs first: a UI baseline covering named states cannot cover a state nothing can reach.

Watch two things. The harness fires entry_hook automatically and once; entry_points are on-demand via fire-entry-point NAME, so adding them changes no existing behaviour. And a screen opened by a method that assumes a running game may need the campaign hook fired first -- record the ordering in the config comment or in the restart notes.

ACCEPTANCE: every overlay screen in the game can be opened by one fire-entry-point call; a runtime pass over a diff touching one of them reports non-zero reach.
close_reason: Five named entry points: campaign, notebook, keys, options, pause. All four overlay screens are now drivable and all four are clean on their first-ever runtime UI pass. A test asserts each entry point's method and scene still resolve, since a rename would otherwise break them silently.

title: Stop the over-promise simulation asserting the RNG draw
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md cycle 81. A fragility this cycle exposed and worked around rather than fixed.

test_the_coverage_map_keeps_its_promise_to_a_pest_that_never_leaves_covered_ground drives a seeded wave 22 and asserted escaped_engaged == escaped. Adding one randf() per mutated pest past wave 20 moved that to 20-of-34.

Demonstrated to be the STREAM and not the feature: with the draws still consumed and the second mutation never applied, the failure is byte-identical. So the equality was a coincidence of one draw, and it had read as an invariant for many cycles.

Cycle 81 replaced it with a floor (most escapes were fought) and wrote the demonstration beside it. That is honest and it does not fix the underlying problem: EVERY future change to RNG consumption in WaveDirector reshuffles this simulation, and the next one will present as a mysterious behavioural regression in a test about coverage.

Options worth weighing rather than one obvious fix. Give the simulation its own RNG, separate from the director's, so wave composition is stable across director changes. Or assert only properties derivable from the setup -- pests_all_covered_untouched == 0 is one and it survived this cycle untouched, which is the evidence that derivable assertions are the durable ones. Or record the wave's composition as a fixture so a reshuffle is visible as a diff rather than as a failure.

ACCEPTANCE: adding an RNG draw to WaveDirector does not change whether this test passes, or it does and the test says so in its message rather than reporting a coverage failure.
close_reason:
Fixed by replacing a COUNT with an IMPLICATION, which is the option the bead listed third and the only one that removes the dependency rather than managing it.

THE FRAGILE LINE WAS A COUNT. Its replacement is universally quantified over pests: escaped_unengaged_all_covered == 0 -- no pest walked out unfought having spent its WHOLE road walk on ground the map was still covering. A reshuffle changes WHICH pests are examined and never whether the sentence holds, so the next RNG change to _build_schedule cannot present as a coverage regression.

AND IT IS NOT A RESTATEMENT OF THE LINE ABOVE IT, which was the risk. Pest._ever_engaged and the test's touched_ever are different predicates: engagement is a strict SUPERSET, because take_damage marks on amount > 0 while a Shield Bug's plate can eat the hit and drop no health. The lane verified the superset by enumerating every write to Pest.health -- four sites, only one of which lowers it, and the mark happens before that one. So the assertion goes red exactly when a damage or hold path stops marking, which is a real defect: the fought ring the player sees is painted off that same flag.

NOT VACUOUS, and guarded to stay that way. Two denominators sit above it: escaped > spawned/3 (the wave really is losing) and pests_all_covered > 9 (the population the implication quantifies over is non-empty). An implication over an empty set is also zero.

THE ONE PREMISE THAT CANNOT BE MADE IMMUNE -- 'this seed produces a losing wave' -- now carries a SCHEDULE SIGNATURE (mutated / double_mutated counts) in its failure message, saying read the schedule before the garden: any draw added to _build_schedule reshuffles it, and that is a stream change rather than a coverage failure. That is the bead's second acceptance clause.

REJECTED, each for its own reason: a private RNG isolates nothing, since there is exactly ONE consumer of _rng and the reshuffle comes from the SHAPE of consumption rather than a competing reader -- and a test driving an RNG the game does not use is a test of a wave no player can meet. N seeds and a distribution would genuinely work but multiplies a 40,000-frame simulation by N in a helper five tests already call. A schedule fixture is the right shape at the wrong cost, since wave 28 is generated rather than tabled; the signature above is the cheap tenth of that idea that was kept.

TWO DRIFTS FOUND IN THE PROSE: the cycle-81 paragraph said the run is 'wave 22 (WAVES + 6)', but WAVES has 22 rows now so the run is wave 28; and the header still asserted 'every pest that reached the exit had been fought', which cycle 81 itself disproved. Both fixed, and the going-stale is now part of the argument.

ALSO SHIPPED: cycle 81's demonstration turned from a paragraph into an executable statement -- set_seed(12345) twice builds the identical wave-28 schedule, and ONE extra randf() burned off the same generator builds a different one. Four seeded simulations rest on that and nothing asserted it.

No game code changed; wave_director.gd is untouched. No player sees any of this.

VERIFIED at the parent, which the lane correctly called the real gate: 882/882 tests, import OK, check_all 19/19.

title: Say that a pest carries two traits, without inventing a third colour
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (81), first entry. PLAYER-FACING.

Pest.apply_mutation keeps the PRIMARY trait's tint on purpose -- a blend of two hues is a third colour nobody has been taught. The non-colour channel composes for free: gait_swing reads is_armoured and is_winged, gait_stretch reads is_hungry, so a paired pest MOVES like both while wearing one colour. That is the two-channel rule paying off in a case nobody designed it for.

What is missing is any signal that a pair is what you are looking at. And the pair is the rarest thing in the game -- under 3% of pests at wave 20 (game/wave_director.gd:51-52 against mutation_chance_for) -- so a player will meet one having never been told the category exists.

A cue that says TWO rather than WHICH TWO is enough and is cheap: the mutation marks drawn at the silhouette edge are already the non-colour half of a mutation's read, so a second mark is a count in an existing vocabulary rather than a new one.

Check the drawn-overlay grammar before choosing a shape -- game/OVERLAY_GRAMMAR.md now has a row for partial arcs and two for solid rings, and a mark that collides with one of those inherits its meaning.

ACCEPTANCE: a paired pest is distinguishable from a single-mutation one with colour thrown away; a test asserts the mark appears for two traits and not for one; the grammar document gains the row or names the exception.
close_reason: ALREADY SHIPPED, in the same cycle that filed this. markers_for (game/pest.gd:556) appends one mark per flag, _draw (:630) iterates markers() and draws each, apply_mutation queue_redraw()s (:529), and marker_fill/_ink (:678,:684) colour each mark from ITS OWN mutation's hue. So a winged+hungry pest wears wings AND jaws, in two hues, on a body wearing one. The test the acceptance asks for exists too: test_a_pest_carrying_two_mutations_wears_both_marks (test/unit/test_combat.gd:451) asserts size 2 and both members. The absence claim came from reading apply_mutation's _tint line and stopping 20 lines short of markers().

title: Make an unshown hint impossible to spend
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (80), first entry.

RunConfig stores two different contracts in one dictionary. HINT_MOVE_PREVIEW (game/run_config.gd:114) is a HINT -- spent when the player is shown something. Milestones.TABLE (game/milestones.gd:54) holds ACHIEVEMENTS -- earned by doing a thing. Same storage, opposite triggers, and nothing in the code distinguishes them.

Cycle 79 proved that matters and cycle 80 fixed one instance: the move tip was recorded whenever the game DECIDED to show it, and a later change displaced the sentence, so the hint burned unseen for a cycle. The fix put the decision in Hud.uproot_shows_tip and had Game ask it, which is correct and is a fix to one call site rather than to the class of bug.

Shape: RunConfig.spend_hint(id, shown: bool) that refuses to record when shown is false, alongside record_milestones for the achievement kind. Then a hint cannot be spent by a code path that did not render it, and the next hint's author cannot get it wrong by thinking of it the way its predecessor's author did.

Consider also whether HINT_ ids belong in Milestones.TABLE at all -- if they are a different contract they may want a different store, and the notebook renders TABLE.

ACCEPTANCE: recording a hint requires passing whether it was shown; a test asserts a hint is not recorded when shown is false; the existing move-tip call site goes through the new path.
close_reason: spend_hint(id, shown) and record_milestones now refuse each other's ids, gated on RunConfig.HINTS. shown is a required argument, so the next hint's author cannot forget the if. Four mutations red. Also answered the bead's open question: HINT_ ids do NOT belong in Milestones.TABLE -- the shelf counts earned off TABLE, so a foreign id would break that guard; noted on -ei83.

title: The move tip can now be spent by a plant that never shows it
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (79), second entry. A bug introduced by cycle 79 and found by writing the entry, not by a test.

The move tip fires on the first arm ever: game/game.gd:1325-1327 checks HINT_MOVE_PREVIEW and records it in the same breath. From cycle 79 the forfeit clause DISPLACES the tip when the plant has upgrades.

So a player whose first-ever uproot is on an upgraded cob gets the money sentence, never sees the tip, and the milestone is recorded anyway -- the hint is spent without being shown. That is likely rather than rare: uprooting something cheap is not a decision worth a four-second prompt, so the first real uproot is disproportionately an expensive plant.

Two fixes and they are not equivalent. Record the milestone only when the tip is actually rendered, which is one line at game/game.gd:1326 and keeps the hint. Or drop the tip entirely on the grounds that a hint nobody reliably sees is not doing its job -- which is a smaller message corpus and one fewer claimant on the row (see the slot bead).

ACCEPTANCE: whichever is chosen, a test drives a first-ever arm on an UPGRADED plant and asserts the milestone state matches what the player actually saw.
close_reason: Fixed: Hud.uproot_shows_tip is the one place the tip's presence is decided, and Game asks it instead of re-deriving it. Verified live with --snapshot-userstate, which restored the save afterwards.

title: Decide what the message row's one extra clause is for
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (79), first entry.

Cycle 79 measured the ceiling exactly. The armed prompt plus the move tip plus the forfeit clause is 1064px against an 876px row, so Hud.uproot_armed_message (game/hud.gd:1731-1745) carries at most ONE extra sentence and the forfeit now displaces the tip.

Three open beads all want that same slot and none of them mentions the others: -fjqp (draw the uproot countdown, which is a cue rather than a clause but competes for the same row), -c3h3 (a flinch), -qoil (a second one-shot hint). Roughly 190px, three claimants.

The useful move is probably not to keep ranking clauses. Three features arriving at one surface means the ROW is the wrong surface for at least one of them, and the selection panel is the obvious second home -- -r722 already wants it budgeted, which is the prerequisite for putting anything there.

Do not close the three beads on this. The deliverable is a stated policy for what the row is for and what goes elsewhere, so the next feature knows before it is written rather than after check_budgets refuses it.

ACCEPTANCE: a written rule for the message row's extra slot, referenced from Hud.uproot_armed_message; each of the three competing beads has a note saying which surface it is now aimed at.
close_reason: STALE: premise false. Its argument was 'three open beads want that slot'; c3h3 and qoil are both CLOSED, leaving one claimant (fjqp).

title: Say that an upgrade is not refunded, or refund it
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (78), fourth entry. PLAYER-FACING, and OUTSIDE this cycle work -- economy rather than drawn cues.

Plant.uproot_refund() (game/plant.gd:541-544) scales PlantCatalog.cost(kind) -- the BASE cost -- by a rate sliding with remaining health. Verified how: grepped for uproot_refund across game/, it is declared once in plant.gd and no plant overrides it.

So a Corn Cobbler carrying 65 seeds of upgrades refunds exactly what a fresh one does. The HUD shows the number (game/hud.gd:1224) and structurally cannot show what it is a fraction of, so the player sees a plausible figure with no hint that two thirds of the investment is not in it.

This may be the right rule. Upgrades are consumed is a defensible economy and the health slide already exists to make a wrecked plant worth less. What is not defensible is that it is a rule nobody stated, discovered by uprooting an expensive plant once.

Two routes and they are not equivalent. Scaling the refund by what was actually spent needs a per-plant record of spend, which nothing tracks today. Saying it in the armed-uproot prompt costs one string and lands on the one row cycle 69 guaranteed a place for -- and message_corpus_check will hold whoever writes it to the budget.

ACCEPTANCE: a player about to uproot an upgraded plant can tell what they get back and what they do not; whichever route is taken, a test asserts the refund against a plant that has been upgraded rather than only a fresh one.
close_reason: Shipped in 600cf8a via the cheaper route: the armed prompt names the forfeited seeds, derived by CornCobbler.upgrade_spend from LEVELS. The budget refused the naive version at 188px over and decided the design -- the tip and the forfeit cannot share the row, and the one about money wins.

title: Refuse to file a bead from an uncited kanban entry
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (77), first entry.

tools/citation_check.py measured it in cycle 77: 249 of kanban.md 323 entries carried no file-colon-line citation at all. The cite rule arrived in cycle 30 and the file is 77 cycles old, so the uncited three quarters is simply everything written before it.

Backfilling 249 citations is the wrong move and this bead is not that. An uncited entry nobody promotes costs nothing being wrong; the cost lands only when one becomes work, and that is where three cycles running produced a bead whose factual claim was false.

So the rule belongs on the PROMOTION path, not on the file: an entry may not become a bead unless the bead description carries a citation for the claim it acts on. That is already CLAUDE.md step 6 in prose since cycle 72. What is missing is anything that notices.

Shape to consider before building: bd descriptions are free text, so this is either a check over open beads for absence-claim sentences with no path-colon-line anywhere (which -thoj already scopes as a one-time sweep) or a step in the filing habit. A checker that reads bd is a new dependency the other eleven do not have -- weigh that before writing one.

ACCEPTANCE: filing a bead whose description asserts something about the code without citing it is caught by something other than my own attention; whatever that something is, it does not require the beads database to be readable by the parallel-safe gates.
close_reason:
REFUTED. No code written, and that is the result.

THE PROPOSED RULE WOULD HAVE CAUGHT NONE OF THE INCIDENTS IT WAS FILED FOR. The bead asks that "an entry may not become a bead unless the bead description carries a citation for the claim it acts on". Measured against every documented false-premise bead in this project's own record:

    bead     citations in description   rule fires?   premise was false?
    -e1u3    8                          no            yes
    -4lnu    0, names no code file      no            yes
    -lk0n    5                          no            yes
    -2ker    4                          no            yes
    -ibvb    21                         no            yes

**0 for 5, and the correlation runs BACKWARDS**: the four most heavily cited beads in the corpus are the four whose premises turned out false. -e1u3 is the clearest -- its eight citations enumerate `create_tween()` sites, and the claim they were marshalled for ("Nothing runs while a plant is doing nothing") was false because both animations are `_process` sinusoids. The citations were the VEHICLE of the error: they are what made "Verified unbuilt" read as established. And -4lnu asserts an absence over a LOG, which no `path:line` can cite at all.

IT WOULD ALSO BE PERMANENTLY RED, which house-static-checker calls worse than no gate. On the live export (479 issues, 80 open): 53 of 80 carry no `path:LINE` at all; narrowing to "names a CODE file but never a line" still leaves 17 of 80 standing red, 21%. And 18 of the 53 are taste beads ("Decide whether...", "Ask whether..."), which the cycle skill's step 3 explicitly exempts: "Taste needs no citation -- assert a preference plainly and let it be argued with."

THE BEAD IS ALSO UNDERSTATED, in the opposite direction from usual. Its "Shape to consider" says "a checker that reads bd is a new dependency the other eleven do not have". That is false on this tree: TWO checkers already read `.beads/issues.jsonl` and both already run inside `check_all.py`, which reports 19 checkers, not eleven. `bead_claim_check.py` already prints `<-- NO CITATION` beside open beads and is advisory BY DESIGN for exactly the permanently-red reason re-derived above. `citation_check.py --beads` already resolves citations living in bead prose -- 479 beads, 967 citations, open gating and closed advisory.

SO THE ACCEPTANCE IS ALREADY MET -- "caught by something other than my own attention; does not require the beads database to be readable by the parallel-safe gates" -- and met by a better-targeted mechanism than the one asked for: `bead_claim_check.py` catches the ABSENCE CLAIM whether or not it is cited, which the 5-for-5 table says is the actual defect class.

THE RESIDUAL GAP, stated so it is not re-proposed: it is not "an uncited bead" but "a CITED bead whose citation does not support its claim". `citation_check.py`'s own NOT COVERED line has always disclaimed that as unautomatable, and `bead_claim_check.py`'s ranking is the working countermeasure.

ONE FALSE SENTENCE FIXED as a consequence, in a file the lane did not own so the parent applied it: `bead_claim_check.py`'s NOT COVERED line claimed "nothing in this repo resolves a citation living in bead prose", which `--beads` has done since it shipped. It now says what is actually true -- neither tool reads the SENTENCE around the citation, which is where the claim is.

VERIFIED: check_all 19 of 19 clean, citation_check --self-check 7 cases OK. No mutation run, because no behaviour was added -- the measurement above is what a mutation would have told me afterwards, run first.

title: Make the citation verifier a tool and run it over the whole of kanban.md
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md cycle 76, and the kanban-staleness-audit edit made the same cycle.

I have retyped the same six-line Python citation verifier in cycles 68, 70, 71, 73, 74, 75 and 76 -- seven times -- and it has caught a wrong citation on three of those occasions, twice because the edit itself moved the lines it cited. That is the transcription disease -iezf describes, on a script rather than a list.

Shape: tools/citation_check.py over any markdown, resolving every  or  backtick citation, reporting one of three states per citation -- resolves, out of range, file missing -- and printing the landed line so a reader can see it supports the claim. House contract applies: stdlib only, parallel-safe, exit 0/1/2, printed denominator, NOT COVERED line, fixture plus a mutation of the checker.

The reason to build it is not convenience. Run over the WHOLE of kanban.md rather than the section being edited, it becomes an audit nobody has ever done: the file is 2700+ lines and its own top says roughly half is stale, and every citation in a stale entry is a candidate for having drifted silently. Expect a large first run and treat it as a survey, not a gate -- adopt a baseline the way lint does rather than trying to reach zero in one pass.

Two known limits to state in NOT COVERED. It cannot tell whether the cited line SUPPORTS the claim -- cycles 68 and 76 both cited a doc-comment line one above the constant they meant. And a citation into a file that has been renamed reads as missing rather than as moved.

ACCEPTANCE: one command reports every citation in a markdown file with its landed line; a first full run over kanban.md is recorded as a survey with counts; the mutation pass is recorded.
notes: CORRECTION: the sentence beginning "resolving every" lost two words to shell backticks when this was filed. It should read: resolving every path-colon-line or path-colon-line-dash-line backtick citation. Second time this session -- the standing note in cycle-log.md says never put backticks in a bd description passed through bash, and I did it anyway. The failure is silent: the word vanishes and only an unrelated "command not found" on stderr betrays it.
close_reason: Shipped as tools/citation_check.py. First full sweep: 146 citations across 23 markdown files, one bad. The real finding is the denominator -- 249 of kanban.md's 323 entries carry no citation at all, so 'all resolve' is a statement about 74 of them. fa81341

title: Give the boss a body, since it already has a mechanic
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md 'Requested directly by James', second bullet, after the cycle-76 audit. PLAYER-FACING, and it is the narrow half of an ask that read as entirely unbuilt for many cycles.

The ask was: at least one boss pest -- bigger health pool, a distinct sprite, a mechanic that isn't just 'armoured but more'.

The MECHANIC shipped. WaveDirector.wave_carries_boss() (game/wave_director.gd:319) feeds the HUD prep note, and game/game.gd:796 documents it: a pest whose species names a split bursts into that many when killed. That is not 'armoured but more' and it is the interesting third of the ask.

The BODY did not. game/game.gd:767 says it outright -- a pest that arrives because a boss burst is the same object. So the boss has no health pool of its own and no sprite of its own, and a player meets it as an ordinary pest that happens to explode into others.

Two constraints already on the board. Pest declares exactly two species (game/pest.gd:16-17) so a third is a real addition rather than a flag. And a corpse currently lingers a flat DEATH_LINGER for every pest (game/pest.gd:200) -- see -rowt, which wants that scaled by difficulty; a boss is the case that makes that bead obviously right.

ACCEPTANCE: a boss is distinguishable from an aphid before it dies, without reading a health bar; its health is its own number rather than a mutation multiplier; the split mechanic still works unchanged.
notes: 2026-08-17 (filing -gsai): the description's absence claims look stale. game/pest.gd:16-18 declares THREE species incl. QUEEN; the QUEEN block at pest.gd:51+ gives her health 80, speed 30, chew 11 s and assets/sprites/pest_queen.png / pest_queen_dead.png exist. Confirm before claiming — this may already be closable; -g1o4 covers the sweep.
close_reason:
ALREADY SATISFIED (cycle 104 sweep, -g1o4). Every factual claim in this bead is now false.

The description says: "Pest declares exactly two species" and "the boss has no health
pool of its own and no sprite of its own, and a player meets it as an ordinary pest that
happens to explode into others."

Verified against the code:

  * FOUR species, not two. `grep -n "^const .* := &" game/pest.gd` gives APHID:20,
    BEETLE:21, SHIELDBUG:22, QUEEN:23.
  * The Queen HAS its own health pool: the QUEEN block in `Pest.SPECIES` carries
    `"health": 80.0` against an aphid's and a beetle's own values -- read the block, it
    is right there beside `speed`, `seeds` and `chew_seconds`.
  * The Queen HAS its own sprite, and a death sprite:
    `"texture": "res://assets/sprites/pest_queen.png"` and
    `"dead_texture": "res://assets/sprites/pest_queen_dead.png"`. Both files exist on
    disk, as does the source `art_src/pest_queen.svg`.
  * It also carries `"scale": 1.45` and `"big": true`, so it is visibly larger than
    anything else on the board, and `"chew_seconds": 11.0` against an aphid's.
  * A player meets it: `grep -c "queen" game/wave_director.gd` returns 26.
  * The mechanic the title refers to is intact: `split_species: APHID`, `split_count: 3`.

So the boss has a body -- health, size, its own art alive and dead -- and had one before
this sweep looked. The bead was filed when it did not; the repo moved and the bead did
not, which is the exact failure -g1o4 exists to find.

Closing with the evidence rather than re-scoping. If the ask is now "the boss should look
MORE distinct" or "the boss needs a health BAR", that is a different, honest bead with a
different premise, and it should say what it wants rather than inheriting a claim that
has stopped being true.

title: Compute the row ceilings the other three surfaces write in comments
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md 'New this cycle (75)', first entry. Enumerated over every row-limited surface in the game, not sampled.

TitleScreen.menu_capacity() (game/title_screen.gd:169-174) COMPUTES its ceiling: it walks hint_y(n+1) + HINT_HEIGHT against the backdrop horizon and returns the count, so adding a destination moves the number on its own.

The other three write the arithmetic in prose and pin it with a test:
  - OptionsScreen, game/options_screen.gd:100-108 -- three rows from 256 at 48 foot at 392, footer at 440, gap 48 against OverlayScreen.FOOTER_GAP of 24
  - the milestone shelf, game/notebook_screen.gd:166-168 -- SHELF_ROW_PITCH 42 x 7 + 3 = 297 against a 300px box
  - RunSummary, game/run_summary.gd:77 -- rows step 38, the seventh foots at 448, BUTTON_Y is 476, an eighth would foot at 486

All three are correct and tested. All three were derived by hand, in three files, by three cycles that could not see each other, and each has to be re-derived by the next person who wants a row. The fourth shows the shape that does not rot and it is the OLDEST of them.

Blocks -1490 (the options panel decision) and the seeds row idea, both of which are 'this surface is full' problems wearing different hats.

Do not force one helper if the four shapes genuinely differ -- two of them measure to a footer and two to a box, and a helper that needs four arguments to express that is worse than four computations. The deliverable is that each surface COMPUTES its ceiling, shared or not.

ACCEPTANCE: adding a row to any of the three fails or fits without anyone re-deriving arithmetic from a comment; the existing tests still pin the result rather than being replaced by the computation.
close_reason: All four row-limited surfaces now compute their ceilings. Three are exactly full; the title screen -- the one that already computed -- has three spare. The test records measured slack per surface rather than asserting fullness as a rule.

title: Run the parallel-safe gates from one command that derives its own list
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md and CLAUDE.md step 5, cycle 75.

CLAUDE.md carries a hand-maintained list of ten stdlib checkers in tools/. Every cycle for the last several I have retyped that list into a shell for-loop to run them, which is a per-cycle transcription of a list that already exists in prose -- the same disease the workflow cured for the work queue when it made bd the only place items live.

Two consequences, both real. A new tools/*_check.py that nobody adds to the CLAUDE.md block is invisible and never runs; and the loop I retype can silently omit one, which no exit code catches because the omitted checker never reports anything.

Shape: tools/check_all.py, deriving its list from glob('tools/*_check.py') rather than from the prose block, running each, and printing a denominator -- 'ran 10 of 10 discovered'. Note the two exclusions it must handle deliberately rather than by accident: mirror_check --fix WRITES AGENTS.md so the runner must call it read-only, and run_json_check exits 2 when there is no run.json, which is the normal state at the start of a cycle and must not read as a failure.

Then CLAUDE.md's block becomes a description of what the command finds rather than the list itself, and step 2 can name one command.

ACCEPTANCE: one command runs every parallel-safe checker; adding a new tools/*_check.py makes it run without editing any list; the denominator is printed and a checker that could not run is named rather than skipped.
close_reason:
DONE. tools/check_all.py runs every parallel-safe checker from one command and
derives its own list.

NOT by the glob the bead proposed. glob('tools/*_check.py') steps over
tools/check_devtools_log.py, which puts "check" at the FRONT -- it happens to
give the right answer today because that file is a Claude Code Stop hook and not
a repo checker, and it would give the wrong one the moment somebody writes
check_something_real.py. derive-the-list names this exactly: ask what a member
would look like that your matcher would step over.

The rule is the house contract itself: a parallel-safe checker is a tools/*.py
whose source declares a "NOT COVERED:" line. Self-maintaining -- a new checker
written to house-static-checker's contract joins the run when it is saved.

Both exclusion lists are tripwires rather than convenience, per derive-the-list's
"when the hand-typing IS the check" section: NOT_PARALLEL_SAFE (import_check.py,
with the reason) and NOT_A_CHECKER (five entries, each a claim with a reason).
The third category is what makes the derivation total: any tools/*.py that is
neither derived nor listed is reported UNCLASSIFIED and FAILS the run, so a new
tool cannot be silently neither.

Its own first run proved that works by finding one: check_all.py itself, which
owes a NOT COVERED line as a house tool but is a runner, not a checker. It now
has its own SELF branch rather than an entry in a list it would contradict.

Both bead-named exclusions handled deliberately: mirror_check is only ever
invoked read-only (no arg is ever passed, and --fix is the one entry in the
parallel-safe list that WRITES), and run_json_check's exit 2 has a
CONDITIONAL_SKIP entry that PROBES for .devtools/run.json and reports "SKIPPED:
no .devtools/run.json yet -- the normal state at the start of a cycle" while
counting it out of the denominator. Named, not exempted.

Current run: "ran 15 of 15 discovered parallel-safe checker(s) -- 15 clean, 0
with findings, 0 could not run" / "CLASSIFIED 22 tools/*.py: 15 checker(s), 1 not
parallel-safe, 5 known non-checker(s), 0 unclassified". Runs them concurrently,
which the parallel-safe property is exactly what licenses.

The loop's list in .claude/skills/cycle/SKILL.md is now labelled a DESCRIPTION of
what the command finds rather than the source of truth, with a line saying so:
adding a checker there does not make it run; giving it a NOT COVERED line does.

title: Decide how the options panel grows before a feature needs it to
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md 'New this cycle (74)', third entry. Blocks -u9uh.

OptionsScreen.PANEL (game/options_screen.gd:109) is sized from the row count on purpose and its header does the arithmetic: three rows from ROWS_TOP 256 at ROW_HEIGHT 48 put the last button foot at 392 against a footer starting at 440, so the gap is 48. OverlayScreen.FOOTER_GAP is 24 (game/overlay_screen.gd:92). A FOURTH row puts the foot at exactly 440 -- gap 0 -- and trips the rule.

That is the good kind of wall. It also means every future option is a panel-geometry decision before it is anything else, and the milestone shelf taught this project that picking the way out while holding a feature is the expensive order.

Two candidate answers, both already precedented here. Grow PANEL and re-derive the arithmetic in its header, which is what the header is for. Or split audio onto its own screen the way Keys already is, which the title screen has room for only if a destination name fits 146px (see the cycle-64 entry on that).

Note PANEL is a hard-coded Rect2 with a comment saying it was DERIVED -- a recorded value with no equality assertion behind it, which is exactly the shape derive-the-list warns about. Whatever is decided, consider computing it.

ACCEPTANCE: a fourth option can be added without anyone re-deriving panel geometry in the moment; the decision and its reason are written where the next person adding an option will read them.
close_reason:
DONE, and answered in the order this bead asked for -- the decision was taken with the
arithmetic in hand rather than while holding a feature, which is the expensive order the
milestone shelf taught this project.

THE DECISION: GROW, not split. The bead offered both and the split loses on its own merits
rather than on convenience. Keys was separated because its rows come from
KeyBindings.ACTIONS, a table that grows every time the game gains a verb, and because a row
there is a capture flow. Audio is two fixed rows in the identical row grammar. A split
leaves Options holding three switches and a door, puts every audio change one navigation
step further away, and spends a title-menu destination slot on a two-row screen.

AND PANEL IS COMPUTED NOW, which is the part of this bead that outlives the decision. It
was a hard-coded Rect2 with a comment saying it was DERIVED -- the recorded-value-with-no-
equality shape derive-the-list warns about, and this bead flagged. `panel_height()` is
derived from the row count, copied in shape from KeyBindingScreen.panel_height(), with the
old 360 kept as a FLOOR so the three-switch layout is pixel-identical and the paper only
grows when it has to.

THE WALL MOVED RATHER THAN VANISHING, which matters: `rows_capacity()` used to measure rows
against a fixed 360 and answer 3, which is what made every new option a geometry decision.
The panel now grows to its rows, so the binding constraint is the 648 VIEWPORT instead --
