title: Decide what plant death means before there are two causes
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (94), second entry. Not player-facing today; the sentence
saying why is that it is a constraint on the next player-facing change to plant death.

"A hungry pest ate your X!" is accurate right now by a coincidence of there being one cause.

Enumerated: Plant.destroyed is emitted from exactly one place (game/plant.gd:1031, health
reaching zero inside take_damage), and Plant.take_damage has exactly one caller in the whole
game -- game/pest.gd:742, `meal.take_damage(EAT_DPS * delta)`, the eating path. Uprooting
does not go near it: commit_uproot frees the plant with play_exit_and_free()
(game/game.gd:1469). Game._on_plant_destroyed names the cause unconditionally
(game/game.gd:1287).

So anything that ever kills a plant another way makes that sentence a lie the moment it
lands, silently, because a message that reads perfectly is not something a test looks at
twice. Candidates that already exist in some form: a Dandelion seed bomb catching your own
bed (SeedBomb currently damages pests only, game/seed_bomb.gd:223), a weather effect, a pest
that crushes rather than eats.

The work is NOT to build that -- it is to decide the shape now, while there is one caller,
because deciding it with two is much more expensive:

  * A cause on the signal (`destroyed(plant, cause)`) mirrors what Pest already does --
    Pest.kill takes a death cause (DEATH_BITTEN, DEATH_BLASTED) and the corpse and sound read
    from it. The precedent is in the codebase and on the other side of the same fight.
  * The alternative, a second show_message call site per cause, is what this project's
    message-corpus discipline exists to prevent: every producer has to be in
    Hud.message_corpus() or the row's budget stops measuring it.

Note honestly that this may never be needed. That is a fine outcome and the entry still
earns its place, because the cost of writing it down now is one paragraph and the cost of
rediscovering it is a shipped lie.

ACCEPTANCE: either `destroyed` carries a cause and eaten_message becomes one of several
producers keyed off it, or a comment at game/plant.gd:1031 states that the signal means
"eaten" specifically and that a second cause must widen the signal rather than add a call
site. The second is cheaper and equally good; what is not acceptable is leaving it undecided.

title: Durable means tracked: .devtools is gitignored
description:
SOURCE: cycle 93 step 5, gap [G-068]. OUTSIDE this cycle's neighbourhood -- the work was the
HUD; this is about where the loop writes things down.

.gitignore:8 is `.devtools/*` with a single exception for verify-runs.jsonl at :9. So anything
written under .devtools/ is invisible to git.

Cycle 92 wrote an owed upstream comment to .devtools/pending-gh54-comment.md and its commit
message said it was "parked at" that path, as though the repo held it. It did not. The text
survived only because cycle 93 ran in the same working tree; a fresh clone, a worktree or
another machine would have lost it silently, and the commit message would still have claimed
otherwise.

This is not a harness defect and not a one-off mistake -- it is the reflex the surrounding
tooling teaches. The loop's own instructions point at .devtools/ for scratch state
(.devtools/tree.json, .devtools/import.log, .devtools/lint.log all appear in CLAUDE.md), so
"write it under .devtools/" is the obvious move, and it is exactly wrong for anything that must
outlive the session.

The work, and it is small:
  (a) Decide where owed work goes. The bead body is the honest answer -- it is in Dolt, it is
      exported to .beads/issues.jsonl, and it is what the next cycle reads. A committed file
      is the alternative when the content is long or is a patch.
  (b) Consider whether CLAUDE.md should say it. Step 5 prefers deleting rules to adding them
      and the file is 805 lines, so this may be a standing note in cycle-log.md instead -- it
      already carries eleven, and "durable means tracked; git check-ignore -v PATH answers it"
      is one line.
  (c) Check whether anything ELSE currently owed is sitting in an ignored path. That is the
      part with an actual failure mode attached, and it is one command.

Do (c) first; it is the only part that could already be losing something.

ACCEPTANCE: (c) is run and its result recorded even if empty; a decision on (a) exists in
writing; and (b) is either done as one line or refused with the reason, since a rule nobody
reads is worse than the habit it replaces.
notes:
Part (c) DONE in the cycle that filed this, since it was the only part with a live failure
mode. `git status --porcelain --ignored=matching .devtools/` lists 44 ignored files. Every one
is scratch (.log / .json / .txt / .jsonl) except .devtools/project.godot.bak and .bak2, which
are the import gate's own backups that CLAUDE.md tells you to make. Nothing owed is sitting
there: pending-gh54-comment.md was the only such file and cycle 93 posted it and deleted it.

So the failure mode is closed and (a) and (b) are the remaining work -- both judgement rather
than risk. Priority stays low accordingly.
close_reason:
All three parts done, and two of them were already done when this was filed.

(c) THE URGENT PART -- done in the cycle that filed this. 44 ignored files under .devtools/,
every one scratch (.log/.json/.txt/.jsonl) except the import gate's own project.godot.bak
files that CLAUDE.md tells you to make. Nothing owed was at risk; pending-gh54-comment.md was
the only such file and cycle 93 posted it and deleted it.

(a) WHERE OWED WORK GOES -- the bead body. It is in Dolt, it is exported to
.beads/issues.jsonl, it is committed, and it is what the next cycle reads at step 0. Cycle 93
proved the point by parking a comment in .devtools/ and having the BEAD be the thing that
survived: the text would have been lost on a fresh clone and the loop would still have
recovered, because -he1l carried the obligation. A committed file is the alternative only when
the content is long or is a patch.

(b) WHETHER CLAUDE.md SHOULD SAY IT -- no, and it already does not need to: cycle 93 added it
as a standing note in cycle-log.md ("Durable means TRACKED -- .devtools/* is gitignored
(.gitignore:8, one exception for verify-runs.jsonl), so anything owed to a future cycle goes in
a bead body or a committed file; git check-ignore -v PATH answers it in one command"). That is
the right home: it is a session fact, not a workflow rule, and CLAUDE.md is 831 lines with step
5 preferring deletion to addition.

So this closes having changed nothing further, which is the correct outcome for a bead whose
value was the check in (c).

title: Enumerate everything the game silently discards
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (93), second entry, and log-devtools [G-068]. Not
player-facing, and the sentence saying why: it is the instrument that makes player-facing
questions answerable at all.

CompostMeter.total_rotted (game/compost_meter.gd:109) exists specifically as the denominator
for total_collected -- the class header argues that a husk count alone would call sweeping one
cheap husk and letting the richest rot a 50% run -- and the post-mortem prints "Compost swept"
off it (game/run_summary.gd:260). Cycle 93 gave the message row the same treatment
(Hud.messages_refused / messages_evicted).

So the game now counts what it discards in exactly TWO systems, and -i366 sat unanswerable for
three cycles purely because the third one it needed did not exist.

The work is the enumeration nobody has done: where else does this game silently drop something
on the player's behalf? The search is for a `return` or a `continue` inside a
full-capacity or already-handled branch -- NOT for the word "drop", which will find nothing.
Known candidates to start from, and this list is a starting point rather than the answer:
  * the message queue (done this cycle)
  * the compost meter (done, cycles ago)
  * whatever caps concurrent pests -- `cmd budgets` reports pest_road_ceiling at 40 of 40,
    which is a budget at its limit and worth knowing whether hitting it discards a spawn or
    defers it
  * Sfx's voice pool: a fixed number of voices means a sound requested when all are busy
    either steals one or is dropped, and cycle 87 established the pool is real nodes

Record the answer even where it is "nothing is dropped here" -- that is the finding that stops
the next person re-deriving it, and it is what the husk and message cases both turned out to
need.

ACCEPTANCE: every place the game can discard something on the player's behalf is enumerated
with the file:line of the branch that discards, and each is marked counted / not-counted /
does-not-discard; the ones worth counting get a counter, and the reasoning is recorded for the
ones that do not so nobody proposes it twice.

title: Is a same-subsystem streak worth checking mechanically?
description:
SOURCE: cycle 92 step 5, and the workflow change it produced. OUTSIDE this cycle's
neighbourhood -- the work was two screens; this is about the loop noticing itself.

CLAUDE.md step 2 now says the player-facing steer OUTRANKS the vary-the-subsystem rule, and
that an override must be named in the cycle's close. That rule was added because cycles 91
and 92 both worked the notebook and the override was correct but unrecorded.

The rule is only worth what the recording is worth, and nothing checks it. A cycle that
works the same subsystem as the last two and says nothing looks exactly like a cycle that
varied -- which is the failure mode step 0 exists for and the reason the mirror became a
tool rather than a note.

The work: decide whether this is checkable at all, and record the answer either way.

  - A checker would need to know which subsystem a commit touched. `git diff --name-only`
    per commit is available and cheap, and "same top-level dir under game/" is a crude but
    real proxy. Three commits in a row touching the same file set, with no "overrode" in
    any of their messages, is a mechanical question.
  - Against it: the honest denominator. This has happened ONCE. house-static-checker's own
    rules say a checker that has never been observed to fire is not a checker, and cycles 89
    and 92 both correctly declined to build one on exactly that ground. One instance is not
    a pattern.

So the likely right answer is NOT YET, and the deliverable is the reasoning plus a note of
what would change it: a second unrecorded override, or a third consecutive same-subsystem
cycle. Do not build the tool to justify the bead.

ACCEPTANCE: the last ten cycles' commits are checked for consecutive same-subsystem runs and
whether each was named; the count is recorded; and either a checker is built because the
count justifies it, or the bead closes stating the count and what number would change the
answer.

title: Trim cycle-log.md's Restarting section, if the CLAUDE.md move held
description:
SOURCE: cycle 90 step 6, from OUTSIDE this cycle's neighbourhood -- the work was the HUD and
a plant's targeting loop; this is about the loop's own narrative file.

cycle-log.md is 115 lines and its "Restarting" section is roughly 40 of them: ten numbered
standing notes plus a paragraph of verb trivia (plant ids, unlocking a Chomp, driving a
click, walking a tween, snapshotting user state, run_tests.py's `--` passthrough).

CLAUDE.md had exactly this problem and cycle 89 fixed it by moving step 3's five citation
rules into .claude/skills/kanban-idea-pass/SKILL.md, taking the file from 826 to 788 lines.
The same move is available here and the same risk applies -- a pointer is not a rule -- which
is why -q1xs exists to check whether that first move held.

So this bead is deliberately BLOCKED ON -q1xs and should not be worked before it. If the
cycle-89 move turns out to have failed, doing it a second time to a second file is doing the
wrong thing twice.

What it would look like if -q1xs comes back positive: the verb trivia is a harness-usage
recipe for THIS project and belongs in a skill (a `godot-devtools-this-project` or an
addition to the existing `godot-devtools-concurrent-launch`); the ten standing notes split
into ones that are really workflow rules (the mirror, the ledger row's deadline, --body-file)
and ones that are session facts (the harness pin, the empty UI baseline). The first group
already has a home in CLAUDE.md.

What must NOT happen: the cycle counter, the last cycle's lesson, what is waiting on the
user, and how to restart are the four things this file exists for, and step 6 says so. Those
stay whatever else moves.

ACCEPTANCE: -q1xs is resolved first; then either cycle-log.md's Restarting section is reduced
to the four things the file exists for plus pointers, with the moved content landing somewhere
a reader will actually open, or this bead closes recording that the cycle-89 move did not
hold and that inlined rules are the better shape after all.

title: Never type a node path; and maybe a local node_hint verb
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md cycle 90, gap [G-065], filed upstream as gh#53. In-project half.

`get-state --node <path>` reports a missing node as `Failed: Node not found: <path>` and
nothing else. Cycle 90 polled /root/Game/Hud/Root/TopBar/MessageLabel fourteen times in a
loop -- the node is /root/Game/HUD/... -- and read fourteen identical failures as a stable
RESULT rather than a stable error. It led to hunting a defect in a feature that had worked on
the first attempt.

The upstream fix (report the longest prefix that resolved, and name the leaf if it exists
elsewhere) is filed as gh#53 and cannot reach this project while it is pinned at 0.38.0 for
gh#43. So the in-project half is a habit and a note, not a patch:

  (a) cycle-log.md's standing notes should carry it: NEVER TYPE A NODE PATH. Get it from
      `find-nodes --class X --where name=Y` or from `scene-tree`, both of which print the
      real thing. This project's own HUD is `/root/Game/HUD` while its class is `Hud`, so
      the wrong guess is the natural one.
  (b) Consider a `devtools_ext` verb -- `cmd node_hint --args '{"path": "..."}'` -- that does
      what gh#53 asks for, locally: walk the path, report the deepest segment that resolved
      and that node's children, then `find_children(leaf, "", true, false)` for the leaf name
      anywhere in the tree. Ten lines, works at the pin, and turns the failure into the
      answer.

Do (a) regardless; it is free. Decide (b) on whether a second person hits this -- one
sighting is an observation. Note that -rvvt proposes a devtools_ext verb for the same
reason (the pause/repaint gap), so if both get built they are the second and third
project-local workarounds for harness gaps, which is itself worth noticing: at that point
the pin is costing real work and -ny3h's cost/benefit has changed.

ACCEPTANCE: the standing note exists in cycle-log.md; and either the verb is built and
demonstrated on the exact path that failed this cycle, or the bead records why one sighting
was not enough and closes.
close_reason: STALE (mandatory half done): cycle-log.md:362-366 carries 'NEVER TYPE A NODE PATH' verbatim including the /root/Game/HUD vs Hud trap. The bead's own bar for the rest is a second sighting; none logged.

title: Check whether moving rules out of CLAUDE.md into a skill held
description:
SOURCE: cycle 89 step 5, and the kanban-idea-pass skill built the same cycle. OUTSIDE this
cycle's neighbourhood -- the work was an autoload guard; this is about the loop's own files.

Step 5 moved step 3's five citation rules out of CLAUDE.md and into
.claude/skills/kanban-idea-pass/SKILL.md, leaving a pointer. CLAUDE.md went 826 -> 788 lines.

That is a move, not a deletion, and it introduces a risk worth naming rather than hoping about:
a reader working from the loop now sees a pointer where they used to see the rules. The
mitigation in place is that the pointer names all five rules in one sentence each and says the
skill is not optional reading. Whether that is enough is an empirical question and NOT one this
bead can answer by reasoning.

The check: at the end of a later cycle, ask whether step 3's entries that cycle actually
followed the five rules, and whether the skill was opened. If entries drift back toward
uncited claims, the pointer failed and the rules belong back inline -- which would itself be a
finding about moving rules into skills, applicable to the four other places this loop points at
one.

This is deliberately a bead and not a note, because it is a measurement that can only be taken
later, and step 6's own rule says an acceptance criterion needing evidence a commit cannot
produce should be split out and said so. This IS that split-out half.

Do not do this in cycle 90. Two cycles of distance is the minimum for the question to mean
anything, and the honest version records which cycles were examined.

ACCEPTANCE: at least two cycles' worth of kanban entries written after cycle 89 are checked
against kanban-idea-pass's five rules, one verdict per entry with the rule it missed if any;
the finding says whether the pointer held; if it did not, the rules go back into CLAUDE.md and
the reason is recorded where the next person considering a move will read it.

title: Decide whether repeated sounds want a per-play jitter
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md 'New this cycle (87)', second entry. PLAYER-FACING, and it has a real tension to resolve first.

The most repeated sounds in the game fire often enough to read as machine-gun sameness: `CORN_FIRED` every 0.62s at level 3 with several cobs on the board, `PEST_KILLED` up to forty times in a wave. The standard fix is a small random pitch jitter per play.

Cycle 87 removed the objection to it. Voices are pooled, and `tune_voice` writes every property unconditionally so nothing inherits a previous event's values — argued in cycle 74 and OBSERVED in cycle 87, where `Voice0` went 1.12 to 1.0 across two kills. So a per-play value is provably safe to apply there.

**The tension, and it is the reason this is a bead rather than a patch.** `test_no_two_events_are_the_same_sound` is currently the only thing keeping two events from collapsing into one sound, and it works by deriving the (file, volume, pitch) triple from the tables. A per-play jitter makes that test a statement about the TABLE rather than about what the player hears — two events 0.04 apart in the table could overlap once jitter is applied.

So decide the shape before writing it: a jitter RANGE per event that the twin check accounts for (assert the ranges do not overlap, not that the centres differ), or jitter only on events with no near neighbour, or a deterministic per-instance variation rather than a random one.

Note also that `REPEAT_MS` already exists to stop a stream of calls becoming one loud sound, and it solves a different half of the same complaint — check whether the sameness is actually audible before assuming it is, since the throttle may already be doing the work.

ACCEPTANCE: sameness is confirmed audible before anything changes; whatever ships keeps the twin check meaningful, and its doc says which of the two the check now asserts.
close_reason: Cycle 113; merged, 835 tests, lint 0, check_all 19/19. Hints page verified live and its notes fixed to wrap inside the pane.

title: Ask whether a rich husk should sound rich
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md 'New this cycle (87)', first entry. PLAYER-FACING.

A kill and the husk it drops are two sounds for one event: `Sfx.PEST_KILLED` (or `PEST_KILLED_HARD` since cycle 87), then `HUSK_COLLECTED` a moment later when the player sweeps it. The kill now says how hard it was. The husk does not — it pays 1.5x or 3x and sounds identical every time.

The seam exists. `HuskLayer.radius_for` (`game/husk_layer.gd:31`) and `glow_for` (`:44`) both read the husk's value already, and `Sfx.kill_event_for` is the pattern to copy: a pure static taking the number, not the object.

**Ask the design question before building.** A kill and its sweep are seconds apart, not milliseconds, and the pitch interval that works for two sounds heard back to back may be inaudible across a gap that long. Cycle 87 deliberately kept the kill interval small because a kill is the most frequent sound in the game; the same reasoning may say a husk needs a WIDER interval, or a different channel entirely, or nothing at all.

Measure first: how long is the median gap between a kill and its sweep in a driven wave? `CompostMeter.lifetime_for` bounds the maximum, and the harness can drive a wave and time the sweeps.

If the answer is that a pitch cannot carry it, that is a finding and this closes. The honest alternative is that the husk's existing size and ring brightness already say "rich" visually, and adding an audio channel to a cue that is already legible is decoration.

ACCEPTANCE: a measured median gap; a stated decision either way; if a pitch ships it goes through the table and the existing twin check, not a per-call override.
close_reason: WONTFIX after analysis: the husk's value cue must land BEFORE the sweep decision, and HUSK_COLLECTED plays after the click is spent. Richest husks also rot in 4.5s so a pitch interval has no reference to be heard against. Visual channel (radius/glow/pips) closes it in the actionable window.

title: Find the duplicates already in the queue
description:
SOURCE: log-devtools.md, cycle 84, and CLAUDE.md step 6's existing rule. OUTSIDE this cycle's neighbourhood — it is about the queue rather than the game.

Cycle 84 claimed a bead asking for a weather readout, checked the code, found none, and discovered mid-cycle that the identical request had been filed in cycle 17 (`-saaw`), measured, and refused — with every candidate string's width recorded in its notes.

Step 6 already says: "If a source points at a bead that is already open, add a note to THAT bead — do not file a duplicate." What it does not say is **how to notice**, and the answer is one command: `bd search "<a phrase from the entry>"`. `verify-bd-item`'s `confirm` step now says to search the queue as well as the code, which fixes it going forward.

This bead is the retrospective half: how many other duplicates are already open? Three are known — `-t0vy`/`-saaw` (this cycle), and cycles 53-56 each filed an item whose own description said "duplicate of the open X, filed only to record the second identification". The queue is 124 items and grew mostly by filing 3-8 per cycle for eighty cycles, so the base rate is unlikely to be zero.

Method that respects the cost of getting it wrong: group open beads by the nouns in their titles (surface, subsystem, mechanic), read each group, and merge only where two items ask the SAME question — not where they ask related ones. `kanban-staleness-audit`'s bar applies: a wrong merge loses an item nobody will think of again, and merging is harder to undo than leaving a near-duplicate.

Where two items really are one, keep the OLDER — it usually carries the measurement, which is the part cycle 84 nearly threw away.

ACCEPTANCE: every open bead is in a named group; any merges are recorded with both ids and the reason; the count of true duplicates found is reported even if it is zero, since zero over 124 items is itself a result about how the queue has been filled.
close_reason:
Done. 90 open beads, 14 groups, every open bead in exactly one group -- proved by set difference against bd list --status=open rather than by reading down the list. Written up in .claude/bead-groups-cycle111.md.

TRUE DUPLICATES FOUND: ONE, in 90. The bead predicted 'the base rate is unlikely to be zero' and it was right, but only just -- 1.1%.

  MERGED: -fdz1 superseded by -8u01. Same file (kanban.md), same skill (kanban-staleness-audit), same sections, same bar. Kept the older per this bead's own rule, and it earned it: -8u01 carries cycle 34's four file:line proofs that its sampled section was 100% stale. -fdz1's two real contributions were folded into -8u01's notes BEFORE superseding -- 'the six oldest sections' is a finishable unit where 'the rest' is not, and the reason those sections rot is that they predate the cycle-31 file:line rule, which is what makes them unfalsifiable.

WHY THE RATE IS SO LOW, which is the more useful finding. The queue's own anti-duplication rules were already working, visibly, in the bodies: -a155 opens 'Sharpens -6e2e rather than duplicating it -- read that one first'; -iiyg cites '-v9px which this depends on and does not replace'; -kihy says 'if they turn out to overlap once opened, fold rather than duplicate -- per step 6'. Three beads that each stopped short of being a duplicate, in writing, because whoever filed them searched first. So this retrospective sweep mostly confirms the forward fix already took.

FOUR PAIRS LOOKED LIKE DUPLICATES AND WERE NOT: -r722/-0y0w are different panels (selection readout vs the shop's name/blurb/price list); -v9px/-iiyg are a dependency ALREADY RECORDED, and in the direction opposite to my guess (v9px depends on iiyg -- the tracker was right and I was wrong); -9vq6/-orcl are two halves (a tool that never reads beads, and the support judgement no tool can make); -8ute/-kihy/-w0wh are a hierarchy.

THE REAL DEFECT IS MISSING STRUCTURE, NOT DUPLICATION. Three relationships lived in prose and not in the tracker. Recorded: -kihy and -w0wh now depend on -8ute. And -w0wh NAMED THE WRONG UMBRELLA -- it scopes itself as 'not the whole document, which is -hwo6's larger job', but -hwo6 audits STYLE.md, a different document; the whole-brief job is -8ute, already open when -w0wh was filed. Corrected in its notes. Nobody filed a duplicate here; somebody filed a CHILD CITING THE WRONG PARENT, which is harder to spot and costs the same -- two people audit one document without knowing it.

WHAT THE GROUPING SHOWS THAT THE COUNT DOES NOT: one group is 17% of the queue. 'Width budgets and the corpus pattern' is 15 beads, bigger than the next two groups combined -- one technique applied down a series of surfaces plus five meta-beads about the technique itself. None should be merged, but the queue is saying the project has one favourite kind of work and is generating it faster than it closes it. -yoc2 ('decide whether the other HUD surfaces deserve corpus-style checking') is exactly the decision that would resolve the group, it sits inside that group, and it is a P2 nobody has taken. Second: 'Open design questions' (7) is the only group whose items cannot be closed by writing code, and three are already blocked on the user.

title: Ask whether the overlays should switch rather than refuse
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (83), third entry. PLAYER-FACING.

_open_notebook, _open_keys and _open_options in game/title_screen.gd all return early when overlay_open() is true, so the three overlay screens are mutually exclusive. Cycle 83 found this by driving them: firing one entry point while another was open silently did nothing, and the verb reported success because the method WAS called and DID return.

For a player that is right in the case it was written for -- a second click on a menu button while a screen is up should not stack screens. It is less obviously right for the case nobody considered: there is no way to go from the notebook to the options without passing through the title menu, and the notebook is the screen whose whole job is to be read alongside something.

Two honest answers. Keep the refusal and accept the trip through the menu, which is two clicks and entirely fine for screens a player visits rarely. Or let a menu button switch the open overlay, which is one line per handler (close, then open) and makes the menu behave like a tab strip.

Check before choosing: whether the menu buttons are even reachable while an overlay is up. _set_menu_active(false) is called on open, so they may be disabled -- in which case the current behaviour is not a refusal a player can trigger at all, and this bead is about the entry points rather than about the game.

ACCEPTANCE: a stated decision; if the menu is disabled while an overlay is open, that is recorded and this closes as a tooling note rather than a UX one.
close_reason: STALE: title_screen.gd:935-946 sets both FOCUS_NONE and MOUSE_FILTER_IGNORE on every menu button, called with false at :860/:886/:913. The refusal is unreachable by a player.

title: Write down that the pause card is the one screen findings must read frozen
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (83), second entry.

Every standing note in this project says to unpause before findings, because a frozen tree catches containers mid-layout -- cycles 60 and 65 both lost time to that, one on a panel mid-entrance and one on a label whose HBox had not finished laying out.

The pause card is the documented exception and nothing documents it. fire-entry-point pause leaves SceneTree.paused true, which is correct: the card IS a paused state, the bridge answers while paused, and unpausing to check it would be checking a screen that cannot exist unpaused.

Cycle 83 got 0 findings on it after 60 settle frames while paused, so the layout does settle -- process frames still tick, only the tree is paused. That is the fact worth recording, since the standing note reads as though nothing settles while paused.

Smallest version is a sentence in cycle-log.md's restart notes beside the existing unpause-before-findings note. Better if the harness ever grows a  flag on an entry point, which would make the exception declarative rather than remembered -- worth a gap entry if it does not exist upstream.

ACCEPTANCE: the exception is stated next to the rule it contradicts, with the reason process frames still tick; anyone reading the unpause rule finds the pause card case in the same breath.
notes: CORRECTION: two words were eaten by shell backticks when this was filed. The sentence should read: "Better if the harness ever grows a paused flag on an entry point, which would make the exception declarative rather than remembered." Third time this session that backticks in a bd description have silently eaten a word -- the standing note says never to use them and I keep doing it, which suggests the note is the wrong countermeasure.
close_reason: STALE: premise false. cycle-log.md:366 already says 'unpause before findings -- except the pause card', in the same sentence as the rule it was said to contradict. Only the parenthetical reason is unwritten.

title: Test whether a computed ceiling actually keeps a surface uncrowded
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (82), first entry. An observation that wants a second data point before it becomes advice.

Measured in cycle 82: OptionsScreen 3 of 3, the milestone shelf 7 of 7, RunSummary 7 of 7 -- every hand-written ceiling confirmed exactly -- and TitleScreen.menu_capacity (game/title_screen.gd:169-174), the only surface that already computed its limit, reports 8 against 5 used.

Three of four are exactly full and the fourth is the one nobody had to re-derive. The proposed mechanism: a ceiling stated in prose is discovered by arithmetic while holding a feature, and by then the feature is what you are defending; a ceiling that is a function can be consulted before starting.

One data point. It may equally be that the title screen simply has fewer things wanting to be on it, which is the obvious confound and the reason this is a bead rather than a rule.

The test is cheap and takes cycles rather than hours: the three surfaces now compute their ceilings as of cycle 82. Watch whether the next several features aimed at them get proposed differently -- -f9zc already competes three beads for one message-row slot, and -1490 and -lp97 were both blocked on this arithmetic. Record what actually happens.

ACCEPTANCE: after five more cycles, a recorded observation of whether any feature aimed at those three surfaces consulted the capacity before being designed; the confound is named either way.

title: Ask whether the width budgets want their own rows_that_fit
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (82), third entry. A question first and a refactor only if the answer is yes.

Cycle 82 gave four surfaces one shared function for does this many rows fit. The same shape exists one level down for WIDTH and is hand-written three different ways:
  - Hud.WORST_CASE_TEXT measures the longest string a readout can hold
  - TitleScreen needs a destination name to fit a 146px cell (cycle 64 recorded shortening a word for it)
  - Game.BUDGET_FLOOR prices seven couplings and check_budgets refuses a build that overruns one

Three mechanisms for one question. The budget system is the most developed of them and cycle 79 proved it can make a design decision when it refuses -- the armed-uproot prompt's two optional clauses became mutually exclusive because 1064px against 876px said so.

So the honest first step is NOT to unify. It is to ask whether these three are the same question. A row ceiling is arithmetic over constants; a width ceiling needs a font, a theme and a resolved Label, which is why the budget system is a runtime check and rows_that_fit is a pure static. They may be the same shape and different worlds.

Deliverable is a written answer either way. If they unify, say what the shared function takes. If they do not, say why in a place the next person asking will find it -- probably next to rows_that_fit, which is where the question now naturally arises.

ACCEPTANCE: a recorded decision with its reason; if the answer is no, rows_that_fit's doc says so, so the question is not re-asked every time someone notices the resemblance.

title: Make a 3x husk look like a 3x husk
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (81), second entry. PLAYER-FACING. Pairs with -rowt.

husk_multiplier() is now a product across a pest's traits, so a hungry winged kill drops a husk worth 1.5 x 2.0 = 3.0. That is the correct economy and it is invisible: HuskLayer.radius_for (game/husk_layer.gd:31) and glow_for (:44) both read the husk's VALUE, so a 3x husk is simply a big one, indistinguishable from a big one for any other reason.

The rarest kill in the game therefore looks like a lucky ordinary one. The game already has a vocabulary for this came from something remarkable -- -rowt wants DEATH_LINGER scaled by the same multiplier -- and doing both would make a rare kill legible twice, at the corpse and at the husk it leaves.

Note the constraint the husk already lives under: its rot timer is drawn as a swept arc at a fixed radius (the partial arc = time remaining row in game/OVERLAY_GRAMMAR.md), so whatever marks a rich husk must not collide with that.

Check before building: value already drives radius and glow, so a 3x husk may ALREADY be visibly bigger than any single-mutation one. If so this bead is about naming the difference rather than creating it, and the acceptance below is the measurement.

ACCEPTANCE: the biggest single-mutation husk and the smallest paired husk are measured against each other; if they are already distinguishable, that is recorded and the bead closes; if not, a second channel says so.
close_reason: Measured, then fixed. Radius and glow both saturate at FULL_VALUE=9, so 6 of the 10 reachable drop values rendered identically -- the acceptance's 'if not, a second channel says so' branch. HuskLayer.overflow_pips is that channel; screenshot confirms v9 vs v14 differ by exactly one pip.

title: Decide whether pairs belong in the campaign or only in endless
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (81), third entry. A decision, not a change.

SECOND_MUTATION_START_WAVE is 20 (game/wave_director.gd:51) and the campaign's fixed table ends at 16 (WaveDirector.WAVES). So paired pests are an endless-only feature and a player who finishes the campaign and stops never meets one.

That is defensible: endless is where variety runs out, which is the argument the constant's own doc comment makes. It is also invisible, and it was arrived at by arithmetic rather than chosen -- 20 was picked as a campaign's worth after single mutations start at 8, and the table happening to end at 16 made it endless-only as a side effect.

Two honest answers. Put a pair in the campaign's last waves -- wave 16 is already described as deliberately sized to land on the pest ceiling exactly, so it is the wave built to be the hardest thing a campaign player meets. Or keep it endless-only and say so somewhere the player can read, which is the notebook (see -ei83, which wants a home for content that currently shows once and vanishes).

ACCEPTANCE: a stated decision with its reason recorded next to SECOND_MUTATION_START_WAVE; if pairs stay endless-only, a player has some way to learn the category exists.
close_reason: STALE: premise false. WAVES has 22 rows not 16 (live wave_count=22), SECOND_MUTATION_START_WAVE=20 (wave_director.gd:80), and _build_schedule gates on current_wave alone with no mode flag (:1138). Campaign waves 20-22 already roll pairs.

title: Name the situations the harness's unused verbs are for
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (80), third entry, and log-devtools.md across many cycles. OUTSIDE this cycle's neighbourhood -- it is about the tooling's discoverability rather than the game.

--snapshot-userstate existed for eighty cycles before anything used it. Cycle 80 needed to clear a persisted flag in a running game to verify a fix; clearing it without the flag would have written the developer's real save, which the harness warns surfaces later as unrelated headless failures. It worked first time.

The pattern, and it has now repeated: step-time --then-pause went unused for 71 cycles until cycle 72 needed a sub-second tween. set-game-speed's argument form was wrong in my hands twice. These verbs are not missing and not broken -- nothing names the SITUATION each is for, so they are found only by someone reading the reference cover to cover at the moment of need.

Deliverable is a situation-to-verb index in this project's own words, in cycle-log.md's restart notes or a skill: verify a fix to a once-per-save behaviour -> launch --snapshot-userstate; catch a tween shorter than a round trip -> pause THEN step-time --then-pause; ask whether a verb exists at all -> list-commands --offline.

Derive it rather than remembering it: read log-devtools.md for every entry where a verb was found late or used wrongly, since that log IS the record of which situations went unserved. Expect the list to be short and the value to be in it existing at all.

ACCEPTANCE: a situation-first index exists somewhere the loop reads at the start of a cycle; every entry names a situation this project has actually been in, with the cycle it happened.
close_reason: STALE (built where asked): cycle-log.md:379-393 is a situation-first index containing all three of the bead's own worked examples. Residual, deliberately not refiled: the entries are undated.

title: Give a missed hint somewhere to be found again
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (80), second entry. PLAYER-FACING.

The move tip fires once per save and then never again, which is right -- a hint that becomes wallpaper is worse than none. But a player who missed it, or who read it while deciding something else, has no route back to it.

The notebook (game/notebook_screen.gd) documents plants and milestones and says nothing about the interactions the hints teach. That is the natural second home for content that currently shows once and vanishes, and it costs no HUD width -- which matters because -f9zc is about three features competing for one row's worth of it.

Scope carefully. This is not put every message in the notebook: it is the hints specifically, which are the ones deliberately shown a single time. Today that is one, so the deliverable is small and the value is that the SECOND hint has somewhere to live before it is written.

Depends on the hint-versus-achievement split (-0q3q) -- if hints stay mixed into Milestones.TABLE the notebook cannot tell them apart to render them differently.

ACCEPTANCE: the move tip's content is findable in the notebook without having armed an uproot; a player who never saw the prompt can still learn the interaction.
notes: Cycle 89 sharpens this. spend_hint(id, shown) now exists (game/run_config.gd:432): a hint the player was NOT shown returns false and stays owed, so the missed-hint state this bead is about is now a real, queryable condition rather than an inference -- has_milestone is false and the hint is in RunConfig.HINTS. Two things worth knowing before designing the surface. (1) The notebook shelf already has a vocabulary for 'a thing you have not got yet': notebook_screen.gd:445 reads earned state and unearned rows are drawn greyed with their note prefixed, so the visual language exists. (2) But hints are deliberately kept OUT of Milestones.TABLE, with the reason written at game/run_config.gd:105-110 -- an id absent from TABLE is invisible on the shelf, and the shelf counts earned off TABLE (notebook_screen.gd:505) so a foreign id cannot push its total past its rows. So this cannot be solved by adding HINT_MOVE_PREVIEW to TABLE; that would put a tip on an achievement shelf and break the count's guard. The surface has to be its own thing, or the shelf needs a second section that renders HINTS separately.
close_reason: Cycle 113; merged, 835 tests, lint 0, check_all 19/19. Hints page verified live and its notes fixed to wrap inside the pane.

title: Give the UI findings baseline something to compare against
description:
SOURCE: CLAUDE.md step 2, the rule added in cycle 79, plus -v9px which this depends on and does not replace.

The UI findings baseline is empty, so every ui_layout finding gates as NEW and there is nothing to compare against. Cycle 79 hit that: one container_layout_drift right after a message-row text change, on an UNPAUSED tree, which the existing pause-transient warning does not cover. Establishing it was a transient took a relaunch, 90 settle frames, a re-trigger and two more runs.

That procedure is now written into step 2 and it is a workaround. The real fix is -v9px, recapturing the baseline -- but a baseline captured while the game is in one arbitrary state is worth little, and that is presumably why it has sat open.

So the question this bead asks is narrower than -v9px and might unblock it: WHICH states should the baseline cover? Candidates worth a capture each are an idle board mid-prep, a wave in progress, an armed uproot with the longest message on the row, and the selection panel open. If the answer is that a single capture cannot represent the game, that is a finding and the honest response is to say so rather than to keep a baseline nobody trusts.

ACCEPTANCE: either a baseline covering named states with the states written down, or a recorded decision that ui_layout gating is not useful for this project and why -- both are better than an empty file that makes every finding NEW.

title: Make LEVELS the cob's single source of truth by name, not by habit
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (79), third entry.

Three pure statics on CornCobbler now read the LEVELS table so that drawing, firing and economy cannot drift from it: kernel_angle_offsets (the firing angles, shared with _draw_muzzle_fan), spread_arc_span (which levels wear an arc, added cycle 70) and upgrade_spend (what has been spent reaching a level, added cycle 79).

That is three instances of one idea with no name. The class header explains the ladder at length and never says the rule, so the fourth question gets answered by whoever asks it, wherever they are standing.

The obvious missing one: what does it cost to REACH level N, which the shop, the selection panel and the armed prompt would each otherwise compute. upgrade_cost() answers only the next step.

This is a small refactor with a documentation deliverable attached, and the documentation is the point -- see derive-the-list for why a table with three derived readers and no stated rule grows a fourth reader that types its own constant.

ACCEPTANCE: the rule is stated on LEVELS itself; any new question about a cob is a pure static over it; a hand-typed number derived from LEVELS anywhere in game/ is either removed or has a comment saying why it is not derived.
close_reason:
Named, and writing the rule down found the exact case it describes.

THE FIND, which is worth more than the refactor: spread_arc_span had ZERO PRODUCTION CALLERS while THREE separate places asserted it had one -- its own inline comment (corn_cobbler.gd:287-293), game/sfx.gd:687 ('the fourth time this project has needed that move: spread_arc_span, ...'), and test_placement.gd:436-439 ('It asserts spread_arc_span, which is the function _draw_muzzle_fan actually reads'). _draw_muzzle_fan was computing the arc from offsets[0]/offsets[-1] -- recomputing the spread beside the table -- and the picture was IDENTICAL either way, which is exactly what let it survive. Three comments and a test header believed a wiring that did not exist. Now wired; that 3-line change is the entire production diff.

THE PREMISE WAS UNDERSTATED. Not three level-taking statics but EIGHT (aim_step_pip_travel, kernel_angle_offsets, spread_for, kernels_connecting_at, single_target_dps, muzzle_pips, spread_arc_span, upgrade_spend). And the ladder machinery has since moved to Plant (ladder_row / ladder_upgrade_cost / ladder_spend), so CornCobbler.upgrade_spend is now a named wrapper over Plant.ladder_spend(LEVELS, for_level).

THE RULE: 'If the answer changes when a row here changes, it is a pure static over LEVELS taking for_level -- never a literal, never a branch on the level number, and never recomputed beside a caller that already had the row in hand.'

PLACED ON const LEVELS ITSELF, not in the class header, and the reasoning for the location is the good part: the class header explains the ladder's DESIGN and is read once, by whoever changes the ladder. The reader about to break the rule is in the opposite posture -- consulting the table for a number at the moment they type the literal. sfx.gd:304 literally reaches in as CornCobbler.LEVELS[2]['interval']; that reader's eyes land on the table's own docstring. The header is the location that already existed and already failed to transfer the rule.

The block names the three failures separately, because their commonality is the part never written down: kernel_angle_offsets = two subsystems asking the same question; spread_arc_span = a call site restating a row; upgrade_spend = a total the table implies and nobody stores.

VERDICT ON 'COST TO REACH LEVEL N': the SAME THING under another name. upgrade_spend(for_level) is literally it, and Plant.ladder_spend is the generic form -- both already exist and both already have production callers. It reads as missing only because upgrade_cost() answers the next step and sounds like it covers the subject. NO fourth static added; instead the LEVELS block says 'do not add a third name for it' and a test walks LEVELS asserting upgrade_spend(n) == sum of steps below n == Plant.ladder_spend(LEVELS, n) at every rung.

No player-visible change is claimed. The arc is bit-identical -- the offsets are symmetric about 0 and float halving is exact, so old and new differ by 0.00e+00.

VERIFIED at the parent: 868/868 tests, lint 0, import OK, suite_reach 0 NEW.

title: Find out whether a 0.45s chew is long enough to read
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (78), third entry. A measurement, not a change.

The chew ring now sweeps closed over the chew (game/chomp_flower.gd:154-156). For an aphid that is 0.45s, which is shorter than a bus round-trip -- cycle 78 tried four ways to photograph it mid-sweep and got none. That is a tooling problem, and underneath it is a design question nobody has asked: is 0.45s long enough for a ring to say anything to a player at all?

The design doc claim is that a Chomp takes a while eating BIGGER pests, so a beetle is the case the readout exists for and an aphid may be a flash nobody parses. If so, the honest answer might be that the ring should not appear for a chew under some threshold, the way the late-bite sprite swap already has LATE_BITE_THRESHOLD.

Measure before deciding: the beetle chew duration against the aphid one, and both against a rough floor for what a moving arc can convey. Then decide whether the aphid case wants suppressing, lengthening, or leaving alone.

Depends on -ip4n, which is the photograph, and a beetle is the easier subject for it for the same reason.

ACCEPTANCE: both chew durations recorded as numbers; a stated decision about the short case with its reason, even if the decision is to leave it.
close_reason:
MEASURED AND DECIDED. The ring stays; nothing is suppressed.

BOTH DURATIONS, as the acceptance asked, and all five rather than two.
Pest.SPECIES chew_seconds: aphid 0.45, beetle 2.6, Shield Bug 3.0, Nurse Beetle 5.0,
Queen 11.0. MUTATION_ARMOURED doubles any of them, so the real range the ring must work
across is 0.45s to 22s.

The number the bead did not have: the aphid is 5.8x shorter than the next one up. It is not
merely the shortest, it is in a different league from every other case -- and it is the
commonest pest in the game.

THE DECISION: NO SUPPRESSION. Three reasons, and the third is the one that settles it.

1. THE RING MEANS BUSY. A Chomp mid-chew cannot grab anything (is_busy() is `_held != null`)
   and the ring is what says so. Suppress it below a threshold and a busy Chomp reads as a
   FREE one for exactly as long as the suppression lasts -- at the moment a player is most
   likely to be scanning for a mouth to throw the next pest at. The bead framed this as
   "is the flash readable"; the more important question is what its ABSENCE says, and its
   absence already means something.

2. IT WOULD HIDE THE MAJORITY CASE. The aphid is the pest the player sees most, so any
   threshold above 0.45s removes the ring from most chews in the game -- leaving a cue too
   rare for anyone to learn, which is a worse outcome than a brief one.

3. THE SHOP ALREADY PROMISED THE FLASH. PlantCatalog's Chomp entry reads: "Eats small pests
   instantly. Big ones take a while -- and it is busy the whole time." A 0.45s sweep reading
   as instantaneous is not a cue failing. It is the cue agreeing with the sentence the
   player was sold before they bought the plant. The ring exists for "big ones take a
   while", and there it has 2.6 to 22 seconds to work in.

That third point is what reframed the item. The bead's premise -- "a design question nobody
has asked" -- was not quite right: it had been answered, in the shop line, and nothing
checked that the answer was still true of the numbers.

SO THE DELIVERABLE IS A RELATIONSHIP, NOT TWO RECORDED NUMBERS. The acceptance asked for
"both chew durations recorded as numbers"; recorded numbers go stale, and this file has
spent several cycles removing exactly that shape.
test_the_chomps_shop_line_is_true_of_the_chew_table derives them from SPECIES and pins all
three clauses of the blurb:
  * the quickest meal is the SMALLEST pest -- not merely some pest. If the Queen were ever
    fastest to eat, the sentence would be false while every duration in it stayed the same.
  * every other species takes at least 4x the aphid's chew. A RELATIVE gap deliberately,
    because "instant" is a fact about perception and no test here can measure one; what it
    can measure is that the two halves of the sentence describe two different experiences.
  * a Chomp is busy for even the quickest meal, with chew progress left to draw -- which is
    the assertion that makes the no-suppression decision structural rather than a comment.

Mutation-tested: aphid 0.45 -> 1.2 fires the gap assertion naming both durations.

A SIDE EFFECT WORTH RECORDING: writing this paid down recorded debt. `chew_progress` was in
tools/suite_reach_baseline.json as a symbol no test named, and the suite FAILED telling me
to re-bank the baseline. Banked -- 43 symbol findings down to 42.

WHAT WAS NOT DONE, and why it is not a gap: no photograph. -ip4n already did that in cycle
14 and pinned what the picture measured. The only runtime question left here is "is 0.45s
long enough for a person to READ", which is a fact about perception that no bridge verb can
answer -- the harness can photograph the sweep and cannot tell you whether anyone parsed it.
If that question ever needs a real answer it needs a player, not a tool.

title: Write down which radii the plant readouts occupy
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (78), second entry.

Three plants own a radial readout in the band between the sprite and the cell edge, and the constraints keeping them apart live in three files plus one test:
  - ChompFlower.CHEW_RING_RADIUS is 22 (game/chomp_flower.gd)
  - CornCobbler states its muzzle fan sits inside about 26 (game/corn_cobbler.gd:71-75)
  - Sunflower puts its gauge nearest corner at exactly 26.0, and test_combat asserts that corner is outside the chew ring

So the band is fully spoken for, and the next plant with a per-instance readout will discover that by overlapping something rather than by looking it up. Cycle 78 rediscovered it while moving the chew ring from 16 to 22 -- the upper bound came from a test assertion in another plant is file, which is a fine place for a gate and a poor place for a fact.

Smallest useful version is a comment on Plant listing who occupies what, which costs nothing and rots. Better is a constant per occupant plus one test asserting they do not overlap, derived from the constants rather than from a list someone typed -- see derive-the-list.

Note the fourth occupant that is NOT in the band and should be said so explicitly: the range rings are 176 and live outside all of this.

ACCEPTANCE: adding a fifth radial readout means reading one place; a test fails if two occupants overlap, and it iterates the occupants rather than naming pairs.
close_reason:
Written down as game/readout_band.gd, and the writing-down found a live overlap nine hand-written assertions across three files had missed.

THE CENSUS WAS BADLY SHORT. The bead named three occupants; there are FIVE, and two of them are marks every plant wears:
  uproot clock  selection_marker.gd  [14.5, 17.5]
  chew ring     chomp_flower.gd      [20.5, 23.5]
  fang crown    chomp_flower.gd      [25.3, 30.7]
  alone ring    sole_cover_marks.gd  [30.0, 32.0]
  reach ring    plant.gd             [63, 193]

THE FOURTH OCCUPANT ARRIVED EXACTLY AS THE BEAD PREDICTED IT WOULD. The fang crown discovered the band by needing to clear the chew ring, argued in prose in its own header and pinned by an assertion in a THIRD file. That is the bead's thesis happening while the bead sat open.

THE FINDING, verified independently at the parent: four marks is six pairs, five of which were written down by hand across five headers and two test files. The sixth is a real overlap -- fang crown outer 30.7 against alone ring inner 30.0, 0.7 px shared. A selected, upgraded Chomp holding no road cell alone puts two of its four teeth under a dash. Neither mark can simply move: the cell edge is 32.0, so there is no room above the crown for a 2.0 px ring. The widest unclaimed slice anywhere in the band is 3.0 px.

The reach ring did NOT become a sixth problem -- the opposite. It is one implementation over eight plants now and the shortest reach in the catalogue is 64, twice the 32 px half-cell, so the bead's prose note about range rings living outside all this is a derived assertion instead of a sentence.

THE SHAPE, and the argument is the good part. Both offered options fail, for opposite reasons: a SHARED CONSTANT makes 'does the chew ring sit inside the band' compare the band to itself, which is exactly the trap that kept the glyph table unwired last cycle; a RETYPED TABLE creates the second copy that table deliberately keeps, for a check that does not need one. What shipped is neither: DERIVED INPUTS, RELATIONAL CLAIM. Every interval is computed from the constant the draw call itself reads, and the claim is not an equality -- nothing asserts the chew ring is at 22 -- it is that four independently authored intervals do not intersect. Move any one constant and it goes red. Two sides without duplication.

NO BEAD FILED for the overlap, deliberately. It is recorded in READOUT_BAND_KNOWN_COLLISIONS with its reason AND GATED: if someone fixes it, the stale row fails and must be deleted in the same commit. A gated record that cannot rot is stronger than a queue entry that can. The two candidate fixes for whoever takes it: FANG_RADIUS 28 -> 27.3 puts the crown's outer rim exactly at 30.0, or the alone ring gives up the outer band -- both are grammar decisions rather than arithmetic, which is why the lane did not take them.

No player-visible change: every constant that decides what is drawn is byte-identical and the four plant edits are doc comments.

VERIFIED at the parent: 888/888 tests, import OK (mandatory -- new class_name), lint 0, check_all 19/19, suite_reach 0 NEW. The 30.7/30.0/32.0 arithmetic re-derived independently through eval.gd rather than taken from the report.

title: Photograph a chew ring mid-sweep, which needs a pest guaranteed in reach
description:
SOURCE: the blocked runtime check in cycle 78's ledger row. The evidence half of -xej7, split out per the rule that an acceptance a commit cannot produce is its own item.

The change landed and the FULL ring at 22px was photographed live, clearing the flower head. What could not be caught is a partial arc mid-chew, which is the shape the whole change is about.

Why it failed, so the next attempt does not repeat it. An aphid chew is 0.45s (Pest chew total) against a bus round-trip of roughly 200ms, so plain polling gets one or two samples by luck. Pausing first makes each step deterministic but stops the wave that has to deliver a pest in the first place. Slowing the game with set-game-speed stops the pest arriving at all. All three were tried.

The technique that should work: remove every Corn Cobbler from the board first, since pests were dying before reaching the Chomp; put the Chomp adjacent to the road entrance rather than mid-route; let a wave run at 1x until a pest is within GRAB_RADIUS; THEN pause and step in 0.15s --then-pause slices, which cannot overshoot a 0.45s window. See .claude/skills/read-a-moving-value for the pause-before-you-step ordering.

A beetle would be easier than an aphid if one can be arranged -- the design doc says the Chomp takes a while eating bigger pests, so the window is longer by design.

ACCEPTANCE: one rendered frame at roughly 50 percent and one at roughly 90 percent chewed, with the arc visible and outside the flower head in both; if the 90 percent frame is NOT legible, that is a finding about CHEW_RING_WIDTH rather than a failed test.
close_reason:
Both frames photographed, on the first attempt, after three earlier failures.

WHAT MADE IT WORK, since the bead asked for the technique not to be repeated wrongly:
  1. spawn_pest a BEETLE, not an aphid. 2.6s chew against the aphid's 0.45s -- five times the window, and the bead predicted this ('the design doc says the Chomp takes a while eating bigger pests').
  2. Chomp at (3,2), adjacent to road cell (3,1). Reach is GRAB_RADIUS 73.6 and the cell centres are 64 apart, so the cell is covered; the diagonal neighbour at (2,1) is 90.5 away and is not. Predicted the grab at x >= 187.7 and it grabbed at x = 187.77.
  3. Cleared the five stray pests the auto-started wave had already put on the road -- the bead's 'pests were dying before reaching the Chomp' problem, in its other form.
  4. PAUSE FIRST, then walk the pest in with step-time --then-pause, per .claude/skills/read-a-moving-value. Coarse 1.0s steps to close the distance, then 0.15s slices.

RESULT: 47.4% and 90.4% chewed, each within a percent of target, both captured with the tree frozen so the pair carries no ambient drift. Two rendered frames, 80x80 crops centred on the Chomp at screen (224,232).

THE ACCEPTANCE'S REAL QUESTION was whether the 90% frame is legible, and the answer is a number rather than an opinion. The ring SWEEPS CLOSED -- it shows time REMAINING, which is OVERLAY_GRAMMAR's own reading of this shape -- so the ink shrinks as the chew completes. chew_arc_end(p) * CHEW_RING_RADIUS is the arc's length in pixels:

    0% chewed   138.2 px
   25%          103.7 px
   47.4%         72.7 px   <- photographed
   75%           34.6 px
   90.4%         13.3 px   <- photographed
   95%            6.9 px

So at 90% there is 13.3 px of 3 px-wide ink. That IS small, and the bead says a small one is a finding about CHEW_RING_WIDTH rather than a failed test.

I AM NOT CALLING IT A DEFECT, and the reasoning is recorded with the number: a chew is not actionable. The player cannot hurry it or interrupt it, so a cue that goes quiet at the end goes quiet exactly when nothing turns on it. What matters is the EARLY reading -- a Chomp busy on a big pest is a lane that needs something else planted in it -- and at 50% the arc is still 72.7 px.

ALSO MEASURED, since 'outside the flower head' was the other half: the sprite is 64x64 so the ring at radius 22 sits inside the sprite's BOX, but clears the drawn head, which is what cycle 78's full-ring photograph already established.

PINNED AS A TEST, because a photograph is evidence that expires and the maths is what survives: test_the_chew_rings_remaining_ink_shrinks_the_way_a_clock_should walks 20 steps asserting the ring only ever shrinks (a clock that grows mid-run tells the player the wait got longer), gates the early reading above 60 px, and RECORDS the 13.3 px late one without gating it -- so anyone who later decides it is too small argues with a measurement instead of re-photographing a 2.6 second window. 23 assertions.

title: Say what the weather is doing while it is doing it
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md older sections, taken from OUTSIDE this cycle neighbourhood per step 6. Grounded in code opened for this bead, not remembered.

WaveDirector.fire_interval_scale_for (game/wave_director.gd:333-334) returns WEATHER_DROUGHT_INTERVAL_SCALE for a drought and 1.0 otherwise, and Game applies it to every plant on wave start (game/game.gd:1210). So a drought doubles every plant's firing interval -- the single largest swing in the game applied to every tower the player owns at once.

What the player is told: the wave banner names the weather when the wave starts (Hud._show_banner via weather_headline/weather_note), and then nothing. The multiplier is live on every plant for the whole wave and no readout carries it. Compare the threat level, which gets a permanent slot on the wave readout for a much smaller effect.

Verified how: grepped for fire_interval_scale across game/ -- it is set at game/game.gd:336 and :1210 and read in each plant fire_interval(), and appears in no HUD file. This is an absence claim and that grep is how it was established.

Note -oo7e is blocked on the user and asks the bigger question (should weather have counter-play at all). This is the smaller one that does not need an answer first: whatever weather does, the player should be able to see it doing it.

ACCEPTANCE: a player mid-wave can tell a drought is active and roughly what it costs, without having read the banner; the readout uses a channel the HUD budget can afford, which is measured rather than assumed.
close_reason: Duplicate of -saaw, which asked the same question in cycle 17 and was MEASURED AND REFUSED for the top bar -- every candidate tag overflows the 312px wave slot. My cycle-77 filing said 'no readout carries it' and verified only that fire_interval_scale reaches no HUD file; it never checked whether the question was already open. Reopening the real question as a WHERE decision on -saaw.

title: Say in CLAUDE.md that a continuation citation binds left to right
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (77), second entry.

Entries in kanban.md use a shorthand nobody wrote down: a full citation followed by bare line references that inherit its path -- game/sfx.gd:86 then :91 then :106. There are 44 of them in the file and tools/citation_check.py was blind to all of them until cycle 77.

Binding them immediately found a reference written as a bare :331 in a sentence whose nearest preceding citation was game/chomp_flower.gd, a 183-line file. The intended target was corn_cobbler.gd, named earlier in the same sentence. Nobody would catch that reading: the prose names the right file twice.

The rule the checker implements, and the one a writer needs to know: a bare reference binds to the LAST full citation before it, in the same top-level entry, left to right -- and an orphan with no full citation before it is dropped rather than guessed at.

CLAUDE.md step 3 requires a file-colon-line for every entry and says nothing about the shorthand, so a writer inventing it again would invent it differently. One sentence beside the existing rule.

ACCEPTANCE: the binding rule is stated where the citation rule is stated; the mirror is regenerated rather than hand-edited.
close_reason: Done in the same cycle as step 5's one workflow change: the binding rule now sits beside the citation rule in CLAUDE.md step 3, mirrored into AGENTS.md by --fix.

title: Read the citation checker's landed lines over the whole file, once
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (77), third entry. This is the half of the audit no tool can do, filed as its own item per the rule that an acceptance a commit cannot produce is its own bead.

tools/citation_check.py resolves every citation and prints the line each one lands on. Resolution is mechanical; SUPPORT is not. Cycle 77 read the output once and found game/plant.gd:172 -- cited in cycle 70 as add_child(_sprite), correct then, pushed 34 lines down by cycle 71's Sway pivot, and now landing on a health-bar comment. It still resolves. Nothing will ever flag it.

The job: run the checker WITHOUT --quiet over kanban.md, read all ~182 landed lines, and mark each one supports / does not support / cannot tell. It is perhaps twenty minutes and it has never been done.

Expect a low hit rate and treat that as the result rather than as a wasted pass -- the value is knowing the rate, since it is the only evidence anyone will ever have about how fast citations rot here. Record it as a number in log-devtools.md.

Do not fix as you go. Separate the finding from the rewrite, per kanban-staleness-audit, and note that this is exactly the pass that skill's mechanical-second-pass shortcut CANNOT replace.

ACCEPTANCE: a verdict per landed line with the does-not-support ones named; the rate is recorded; anything wrong is fixed in a separate commit from the survey.

title: Make a hard-won kill sound like one
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (76), second entry. PLAYER-FACING. Pairs with -rowt.

Sfx.PEST_KILLED is one event for every death. An aphid you sneezed on and a hungry armoured beetle that soaked four volleys arrive as the same impactSoft_heavy_000.ogg at -3.0 dB.

The game prices that difference twice already. MUTATION_HUSK_MULTIPLIER (game/pest.gd:103-107) pays 1.5x or 2.0x for the harder kill, and cycle 74 gave the mixer a direction: losses go lower, gains go higher. A harder kill is a bigger gain, so it wants to sit above the base kill.

The obstacle is real and is the interesting part of this item. Sfx.play(event) takes an id and nothing else, and PITCH is keyed by id. So this means either new event ids (pest_killed_hard) or a per-call override on play(). The second is wider than it looks: every existing call site becomes a place where a caller can disagree with the table, which is exactly what tune_voice was extracted to prevent. Read .claude/skills/extract-a-testable-seam before choosing -- the seam is the thing at risk.

If new ids win, note they must also be added to the SOUNDS and VOLUME_DB tables and will be checked by test_no_two_events_are_the_same_sound, which is the gate that will tell you whether the new sound is actually distinguishable.

ACCEPTANCE: two kills of different difficulty are distinguishable by ear; whichever route is taken, tune_voice remains the only place voice properties are written, and a test asserts that.
close_reason: Shipped: PEST_KILLED_HARD is the same impact pitched 1.12 at -1.5dB, routed by Sfx.kill_event_for(husk_multiplier). Verified live -- a 3.0x pest tuned a real pooled voice to exactly those values, and a plain kill afterwards retuned the same voice back.

title: Let a pest carry two mutations
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md New this cycle (76), first entry. PLAYER-FACING.

Pest.mutation is a single StringName (game/pest.gd:284), applied one at a time by apply_mutation (:455), and there are three -- armoured, winged, hungry (:94-96). Two species (:16-17) times three mutations plus plain is eight kinds of enemy, six of them mutated.

Endless mode escalates health, speed, the beetle column, and MUTATION_CHANCE from 0.4 toward a cap of 0.85 (game/wave_director.gd:22, :29-30). Every one of those dials raises intensity. None raises variety, so past the cap the player meets the same eight things, more often, faster, with more health, forever.

A pest carrying two mutations is the cheapest new kind available. apply_mutation already composes onto whatever the pest is, and MUTATION_HUSK_MULTIPLIER (:103-107) multiplies naturally so the payout stays coherent without a new table.

This needs decisions made up front rather than discovered: a cap (two, not three), a wave floor below which it cannot happen, and what an armoured-winged pest actually means -- winged is documented as unreachable by a Chomp and armoured as double chew time, so the combination may be unkillable by one of the two plants that can kill it. Check that before building, not after.

ACCEPTANCE: a doubly-mutated pest can appear past a stated wave; it is killable by at least two distinct answers the player can buy; the husk payout is derived rather than special-cased; a test asserts the combination the design decided is illegal cannot be rolled.
close_reason: Shipped: pests compose mutations, the payout multiplies across them, armoured+winged is excluded for a mechanical reason, and WaveDirector rolls a second trait past wave 20 at 8%. The bead's own check-before-building instruction is what turned the design around.

title: Audit the notebook against three cycles of new mechanics
description:
SOURCE: kanban.md older sections, via step 6's outside-the-neighbourhood rule. The notebook is the one player-facing surface untouched in the last seven cycles, and it is the surface whose whole job is to describe the game to the player.

Cycles 69-75 added or changed: a third message priority rung with an armed-uproot prompt that now pre-empts (MESSAGE_DEADLINE), a spread arc whose presence marks a Corn Cobbler level, an idle breathe on every plant, a corpse whose shape names its cause, and a pitch axis on the sound palette where losses go lower.

The question is not whether the notebook is wrong -- it is whether it still claims to be complete. Its shelf and its drawing pages were written when the game was smaller, and kanban-staleness-audit bar applies to a screen exactly as it does to a backlog entry: open the code that would contain the claim before writing that it is missing.

Verify before claiming anything, and say in the finding HOW. Two of my last four absence claims about this codebase were wrong, both because the enumeration was over the wrong set.

ACCEPTANCE: a verdict per notebook page -- accurate, drifted, or silent about something the player now meets -- with a file:line for each; anything worth adding becomes its own bead rather than being fixed inside the audit.
close_reason:
AUDITED. 16 pages, a verdict and a file:line for each, three findings filed as their own beads.

FIRST, THE BEAD'S OWN PREMISE IS STALE, and the loop's confirm-before-claim step is what caught it. The description says the notebook "is the one player-facing surface untouched in the last seven cycles". It has been touched five times since: 819567c (told the player they may build on the road, and SPLIT the page that held it), a3a9b58 (the ninth plant's page), 6498493 (the lane-pressure hatch grammar row), 1de7a26 (hint notes assigned last so they wrap), 0fba521 (the hints page itself). The MOTIVATION was stale; the ASK -- a verdict per page -- had still never been performed, so the bead was worth doing as written.

THE PAGE TABLE, derived by parsing PAGES rather than read off the screen:

 p3  :403  bunch-of-corn upgrade   DRIFTED  -> filed -hvdj

 p11 :464  Salve Aloe              ACCURATE as written, and see -djvk: its subordinate clause is the notebook's ONLY mention of weather
