title: Bisect your own change before auditing the tool
description:
SOURCE: cycle 97's debugging, and it is the cheapest thing learned this cycle.

When suite_reach_check reported four symbols as unreached while they were plainly named in
real code, I spent several minutes on source-reading: probing strip_comments in a REPL,
checking the file for mixed line endings, reading STRING_RE, hypothesising about `#` inside a
string literal.

What actually found it was three commands:

  git stash push -q test/unit/test_placement.gd
  python tools/suite_reach_check.py; echo $?     # -> 0, clean
  git stash pop -q

Ten seconds, and it converted "the checker is broken" into "my edit did this" with no
reasoning at all. The reasoning afterwards was still needed to find WHICH part of the edit,
but it was reasoning over one file's diff rather than over a checker's internals.

I reached for source-reading first and the bisect second. That order was wrong and it is
worth writing down, because the instinct when a TOOL disagrees with you is to audit the tool
-- and this project's tools are unusually well-documented, which makes auditing them feel
productive.

The rule: when a gate that has been reliable disagrees with something you can plainly see,
BISECT YOUR OWN CHANGES BEFORE READING ITS SOURCE. `git stash push <one path>` is the whole
technique and it works per-file.

Where this belongs is a judgement. It is not a workflow step (step 5 prefers deleting rules
to adding them and CLAUDE.md is 817 lines), and it is not really about the harness. The
candidates are a new short skill, or a section in an existing one -- read-a-moving-value is
about not drawing false conclusions from a reading, which is adjacent but is about the
GAME's values rather than a tool's output.

Note honestly: this is one instance. The bar this project uses for building a skill is two
independent identifications. So the right outcome may be to record it here and wait.

ACCEPTANCE: a decision recorded on where this lives; if it becomes a skill or a section, it
names the cycle-97 case and the three commands; if it waits for a second instance, this bead
says so and stays open as the first identification.

title: Should the message counters get a devtools verb?
description:
SOURCE: cycle 96, and OUTSIDE this cycle's neighbourhood -- the work was the message row; this
is about the four counters it now carries and where they are read.

Hud now has four counters that exist purely to answer questions about what the player did not
see: messages_refused, messages_evicted, messages_preempted, messages_retired. Three of the
four were added in the last four cycles, each to answer one bead, and all four are readable
only by get-state against a running game.

That is fine for a measurement and poor for a habit. Nothing surfaces them, so the next person
suspecting a message problem has to know the counters exist before they can look. Compare
`cmd budgets`, which exists precisely so the seven couplings can be priced without knowing
their names.

The candidate is a `cmd messages` verb in devtools_ext that reports all four plus the current
row state (text, seconds left, priority, pending count) in one call, the way `cmd budgets`
reports every budget.

Two honest arguments against, and they should be weighed rather than dismissed:
  * The counters are diagnostic scaffolding for questions that are now ANSWERED. -i366 closed,
    -trn1 closed, -gtne closed. A verb making them convenient may be building a tool for a
    question nobody will ask again.
  * house-static-checker's denominator rule, applied to verbs rather than checkers: a verb
    never used is not a verb. `cmd budgets` earns its place because the budgets change every
    time the HUD does; the message counters may be stable now that the row's behaviour is
    settled.

The tiebreaker is -k1 (the re-measurement of cycle 93's answer). If that work wants these
counters read repeatedly across several scenarios, the verb pays for itself immediately. If it
is one read, it does not. So do this AFTER that, or not at all.

ACCEPTANCE: a decision recorded either way; if built, `cmd messages` reports all four counters
and the row's current state in one call and is used by the re-measurement rather than added
speculatively; if refused, the reason is written where the next person who thinks of it will
read it.
close_reason:
BUILT, in aaeb8f0, and the bead's own tiebreaker is what decided it.

THE TIEBREAKER, quoted: "The tiebreaker is the re-measurement of cycle 93's answer. If that work wants these counters read repeatedly across several scenarios, the verb pays for itself immediately. If it is one read, it does not. So do this AFTER that, or not at all."

That work is -gd27, closed in cycle 128. It read all four counters EIGHT times across FIVE scenarios -- four purchases during a live wave, a purchase on a quiet row, a purchase over a held ambient line, twelve pest kills with no purchase, and a synthetic five-post burst -- each read a `find-nodes --class Hud --property messages_refused --property messages_evicted --property messages_preempted --property messages_retired` line. So the condition the bead set is met on the evidence rather than on my judgement, which is the point of setting it.

AND THE TWO ARGUMENTS AGAINST, which the bead asked to be weighed rather than dismissed:

"The counters are diagnostic scaffolding for questions that are now ANSWERED (-i366, -trn1, -gtne all closed). A verb may be building a tool for a question nobody will ask again." -- FALSIFIED by the work that was supposed to close the last of those questions. -gd27 re-opened -i366 and CORRECTED it: the row does drop lines. The counters are not scaffolding for settled questions; the settled question turned out to be wrong.

"house-static-checker's denominator rule applied to verbs: a verb never used is not a verb." -- Honoured literally. `cmd messages` was used before this bead was closed, and used to get an answer nothing else could: see below.

WHAT IT REPORTS, per the acceptance ("all four counters and the row's current state in one call"): refused, evicted, preempted, retired; row_quiet, row_text, row_seconds_left, row_priority; pending (the queue's entries, oldest first); queue_max and min_readable so the numbers can be read without opening hud.gd; and refused_log. The one-line message names the two things a reader acts on --

    row quiet | refused 0, evicted 0, preempted 0, retired 0 | 0 pending

ONE ADDITION BEYOND THE ACCEPTANCE, and it is why the verb earned its place immediately. `Hud.messages_refused_log` records WHICH lines were refused, capped at 8, newest kept. -47v7 filed the severity of the double-purchase defect as unestablished -- three refusals against four posts per purchase, so at least one got through, and the count is identical whether the player lost a cosmetic flicker step or the reveal naming the plant they just bought. `_queue_message` had the text in hand and discarded it.

The first real call settled it:

    two purchases back to back ->
      refused 1
      refused_log ["The packet held a Chomp Flower!"]
      row "The packet held a Barrier Bramble!" | 3 pending

It is the REVEAL. The player is told what the second packet held and never told what the first one did. That is the serious reading, and -47v7 is updated with it.

The log also survives its own frame: read again after the row had cleared (row_text "", 0 pending) it still named the dropped reveal. Same property that makes findings_last.json worth having -- a transient stays diagnosable after the moment that produced it.

TWO HOUSE GATES FIRED ON IT, both on their first run after the verb was registered, and both were right:
  test_every_positional_devtools_verb_refuses_a_call_with_no_position -- failed until
  `messages` was classified. It is in DEFAULTED_VERBS with the reason written beside it: a
  verb that exists so you need not know the counter names must not require you to know one.
  suite_reach_check -- named all four new accessors as reached by no test. Covered rather
  than waived, including the assertion that message_queue_snapshot returns a COPY: a debug
  verb that hands out the live Dictionaries lets a caller edit the queue by looking at it.

VERIFIED: name_check 0 errors, import clean, lint 0/0, suite 916/916 with 18021 assertions, check_all 19 of 19 clean, findings 0 across 4 of 5, quit reported no user:// change. Red-then-green on the cap. Ledger row recorded before the commit; hud.gd and commands.gd both reached.

title: Give Pest a last_survivable_leg() instead of re-deriving it by eye
description: Source: kanban.md 'New this cycle (27 of 30)'. Three test files build pests with hand-set _leg values against hand-written routes, and the relationship between 'a route of N points' and 'the last leg a pest can sit on without escaping' is _route.size() - 2, written down nowhere and re-derived by eye each time. Getting it wrong by one is exactly this cycle's bug. Either expose it on Pest or give the tests a helper that places a pest at a FRACTION of its route, so no test does the arithmetic.
close_reason:
Answered by refusing BOTH shapes the bead offered, and the reason is that the bead's arithmetic was wrong.

THE PREMISE, DERIVED FROM Pest RATHER THAN FROM THE BEAD. There are TWO numbers and the bead conflates them:
  * _route.size() - 1 is the last leg THE MODEL HAS. _advance escapes when _leg >= _route.size(), so a pest on size()-1 is alive and walking its final step. This is already written down once, in production, as enter_road_at's clamp: clampi(leg, 1, _route.size() - 1).
  * _route.size() - 2 is the last leg A HOSTED TEST MAY PARK ON, because instantiate_scene's settle frames call _advance before the test body runs and walk a final-step pest off the board.
The bead calls size()-2 'the relationship'. It is not -- it is a fact about the HARNESS, not about the game. Shipping it on Pest would have named as unsurvivable exactly the leg enter_road_at clamps TO.

'RE-DERIVED BY EYE EVERY TIME' WAS ALREADY HALF FALSE. Five hand-set sites across three files: test_combat.gd:297 (correct, with a five-line derivation above it), test_placement.gd:4313-4315 (correct, and cites test_combat's derivation by name), test_selftest.gd:9533 (already inside a _pest_partway helper, callers nowhere near the end). It was derived once, at length, and cited. What was missing is that the derivation lived only in a comment nothing checked.

BOTH OFFERED SHAPES REJECTED, each for its own reason:
  * A Pest method would be dead API -- nothing in game/ wants 'the leg before the last', so lint's orphan pass and suite_reach_check would both be right to flag it. And a method returning the TRUE number size()-1 just duplicates a one-line clamp no caller needs.
  * A fraction helper is MORE arithmetic, not less (0.75 of what, to which leg?), and its failing value is 1.0 -- precisely what someone reaching for 'at the end' would type. It would reproduce the off-by-one with a friendlier name.

SHIPPED INSTEAD: the relationship made EXECUTABLE. A new test drives _advance by hand with NO HOSTING AT ALL -- a pest on size()-1 is off the board when that leg ends; a pest on size()-2 survives the identical walk and lands on the final leg; enter_road_at's clamp is read rather than retyped. Plus a header on _advance naming both numbers and why the second is deliberately not exposed, and the test_placement citation now points at the checked test rather than at another comment.

Two traps handled by construction, both worth keeping: no instantiate_scene, so settle frames cannot destroy the precondition; and the escaped pest is NOT freed, because _escape() already queue_free()d it and a double free would abort the method silently into a [PASS]. Stride is leg_length + 1.0 deliberately -- landing exactly on a waypoint exits the while loop with _leg incremented and the escape check unrun, which would have made the second assertion pass for the wrong reason.

title: Decide whether a drought should slow the non-shooters
description: Source: kanban.md 'New this cycle (18 of 30)'. Plant.fire_interval_scale is read by CornCobbler and Dandelion only; Chomp, Sundew and Sunflower pace themselves by other means (is_busy(), droplets, a growth gauge), so a drought slows two plants of five. That is arguably right -- a drought should hurt shooting, not chewing -- but it is an accident of which plants happen to read the multiplier rather than a decision anyone wrote down. Decide it, then either write the reasoning into Plant.fire_interval_scale's doc comment or extend it.
close_reason:
Answered NO, with a different reason per plant rather than one rule five times.

NUMBERS STALE, SUBSTANCE LIVE. The bead says fire_interval_scale is read by CornCobbler and Dandelion only -- two plants of five. It is read by THREE of EIGHT: Nettle reads it too (nettle.gd:249), and Nettle, Mint and Aloe did not exist when the bead was written. What was true then and is still true is that the split was an accident of which files happened to read the field.

THE DECISION: a drought lengthens a repeating ATTACK interval and nothing else.
  - Chomp -- a chew's length belongs to the MEAL. Lengthening it lengthens how long the pest is HELD exactly as much as how long the flower is busy: a nerf on a thin lane, a buff on a crowded one. A weather whose SIGN depends on the board is not a readable event, which is the same standard weather_for already applies when it refuses to run rain and drought over one wave.
  - Sunflower -- its clock IS the seed economy, and drought already pays +50% on kills. Slowing it moves two numbers against each other so the total barely moves.
  - Sundew -- an aura has no rate to multiply.
  - Mint -- it never acts, and its output lands on plants the drought is already slowing; composed_interval multiplies both, so slowing the Mint applies one weather twice to one shot.
  - Aloe -- repairs between waves where nothing races it; inside a fight it loses to Pest.EAT_DPS by design.

REJECTED: 'drought slows everything', and the shorter-but-wrong 'drought slows everything that engages' -- PlantCatalog.engages is true for Chomp, which is not slowed, so the key cannot express the boundary.

The player-facing sentence is unchanged and was already right: the drought banner says 'Everything shoots half as often.' What changed is that SHOOTS is now the specification rather than a description of whatever the plant files happen to do, gated so it cannot drift back into an accident -- the affected set is derived from the plant scripts (via gdsource so a doc-comment mention does not count as a read), so a ninth plant that starts reading the field fails the gate.

No new visible effect is claimed, because there is none. VERIFIED: 847/847 tests, lint 0.

The pause card now right-aligns its keys against a gutter (game/pause_screen.gd:_build_key_list); KeyBindingScreen centres its RowKey%d labels in a fixed 140px column (game/key_binding_screen.gd:85), neither derived nor matching. The repo has other prose that must agree with something: the parallel-safe gate list in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md must name every tools/*_check.py that exists (it is hand-maintained and a new checker can be forgotten -- three were added in three cycles), and the harness section's verb table must not name a verb list-commands does not report. Both are derivable rather than hand-checkable, which is the derive-the-list shape. Low priority: no instance of either drifting yet, unlike the mirror, which had two.
close_reason: STALE: first half obsolete by design -- check_all.py replaced the hand-maintained gate list and derives it (live: 19 of 19, 0 unclassified). Second half sits inside the scaffold-regenerated block and is upstream's.

title: Show the key hint on the HUD's own buttons
description: Source: kanban.md 'New this cycle (15 of 30)'. The HUD's 'Grow the next wave' button has a keyboard verb behind it and never says so -- a player who rebinds a key sees it only on the two screens that own bindings. Drawing the hint from KeyBindings.label_for() makes a rebinding visible where the player actually is. Depends on the legend column split: this would be the third surface to show key names, and the pause card just spent a cycle learning that a key name a player chose can be far wider than one we shipped.

title: Widen SHORT_NAMES to the keys the engine names badly
description: Source: kanban.md 'New this cycle (14 of 30)'. KeyBindings.SHORT_NAMES (game/key_bindings.gd:121) covers 8 of the ~100 bindable keys -- Esc, four arrows, Space, two Enters. Everything else falls through to the engine's own name, fine for F1 and poor for punctuation (KEY_BRACKETLEFT renders as something no player calls it). Do it with the derive-the-list recipe rather than one complaint at a time: derive the set the engine names badly, assert SHORT_NAMES covers exactly it, plant both directions.
close_reason: Lane 1. The premise was UNDERSTATED, not wrong: the Key enum has 193 constants (read out of the harness's cached engine index, not from memory), so the real denominator is ~190 rather than the bead's ~100, and the punctuation family alone is 32 keys. Done with derive-the-list as the bead asked, and the hard part was that 'names it badly' is a judgement, so it split into two mechanical predicates, both stated in the source. (a) The engine spends more than one character where the key prints a glyph -- inside the printable block the glyph IS the keycode, so this becomes arithmetic; it fires on exactly 32 keycodes and adds ZERO table rows, since key_label falls through to a new glyph_for. (b) The engine spends an abbreviation nobody says where the key prints no glyph -- names beginning 'Kp'; the keys derive but the values ('Num 0') are a choice, so those 15 rows are recorded and asserted equal to the derived set in both directions. The residue of 7 is honestly a curated list and is gated as one, with a comment saying not to 'fix' it. Two findings recorded rather than churned: KEY_SPACE and KEY_ENTER's short names are identical to the engine's and shorten nothing, kept as pins.

title: Reuse SelectionMarker's pattern for a placement preview cue
description: SelectionMarker (plant-tower-defense-42t) is a sibling Node2D drawn independent of a plant's own _draw() override. The same pattern (corner brackets, dimmer/dashed) could show 'this is where the cursor would place a plant' before the click lands, reusing the exact node/technique instead of inventing a new cursor overlay concept.
